Summary of the Report presented at the Sixtieth Annual Meeting, held on 4th March, 1909. ORDINARY BRANCH.—The number of policies issued during the year was 80,379, assuring the sum of £7,614,898, and producing a new annual premium income of £440 376. The premiums received during the year were £4,616,337, being an increase of £135,960 over the year 1907. The claims of the year amounted to £2,812,962. The number of deaths was 8,389, and 15,322 endowment assurances matured. The number of policies in force at the end of the. year was 866,797. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH.—The premiums received during the year were £6,925,755, being an increase of, £264,124. The claims of the year amounted to £2,670,345, including £72,696, the proportion of bonus paid since the date of the last Annual Meeting. The number of claims and surrenders,including 4,355 endow- ment.assurances matured,,was 310,722. 'the number of free policies granted during the year to those policy holders of five years' standing and upwards who desireo, to discontiune their payments, was 145,261, the number in force tieing 1,395,929. The number of free policies which became claims during the year was 40,094. The total number of policies in force at the end of the year was 17,963,17; their average duration exceeds eleven and a quarter years. The assets of the company, in both branches, as shown in the balance sheet are £71,958,859, being an increase of £3,952,575. over those of 1907. In the Ordinary Branch a reversionary bonus at the rate of £1 12s. per cent. on the original sums assured has again been added to all classes of participating policies issued since the year 1876. The Directors are pleased to announce an increase in the Industrial Branch bonus. All policies of over five years' duration which become claims either by death or maturity of endowment from the sth of March, 1909, to the 3rd of March, 1910, both dates Inclusive, will participate. This bonus willbe paid by way of addition to the sums assured of :

Z per cent, on all policies becoming claims upon which at least five but less than ten years' premiums have been paid. £lO per cent, on all policies becoming claims upon which at least ten but less than twenty years' premiums have been paid, and £l2 10s. per cent, on all policies becoming claims upon which at least twenty years premiums have been paid.

Trish Industries.--The shamrock and Irish industries will be much to the fore next week. The Queen has ordered a large supply of shamrock from Lady Limerick's farm at Dromore, tor distribution to the Irish Guards, on St.lPatrick's Day, larch lith. On this date the Irish Industries sale will be open in London at Devon- shire House, and it is hoped that the Queen and the Empress Marie of Russia will be able to visit the sale, Lady Granard, the new American bride, who has not yet, visited her husband's Irish estates' will make an inter- esting addition to the many distinguished Society women who will sell. Lady Aberdeen alwass takes an active interest in the sale, and she is also busy with preparations for the great fancy-dress ball at Dublin Castle on the 35th. Its chief feature will be the pageant illustrating Irish industries. The gentlemen are to wear poplin ties and wastcoats and as is usual at Lady Aberdeen's balls, the ladies are requested to dress entirely in Irish materials. • False Trade Descriptions.—Much that is sold as Irish lace and Irish linen, never saw Ireland, and the Board of Trade are again taking action to prevent these frauds. A short time ago they took proceed;ngs against a firm for misrepresentation of this kind, with respect to lace goods, and more recently complaints have been made of firms offering for sale ties described as real Irish poplin, and handkerchiefs of Irish linen, whilst it is alleged in neither case the goods warranted this discription. The Merchandise Marks Act was designed to prevent false trade descriptions and it is just as well that shop- keepers should be reminded that this kind of thing cannot be done with impunity. Skimpy Skirts es Curtseying.—Tt was noticeable at the two Courts that the Directoire mode is not con- ducive to an elegant curtesy—lndeed iii several instances, .wearers of sheath-like skirts found it impos- sible to manage anything better than a curious kind of " bob " when " passing the presence " a state of affairs scarcely calculated to please his Majesty, who very murh prefers the graceful sweep almost to the gronnd. Moreover it was proved conclusively that skimpy Direeteire gonna do not set off, or blend with the long Court tram nearly ss well as the fuller and more flowing skirts which promise to find favour at the later Courts. The King's Sojourn Abroad.—Before leaving for -Biarritz, the King caused it to he announced that his journey South was to be regarded as a necessity of health rather than a holiday. Lost sear Mr. Asquith had to go to Biarritz to submit his proposals for a new ministry consequent upon the death of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman. and no doubt this official announcement was in consequence of the comments that were then made as to the inconvenience of his Majesty being abroad at such a time. But as on all these occasions, it is on medical adsice that the King goes abroad for the months of March and April, spend- ing the first three or four weeks at Biarritz. His Majesty occupies the same suite of rooms in the Palace rto tel as be has taken for the past three years and entertains numerous guekts at luncheon and dinner parties during his stay. His Majesty has also a private sitting room at the Golf Club,as is a frequent spectator on the links. The Kilts does not. play golf, but often amuses himself as croquet, which he thinks a very fine game, and a court adjoining the golf course is specially ' set apart for his Majesty's use. Gypsying in a Caravan.—Lady Arthur Grosvenor whose husband is now heir presumptive to the dukedom of Westminster, spent a good deal of last summer gypsying in a caravan, and was known on the road as "Sara Lee." She is, like Mr. Geo. R. Sims, a student of the gypsy race, and is a writer of some authority on the history of the Romany langtrace. Of late years the nomadic craze has become quite fashionable, and as soon as the spring advances, the corayanners will be busy planning their excursions. They are tidy and orderly folk, and are welcomed by the county side, but the gipsy race is rapidly disappearing.—Every man's hand is against them, the police, the farmers, the school authorities, all regard them as a nuisance and they have ceased to provide picturesque material for the novelist and play-wright. " Weyer he Cats."—An American Evangelist recently tried a new method of putting a stop to gossip and scandal.—those" " cattish amenillties " of society—to which the Bishop of London referred the other day at a distribution of prizes at a girls' school.—" Never be Cats" he advised the scholars, by which he meant those people who spend their lives thinking and saying ill- natured things about others. The American idea was to invite all the gossips in the neighbourhood to a weekly tea-party, for a sort of slandering competition, it being thought that if they were allowed to hammer away at their neighbours foibles to their hearts content they would use up all the available material, and have nothing left to gossip about. Needless to say the plan was foredoomed to failure, and the gossip sub voce went on as badly as ever. No one is lovable who thinks and says ill-natured things of others, but it is to he feared that the" old catty" spirit which the Bishop of Lon- don denounced, is ineradicable in many, who can always See everybody eyes faults but their own. Care and Commonsense.—An old lady whose years now number more than fourscore, was recently asked to what in particular she ascribed her early life and splendid health. "To keeping my feet warm and slry," was the answer, and undoubtedly we should do well,as far as possible,to follow such an excellent example. Wet, cold feet cause more trouble and sickness generally than the average person would deem possible, and in this direction women are greater offenders than men. The working girl for example has a tremendous affection for dressy—all too dressy—outdoor shoes, and bearing the thinnest of thin soles, and these she calmly dons all the year round.. Fashionable, leisured girls and women too rarely wear anything outdoors but shoes of the daintiest description, only the soles are of leather instead of paper, and the wearers perchance possess a carriage, or the opportunity of taking cats, and the additional advantage of being able so speedily change their shoes should they become damp. But even so, all this is a vast mistake, and footgear of varying substance should find a place in the boot cupboard. If only a limited supply is forthcoming our first ease should be for strong boots with good thick soles, calculated to resist the worst our climate can manage, and further the useful half, or entire solos!), for] such weather as has fallen to our share of late.

111-fitting Underskirts.—Underskirts are in vogue again, and the exhibition of such garments ready-to- wear in sbopland, causes us once again to marvel at the ulter-absence of progress in this direction, as

regards cut and fit. As a rule, the ready-made under- skirt is decidedly too long, too full about the hem and flounce, very ill-setting over the hips, and concerning the waist, we might almost be living in the days of Noah! For the superfluous inches of the waist, and these are generally many, are provided for by means of a string, which gathers them up into a bunch behind! So much is done for us in the way of really well-cut ready-made skirts, that it seems curious indeed that nothing better can be offered us in the shape of ready- made underskirt s.

A Novelty.—The fine serge skirt and satin coat idea, sounds a little funny, but modistes approve of it, for smart afternoon wear. The colour of skirt and coat matches perfectly, the only relief being that of the trimming appearing ripen the revers, collar and cuffs of the coat. This trimming just now is taking the form of velvet or elaborate braiding, and the cost is long and much slash4up, panel fashion. Knock-about Costnmes.—For useful little knock- about costumes, the tailors are advocating the small check skirt. The coats are loosely fitting, the skirts kilted, and sufficiently short to permit the wearer to walk in comfort. A rough straw hat, in the same shade as the coat should complete such a toilette and the trimming shonld consist of ribbon only in some bright shade in evidence in the skirt and taking the form of sharply pointed wings. The Old-World Cane.—Vet another attempt is about to be made to induce us to carry the tall cane, but save in a comparatively few instances, it is not likely to prove any more successful thsn in the past. For useful, ordinary walking sticks however, there is decidedly increased demand, while that for umbrellas, en-tout-cas, and sunshades, is going down. The favourite handle lor umbrellas surd en-tout-cas is again the crook, and there is a positive craze for tbe tortoise shell variety. " Kingsmend."—The Baroness von Hutton is giving ns a new novel " Kingsmead " which will shortly be published by Messrs. Hutchinson-Pam is a figure of the story and readers of "The Halo " will feel more than usual interest in Tommy, Earl of Kingsmead. The story is a delightful one, and quite as fascinating as the other works of this most charming writer.
MADGE.

THE PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY. The annual meeting of this Company was held on March 4th last. We are again able to congratulate this Company on an extraordinary, and an almost phenomenal accession of new business in both branches, which was even greater in the year 1907 than in the year 1906. This was partly due to the satis- factory state of the trade of the country, and partly to an increased bonus in the ordinary branch, to increased tenefits in the industrial branch, and to the intro- duction of the system of profit-sharing in the latter branch. In the year 1908, however, not only base the general commercial conditions been less favourable, but we have had a serious strike in the North-Eastern Counties of England. and what threatened to be a still more serious strike in Lancashire. Fortunately, it did not attain such dimensions as were at first anticipated. Injurious as the results of these labour troubles must always necessarily be, both to those who are immedi- ately concerned in them, and to institutions which, like the Prudential, derive their main sources of income from the industrial classes, they are greatly ; alliated by the policy tbe company have always pursued in such cases, a policy which is both generous end wise. It is a cause for congratulation that in spite of these difficulties, and in spite of the very unsatisfactory state of the trade of the count,y, they are able to repdrt the very large increase of £264,121 in the premiums receivkl in the industrial branch, and an increase of £135,960 in the ordinary brattish. While the magnitude of this business is apparent, in any analysis of the causes of death, it is perhaps in cases of accident, that the benefits of llfe assurance are conspicuously evident, and several unhappy episode.; of the year afford typical illustrations of this fact. Out of a total number £',329 deaths from accidents of various I kinds, DO less than'l,l67 were deaths by drowning, and 551 were in collieries, while the new dangers to which modern scientific inventions lay us open are illustrated by the fact that in the industrial branch last year there were no loser than eleven deaths from electric shocks. In the colliery accident near Newcastle, on February oth, 1908. out of fourteen lives lost, eight were assured with the Prudential. A gain,on June 22nd last,the Brixham trawler "Fear not"was lost with the whole of her crew of five hands,and all were assured in the company. Even the I earthquake at Messina was responsible for two claims which amounted to £4B. Although not coming strictly within the operations of the year under review, we may mention the recent terrible colliery disaster at the West Stanley Mine. Here the number of Jives lost was, 168, and of those, seventy-three were assured in this company for the aggregate amount of £1,378. It is noteworthy that the Warrington district contributed its fair share of the Company's success last sear. In spite of trade depression the local Superintendent was able to report a large accession of new business in both branches. A point of interest to the public and trades- men of tbe town is the fact that through the local office no less a sem than £17,727 3s. 2d. was paid out in claims last, year, which amount when placed in circula- tion through local channels is bound to contribute to the prosperity of the town.

div.head: o.lxammer. Saturday, March 13, 1909,
div.p: The o.lxammer. Saturday, March 13, 1909,
MESSRS. RICHMOND, LTD. A Trying Year, hut a Good Profit.

The eighteenth ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Ltd., was held at the offices, Academy-street, Warring- ton, at noon, on Thursday. Mr. Thomas Dwerryhouse (chairman), presided, and amongst others present were: —Messrs. Horace M. Thornton (vice-chairman and managing director), John Cox, J. F. Atkins, M. 8., John A. Ransome, (managing director), and J. W. Glover (directors), Louis A. Voisey (auditor). James W. Slack (secretary). F. G. Taylpr (Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co., solicitors to the company), Aid. J. Smethurst, Wm. Duff and John Booth. THE REPORT. The DIRECTORS, in their report, stated that the balance standing to the credit of profit and loss account (after deducting debenture interest), including the amount brought forward as per balance sheet, was £20,699 us. 4c1., which the directors recommended be appropriated as follows :—Depreciati ens on buildings, patterns, plant, showroom fixttires, &c., £5,763 95.; dividend on preference capital at the rate of 6 percent. per annum, for the year ended December, 31st, 1908, £5,933 3s. 9d.; dividend (free of income tax) at the rate of 10 per cent, per annum on the ordinary capital, for the year ended December 31st, 1908, ;8,036 125.; balance to next account, subject to directors' remuneration, £966 Cs. 7d. After placing the entire cost of advertising as in former years against revenue, the directors recom- mended dividend at the rate of 10 per cent per annum. Owing to the depreciation on investments the directors _recommended that the sum of £5,000 be withdrawn from mews° to meet such depreciation. The company's works and various branches were in good condition, and , had been maintained out of revenue. The retiring directors were Mr. John Coxon and Mr. J. W. Glover. Their re-election by the Board was reported in accord - !Mee with the Company's Articles of Association. The auditor, Mr. L. A. Voisey (chartered accountant) retired, and was recommended for re-appointment. THN CHAIRMAN AND THE YHAR'S TRADE. The CHAIRMAN in moving the adoption of the report, said the shareholders would no eoubt hriveperused the report and accounts presented for the half-year and found that they are not sir favourable as those in pre- vious years. and they would natut ally want to know why that was so. At their last meeting after the Ameri- can financial crash he remembered remarking that their prospects we' e very good and that so far they had not felt any ill effects. But that crash was far reaching ; they were suffering from it to-day and might do for some time to come. One effect of this state of things was a feeling of uncertainty among tbe trading com- munity and consequentl) a lock up of capital; people who had itwcatld not part with it,and trade was suspended with the natural results. They read in the papers from day to day of companies whose trading had covered the same period as their own, reporting diminished divi- dends, in many cases no dividends, and of otheiS where the assets had been mortgaged to enable them to keep going on at all. It was hardly to be expected that their company selling articles of luxury (for gas cookers and fires were luxuries which could easily be dispensed with in bad times) could escape a itbout loss and they had not done so. Instead of increasing their sales which had been done yearly for some time, this year they had suffered a diminution. Competition had been as keen or perhaps keener than ever consequent upon the smaller amount of business to be had. Raw materials during the year kept well up in prices. A curious feature of the year's trading was the comparative high price of metals. It had usual been the case tbat when trade was bad, prices of materials gave way but this was not the care in the year under review. They were having some relief at the present time in this direction and they hoped it might last. It Was not a safe thing just now to make any forecast for the present. year, seeing that trade as taken from the February Board of Trade Return was at its lowest depths, but they could hope that when the Americen Tariff and our own Budget, events which could not long he delayed were settled, con- fidence would be 'restored, in which case they might look forward to a sharp revival of trade and increased profits. Dealing with the report in detail,the Chairman referred to the fact that there was an increase of £9,607 in the amount allocated to freehold and leasehold works and other buildings, &c. One portion of that increase was due to the fact that in disposing of r.art of their London premises they had had to buy out a previous lease at a cost of £7,0e0. The remainder was represented by necessary additions to works, tools, &c. They were glad to have effected the sale of part of the London buildings and it left them with several hundred pounds to their benefit. The increase paid for itself and would be wiped out in the course of a few years. A favour- able point in the balance sheet was that while the firm owed £15,000 other people (seed them £46,000. Although in some respects the balance sheet did not please the directors, still on Abe whole it anti healthy and sound. Wit b regard to dfpreciat ion of investments, the £5,000 which they pragaosed to take from the reserve fund would go principally to one investment. —George Newton, Ltd. That business was bought many years agt, but unfortuuately things had not gone as well as they had expected, with the result that there bad been a loss. Things were brought to a head recently by their having to remove the business from Oldham to Manchester, and to put it on a sound footing they proposed to take the course recommended in the report. Altogether their investments were a very good feature, some of them bens°.' worth considerably more than the amounts stated. Taking everything into con- sideration, the firm had not done very badly, and they hoped in the coming year to benefit by the reduction in the cost of the materials. Alderman Smethurst, alluding to the sale of part of the London works, said he was alwass strongly opposed to the taking of a Lancashire foundry business to London.

Mr. H. M. THORNTOg, in seconding, confirmed whit the Chairman bad said with regard to the soundne,s of the balance 1-heet. ,The item which pa? ticularly appealed to those vtho were actively employed in the business was that of the trade stocks. The year before the late Mr. Richmond's death the stocks amounted to between £60,000 and £70,000. Year by year they had been able to reduce the amount until now be believed it bad reached the lowest point in the later history of the company—£323BB4. They were satisfied that the stock was worth every penny of that sum. With regard to G. Nest ton, Ltd., they were making very special efforts to improve the business and they hoped that, although tt ey .had wisely depreciated the investment, they . . . . .

mould eventually see iLs value in their -books figuring at a larger amount than it had now been deprecated to. As the Chairman had said, their returns duriing the past year bad been less, but they had not decreased to such an extent as to make them feel real trouble in that direction, and they knew some of their competitors were in a worse position. There were now greater demands upon them from the gas world generally,conLinued Mr. Thornton, for a more scientific article than ever was produced before in the gas stove business and therefore the firm had in the last few years laid ttemselves open scientifically to treat all the apparatus rent out of their workshops. To-day he believed they stood equal to any gas stove manu- facturer for an article produced scientifically and artistically. In conclusion Mr. Thornton paid a tribute to the loyalty of the staff and said it was only by con- tinuing to pull together, master and men, that they could maintain and strengthen their position. The resolution was carried unanimously. THE DIVIDEND.

The CHAIRMAN moved "That a dividend at the rate of 10 per cent. per annum (less 5 per cent. already paid) for the year ended December 31st, 1908, free of income tax, he now declared and paid." He said they would havitliked the amount to be the same as last year, but under the circumstances they ought to bs satisfied. M2ny companies lind not been payihg an3tbing of late and there was no doubt times bad been very bad. Mr. JOHN COXON seconded and sad that in view of
the great commercial depression throughout the wonl . .

a teii per cent. dividend -WB3 not entirely unsatisfactory The business had been well looked after by the Directors and every deparq.nrcnt was managed in a most business like way. They could, therefore, only hope for the best. The resolution was agreed to. DIbECTORS' REM UN ERATION.
Mr. DUFF moved "That the sum of £7OO be placed at the disposal of the directors for their services curing the sear 1908." Mr. Johu BOOTH seconded and the proposition was approved.

div.head: CORONER'S STRONG CRITICISM.
div.p: CORONER'S STRONG CRITICISM.

At the-Eariestosn Tour' Hall on • 'Thursday Coroner Brighouse held an inquest, into the circumstances sur- rounding the death of Ellen Clarke, aged thirty-four, a married woman, of Houghton-street, Earlestown.— The doctor who had attended the deceased gave a death certificate, but information reached the coroner that the woman had been attended by a woman named Mrs. Durber, who had been struck off the midwives' roll. He, therefore, directed the police to make the fullest inquiries and to have a post-mortem examination made of the body.- -The Coroner called Mrs. Dnrber into the room and strongly condemned her conduct in attending midwifery cases after being struck off the rolls. He said that with the aid of her solicitor she had discovered a flaw in the Act of Parliament which 'enabled her to continue to attend cases until April 1, 1910, but after that date she would be liable to heavy' penalties.—On the evidence of Dr. Unswortb, of St. Helens, who conducted the post mortem, and expressed the opinion that death was due to natural causes, the jury returned a verdict in accordance. At the same time they endorsed the Coroner's condemnation of Mrs. Durber.

div.head: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
div.p: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
MR. A. H. CROSFIELD M.P. SUPPORTS THE BILL.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. spoke in the House of Commons last Friday evening in support of the Day- light Saving Bill. He said : In the course of the debate reference has been made to the evidence given by my firm, and to the experiment which they suc- cessfully carried out, as constituting in part an argument in opposition to the Bill. Mr. Dundas White: Not an argument against the Bill, but as showing that firms can do this thing for themselves.. Mr. Crosfield: Quite so. The hon: member quoted the experience of Messrs. Crosfield as showing what could be done by individual action. If, as the result of the experiment, the firm had thought that individual action was sufficient, they would hardly have taken the trouble to come and give evidence in support of the Bill. They were convinced, in. fact, that individual action of itself was not sufficient; The last speaker, the hon. member for Dumbartonshire, did not attach sufficient weight to considerations as to the inter-dependence of different parts of the community in relation both to the different branches of industry and to different ,forms of recreation. This was why my firm, although they found the earlier ! hours were of the greatest possible benefit, and , although they had been asked to adopt the system in ' the winter as well as in the summer months; felt that in a town like Warrington, for instance, individual action was wholly insufficient. The ground has already been so well covered that I need not detain the House for more than a few minutes; but I do wish to emphasise the point to which I have alluded. It seems to me the arguments in favour of the Bill are altogether overwhelming. The objections that have been , raised certainly deserve consideration— objections such as those stated by the hon. Member j for Rye, speaking from the agricultural standpoint. j What the House really has to deal with is the very difficult question of altering a custom, and the question is how we could best do so. If the custom is altered I submit it will be to the 'immense ad+antage of the great majority of the people; while as regards the minority I have -not the slightest doubt that the conditions of labour and work, as in the case of the agricultural population, could be re-adjusted to meet their case. I hold strongly that for the working-class population more particularly, and the great, mass of the urban population, represent- ing perhaps three-fourths of the whole country, the advantages of this Bill from the physical, mental, and moral point of view can hardly. be overstated. (Hear hear.) I might give just one illustration, and that is in reference to a recreation, which is perhaps the most important of all the recreations we have in some ,districts of Lancashire and Cheshire. It is quite 'astonishing to wha't an extent of late years the old English game of bowls has been developed in Lanca- shire, Cheshire, Yorshire, the Midlands, and other districts of England. Instead, of thousands, there are now actually hundreds of thousands of people in the United Kingdom who enjoy that game of a summer evening. If this Bill becomes law, not only during the middle of the summer, but in the early and latter part of the season, they will be able to pursue that pastime to a much greater extent. It will be a vast boon, especially to the working classef, to be able to remain in the open air and enjoy that game for an hour longer at the end of their day's work. It has been said in the course of this debate that people conld take their recreation early in the day instead pf late, but I am afraid that the working classes would hardly find that practicable. Men have their work to do first, and recreation comes afterwards. Besides the members of the Bowling Association, there are many other sections of the community who would be only too glad to enjoy a similar boon—in particular, and in a very special degree, the vast army of clerks and of many salaried officials. I have heard of people who allege that you can have too much - sn- shine. Indeed, one occasionally comes across th-ose who say that they suffer from a surfeit of sunshine and are bored with the blue .sky.. Since I came to dwell in London I have not met with any body who was afflicted with boredom of that deseription.(Lauphter.)l think,indeed,that most of us in - London, as well as in Lancashire, would be very glad to take whatever was going in the way of sunshine .and blue sky. As regards the London climate, they will probably agree with Byron's description, written a century ago, where he complained of— "That sort of farthing-candle light which glimmers Where reeking London's smoking cauldron simmers." (Laughter and Cheers.)

Sir Frederick G. Banbury: The hqn. Member has found the experiment so successful that he would like other people to be compelled to carry it out. I under- stand from the hen: Member that he has found the experiment in no way detrimental to himself or his staff, and so he has done it. Others can do the snme.
Mr. Crosfield : I support, because so many other people cannot do what we have done.

div.head: Mr. Holman Kingdon's Arguments Messrs. Crosfield's Experiment.
div.p: Mr. Holman Kingdon's Arguments Messrs. Crosfield's Experiment.

At the annual meeting of the Associated Chambers of Commerce held lest week in London, a resolution approving of the Daylight Savings Bill was proposed by the ex-President of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Holman Kingdon, M.A., and practically carried unanimously. In the course of his speech Mr. Kingdom said : There can be no question of the advantages to be gained by .bringing . more elaylight and sunshine into our live, if this can be achieved without undue interference with existing conditions. Time is purely arbitrary and should be arranged to give the greatest benefit to the greatest number. To put this in another way, time should be so arranged that, having regard to the working day, that is the period between when we Fet up and when we go to bed, there should be, during this period, as much light as possible and as little darkness. During the winter months little or nothing can be done, because we cannot alter either the number of dark hours or the number of light ones, and, provided we are up and about when the light commences and when it ends for each day, no human agency can effect any improvement; but in the summer months th'e case is quite different. Here, except perhaps when. we are In the second half of June, it is still dark before we go to bed and yet is broad daylight many hours before the world at large awakens. Now, if we could only take off some of the wasted hours of daylight in the early morning in the summer months and add them to ths end of the day, the number of hours of daylight during the working day would be increase, and an incalulable boon conferred on the community generally. The " Daylight Saving" Bill shows the means by which this may he achieved. The proposal is that all our clocks shall be put forward one hour on a certain Sunday in April every year and put back again to an equal extent on a certain Sunday in the September following,—no interruption to our daily life, no altera- tion in the hours when we are accustomed to carry out our respective duties, no getting up earlier in the morning—merely the trifling inconvenience of having once a year a day of twenty-three hours, and later, also once a year, one of twenty-five hours. Any traveller knows that this is so slight as to he entirely negligible. To bring home to every one the amount of additional daylight that could be brought into our lives by these means, a man, in twenty-five years, would have gained a who! year of daylight; when fifty years old, two years, arid at seventy-five, three years. Remember,-too that more daylight means less strain to eyes and nerve and brain ! It is quite impossible for any individual to obtain these advantages unless the means of getting them are uniformly adopted by the whole community. My own firm Messrs. Joseph Crosfleld and Sons,Lirnited ot Warrington. has endeavoured to anticipate this Bill by starting work earlier in the morning and leaving off earlier in the evening ; but, though results have been satisfactory and appreciated by the staff, it has been impossible to do this to any serious extent •because other important matters such as train services, the delivery of letters and so on cannot be altered to the same degree. If, therefore, the commercial community want these advantages—and the proposals ought to appeal to everyone who is engaged in routine work of any deseription whatsoever the greater portion of the day and who desires more opportunity for healthy recreation under the light of Heaven—let them support through their local Chamber of Commerce and by invokipg the assistance of their members of Parliament the proposals of this" Daylight Saving "Bill, and let us all remember that, in bringing more sunshine into the lives of other people, we shall ultimately bring more sunshine into our own. (Cheers.)

div.head: CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP.
div.p: CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP.
A Race In a Blizzard.

A blinding snowstorm raged throughout the race for the National Cross-country Championship which was decided on S%turday at Haydock Park racecourse. The conditions were such as to severely test the stamina of the hardiest man and the majority of the competitors finished in a state of complete exhaustion. There was a fairly large contingent of spectators from Warrington an,t their favourite for the championship was C. J. Straw, of Sutton Harriers, who obtained premier honours in 1906. As events proved, however, they were disappointed, Stra,v being hopelessly beaten. A fourth of the distance of ten miles was over ploughed land, which, owing to the conditions proved exceedingly- difficult to traverse: The entry Of nineteen clubs con- stituted a record for the race when held in the North, though the number was six less than last year at New- bury. Owing to a grievance with the Southern Association on the question of the International, there were no entries this time from clubs in the South. Altogether the field numbered, 183 runners. After the first lap the race practically resolved itself into a struggle for supremacy between J. Murphy, of Hallamshire, the Northern champion, and A. J. Robert- son, of Rirchfield, last year's National champion, with W. Coalea of Thrmeston, the Midland championin close attendance. Over the last stretch a grand race ensued between Murphy and Robertson. and though the latter at one time looked like getting the advantage, owing, to his superior clearing of obstacles, the Hallatushire man was on terms in the straight for home Here a splendid struggle ensued, and Murphy, outstaying his opponent, won by about a dozen yards. whilst Coates. who made up a lot of ground towards the end, was a safe third. NOTES BY" MUST."

There has been quite n lull since the Cup-tic-- and it is. perhaps as well. The soreness and.bitter- ness of the unexpected defeat will take a while to wear 'off. Though I don't suppose either critics or Committee will change -their views materially, still things will be seen in a slightly altered perspective in the course of a week or two.

The second round for the Cup will be played to-day, the matches being as follows : Broughton Rangers V. Salford. Leigh v. Wakefield Trinity. Swinton v. Oldham. • Halifax v: Beverley. Runcorn v. Hull. Hunslet v. Leeds. Huddersfield v. Barrow. Wigan v. Keighley. •

Warrington's interest in the struggle for the pot" will be centred in the Leeds—Hunslet engagement. It will be interesting to see how far the Leeds luck will take the conquerors of Warrington., On paper they are already dead and buried at Parkside, but then there was a grave dug for them at Wilderspool ! Will it be another case of the threatened living long? If Leeds are knocked out,could we not arrange a little friendly with them just to show that the form of a fortnight ago was all wrong?

Good-bye to the Kangaroos! The Australian team left old England on‘Thursday by the White Star Line, and were seen off at Liverf)ool by a number of N.U. officials including Mr. H. Ashton of Warrington. They have had a moderately successful season, playing 43 matches, winning 17, losing 20, and drawing 6. Financially they had just about paid their way. As a side they have given us good football and proved equal to the best the Union could produce. Good- luck go with them

The only players who remained behind were Dean and Anlezark (Oldham), Morton and Devereaux (Hull) McCabe (Wigan) and Walsh (Huddersfield). Rosenfeldt is axpected to return to the Fartown Club, and Bolewski has signed on for Leigh for next season. There were high .1- opes that the crack full back would have come to Warrington, but Leigh seem to have offered i the best tents and snapped up his signature at the last minute. Whether he will— if he returns—prove worth £2OO is open to question. It is a big sum to place in one investment. War- rington are not relaxing their efforts in view of next season, and a Kangaroo may yet find a home at . Wilderspool.

Warrington will to-day entertain Bradford in a friendly, and as the Tykes are always popular visitors to Warrington they should draw a respectable crowd. Barrow away is Warrington's next League match.

The team for to-day is noticeable from the fact that Fish has not been selected: Tilley; Treharne, Dickenson. Taylor' Landor ; Brooks and Jenkins; O'Neill, Dowell, Thomas, Shugars, Belton and Boardman.

The "A" team go to Pemberton with serious inten- tions. Their Championship of the Combination is assured if they win, and they certainly should with such a side as the following: Mclntyre; Bradshaw, Cartwright, Jordan and Hockenhull ; Lees and Lloyd; Chesters, Naylor, Harmer, Bradshaw, Harrison and P. Boardman.

•Oar fooball prize scheme is booming. There is no end of neck-craning when the" Examiner " photo- grapher comes round, and you never know in which corner of the field the winning photo will be snapped. So far they have both been on the popular stand, but there was no crowd anywhere else last Saturday. The prize money last week was claimed before 12 noon on Saturday by Edward Kearns, of 59, West- street, whose portrait was recognised at a glance by both himself and his friends.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
REV E G. E CARLETON'S
EDUCATION BILL.
Lively Discussion.

A highly controversial measure in the form of an Education Bill introduced by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton (Minister of Education) occupied the atten- tion of the Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society on Tuesday 'evening and gave rise to some- what heated discussion. The Bill, which was pub- lished in full in last week's" Examiner," deals almost entirely with the religious question and seeks to pre- serve denominational teaching in the schools. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, in submitttng the measure to the House, said he was afraid he was rather rash in undertaking a task whi& had proved quite beyond the powers of certain Liberal statesmen. In some respects he was in a better position than they to deal with the question, inasmach as he was not hampered by any election pledges or by any overtures made to opposite parties previous to the last election. Promises were made to passive resisters on the one hand, and the Roman Catholics on the other. How they were to betept was never explained. He supposed it did not matter very much so long as the exigencies of the election were served. (" Oh !oh !." from the Opposition.) The election was won and the gentlemen opposite got credit for their promises. The time passed and those political 1.0.U.'s came back to be redeemed and that was the reason they had the four Education Bills of the present Government—four attempts on their part to satisfy their creditors all failures. They were, there- fore, still in the position of undischarged bankrupts. One of the features of those attempts at legislation .was the inconsistencies into which the Government were led. They wanted to unify education, and to promote one great national system, but their prc - fessions ended in the schemes for contracting out. From first to last there was differentiation rather than unifica- tion and the differentiation in every case was in favour of those who in the past had made no sacrifices for education, as against those who had. In the Present Bill the Government had no liabilities of that kind to meet and they did not propose to pay court to any particular party. There was going to be no favouritism. They woullt try to do what was fair` and just by all, and they did not set out with the idea that "minorities must suffer," for" minorities equally with majorities, ware entitled to Cie protection of the law and of the Constitution which knew 40 such distinction as majority or minority in the Government of the country. He had never been able to make out how it was that the passive resisters received such consideration from the party opposite, when they claimed the option to obey or disobey the laws made by the people through their representatives. He himself did not take the passive resisters very seriously, The kind of martrydom to which they were subjected was somewhat doubtful. They'always paid in the end and if they liked to pay- their rates at the Court, he for one should rot object. It might give a little more trouble but in these days when occupation was scarce, it might help somewhat to meet the unemployed problem. (Laugh- ter.) In the Governmont Bill there was tO be perfect impartiality of treatmeht in dealing with the various religious denominations and in order to secure that, they proposed that the parents should have a voice in the moral and religious bringing-up of their children, and that that voice should be respected. How was it . that the gentlemen opposite always wished to have the power of ignoring the views of the electorate when it suited their purpose ? (Laughter.) He was not surprised that they quarelled a little with the House of Lords, because that wac, the one institution which in4isted that they should consult the electorate from time to time. (Laughter). The admission form which it was proposed to use in the elementary schools, with the object of aseertaining the religious belief in which the parent desired the child to be instructed, had been introduced into the Warrington Grammar School with Most excellent fesults—(a voice : " Question ")—and there had been no friction whatever. The Bill pi oposed that if the required standard of secular education was attained, it should not be within the power of any authority—not even a Welsh authority—to inflict a fine or disability upon any school or denomination, and any attempt to act in that way would be met by the Board of Education taking steps to relieve such authority or committee of their authority, while making them responsible for the injury inflicted upon individuals. The Bill. aimed at economy—which he was sure would be very acceptable to the gentleman opposite. No community was justified in indulging luxurious tastes on borrowed money. He was of opinion that the work of education in the past was as well done in the modest parochial school with its modest equipment as in the more expensive edifices that were now arising. He contended that the narrow policy of Free Churchmen was unfavourable to economy. They looked forward to the time when the ample municipal accommodation would be a very good excuse for closing voluntary schools, and so inflict the loss Of those schools upon the community. He did not object to unsuitable schools being replaced but it was necessary to watch carefully, so as to prevent narrow- minded men exploiting the rates for their own pur- poses. Any amendment 3 to the Bill would be fairly considered and accepted if they did not contravene the, peinciples of impartiality, economy, toleration, and educational efficiency in all department of religious knowledge. The PREAUER (Mr. W. H. Sansfieldl in seconding the adopt:on of the measure, said the Goveinment had done their hest to placa the question above party and to do justice to themselves as well as to other's. They had endeavoured to give public control over the spend- ing of public money. It was".net until 1870 tlAat the Goveinment of the conntry took charge of education. There were then" 6,382 Church of England schools, besides Roman Catholic schools and other voluntai schools. The Education Act of 1870 was passed to supplement, not to supplant, the Volun- tary schools. From 1370 to 1102 there were built 13,487 Voluntary • schools. The Government gave building grants of £1,500,000 towards 5,102 of those schools and the rest of the schools were built entirely without grants, by private suliscriptions church collections, Sz. Altogether the Church of England had spent £50,000,000 upon its schools. Between 1870 and 1902 the voluntary schools earned a grant from public funds but in addition the Church of England raised the sum of £6,771,236 from private endowments. Why had denominationalists raised these immense sums? Because they had built the schools for the definite and specific object of maintaining that religious teaching which they believed in. The volun- tary schools comprised half the schools of the land in the number of places they provided. Mr. Stanfield dealt in detail with the provisions of the measure and contended that it dealt fairly with the difficulty in the 8,000 single sohnol areas. Their desire was to devise such a Bill that the passive resisters would cease from resisting and that they would not raise up active resisters on the other hand. Mr. J. UPSON (L., Southampton) moved that." this very remarkable Bill" be read that day six months. He must confess that when he listened to the two previous speakers be was in some doubt as to who was the framer of the Bill. They certainly got very much more elucidation of its meaning and intention from the Premier than they did. from .the Minister of Education. He could not congratulate the Minister of gducation upon the speech he had made. Instead of explaining the intention of the Bill and its clauses, his speech largely partook otf the nature of an attack open the passive resister and an explanation of the deficiencies and delinquencies of the Free Churches. Coupled with that, there Was a remark- able lament for the old condition of affairs when educa- tion hung upon the skirts of charity and depended upon jumble sales, church collections and every other odd and ronarkable way of collecting mouey. and was consequently only very partially carried' out. They were asked to believe that there was no intention to be unfair or unjust. He had never read a Bill which was more unfair or more unjust. than the present measure. He gathered from the Minister of Education that the responsibility for the building of the municipal schools and for the present expenditure on education was largely due to Free Church tepresentatives. He did not know that there was luch a large proportion of Free Churchmen on the Town Council, but if it were a fact that the magnificent-schools which were rising in this borough and their adequate equipment and staffing were owing to the action of the Free Churches, it was a fact of which they were proud. (Cheers.) The Minister of Education was ill-advised to speak of the confisca- tion of trusts, because the charge came will bad grace from a gentleman whose church was enjoying endow-

ments from trusts which had been violated from their original purpose. The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON : Nfay I ask the hon. gentleman if he will give the Act of Parliament by which that transfer was effected? There is no such act.

Mr. UPSON : I will give you what is better—an illustration. The Minister of Education is a governor of the Warrington Grammar School. I have a copy of the original trust of that school and the terms for the endowment of that school being enjoyed are that Masses should be said regularly for the repose of the souls of Sir Thomas Boteler, his dame Nlarjorv. his heirs and his ancestors. (Nationalist cheers). Continuing he said that so long as the party opposite were enjoying the alienated endowments of such trusts, they were complacent and said nothing, but when a Liberal Government put out its hand to touch the old and obsolete trusts under private management, for the good of the people of this country at large, there was a terrible hubbub and outcry. It was objected that the late Liberal Government's Bill was not an Education Bill, and he thougnt that taunt might be returned with emphasis in the present case. The Bill might very properly be called a Religious Bodies Endowment Bill. The proposed milt to voluntary schools, taking each child's Place as being worth about ' £7, would mean about a 241. rate. He did not know whether the members of that House had any knowledge of the terrible odium that the church rate brought to a certain section who enforced its payment in certain .parts of the country, but he maintained that such a rate as that proposed in the Bill would meet with even greater opposition. The Bill represented the violation of a principle which they were all beginning to accept— that was to say the door of the voluntary school was absolutely closed while that of the Council school was open to everyone. There was also the violation of the principle of public control. The Premier had told them that they were trying to do justice to all. He (Mr. Upson) was glad to hear the belated confession or to infer from the statement that Free Churchmen had in the past suffered injustice. There w6re 8,000 village schools but until now they had never heard from the other side an expression of the injustice of compelling children of all denominations to go to those schools The Bill perpetu ited private management, and it subordinwed the interests of the

child to the Church, and limited the expenditure upon education. Great care was taken not to say anything about the price of the land on which the schools were to be built. but ti at was not surprising because the land was held by members of the party opposite, and when it was required for schools the highest price was extorted, to the very uttermost farthing. The children of the working people should have their education givers to them in up-to-date buildings, with modern applianciscr. and there should be nevlimit'of ill per 'head for buildings and apparatus. The Opposition considered the Bill was ludicrously undemocratic,ll foolishly retrogra.de and absurdly uneducational, and therefore they should offer it their strongest' resistance. (Opposition cheers). Mr. W. FußsEss(L.. N. Bristol) formally seconded. Mr. C. RODDY (N., East Mayo) supported the Bill because he believed it was the best effort yet made to settle the education question. The best feature was that, contracting-cut was abolished. It gave Catholics the right to use the ,soools which they had built at great sscriflce. for they were the poorest section of the community. To deprive them of that right would be p7thing short of robbery. He would like to ask (1) what was undenominational teaching; (2) since, all denominations psid rates why shoPld they not, have an equal right in the distribution ; (3) why should not teachers who had to give religious teaching be tested as to their capacity for doing ? The Bill would take away the impossible burden from the shoulders of the Catholics. -

Mr. R. Dom.: (secr.taty of .the Board of Education) contended that the Bill was to an unbiassed mind a most honourable solution of the edncation difficulty. Tt recnenized the great work done by people who were

devotel to their faith and who had not hesitated to carry on the slholls for the purpose of continuing the. teaching of the faith for which the schools were built He eontenled that education without religion was not really education. The repeated use by Mr. Done of thA word "Noncon- formist" drew a vigorous protest from Mr. E. LLOYD- .TONES (L94,1.r of the Opposition) who declared that he wag a Free Churchman.

JARMAN— (L, Button-on-Trent), protested ag4inst the mest un-called for sneers of the Minister of Education at Free Churchmen. They must remind him that they const;tnted at least one-half of the people o 7 the Country and to be continually accusing them of narrow-mindedness did not show that. the rev. cootie- men possessed is very broad mind himself. He bad sated that it had proved beyond the power of Liberal statesmen to effect a settlement of the question. That was not, so. Liberal statesmen had had the power and would have affected a settlement but for the House of Lords. They had had plenty of remarks as to the rights of parents and at the same,time they wee told that the last election was won on education 1.0.U.'5. If that were so, the election mist have been won by the influ- ence of the parents expressed through the ballot box. Education was one of the questions before the country at the last, election and the 1.0.U.'s would have been honeurahly redeemed, had it not been for the Houso of Lords. He frankly admitted that the Roman Catholics had a grievance if they were not allowed to have some measure, at least, of their teaching in their own schools. He would, however, point out that the religious diffi- culty did not exist before the 1902 Act and the troeble arose when the schools were placed on the rates. The allocation to denominational teaching of-the 3 per cent to be paid to voluntacy schools in lieu of rent appeared to admit that Free Churchmen were just in contending that denominational teaching should not be 'placed on the rates. The Bill was objectionable because it retained obnoxious tests. The right to teachetships in the voluntary schools remained with the denomi- nationalists and they would also have right of entry into Council schools and in single school areas. The alternative proposal by the Opposition, as put forth in their Bill when they held office, was secular teaching so far as the State was concerned, and religious teaching at the expense of the denominations which wanted it.
_ . Mr. T. RIGBY (N., Cork City) said It was impossible to teach any code of morals which was not bound up with religions teaching. The National Free Church
Council had had raje_cted the secular solution as being no _
;Motion at a-11. Cr..uper-Templeism created -an atmosphere of indifference and scepticism. The Government Bill was an honest attempt to put educe-
on on a true and lasting basis.

The Rev. C. HARVEY-COOK (L., Ashford, Kent) emphasised that there wag a great difference between .Pcular teaching and the teaching of secularism. He admitted that they on that side of the House were asking the Anglicans and Roman

_ Gttholicsto make a large sacrifice. They were asking that these gentlemen who lad been in power so long should, for the good of the nation's education, vacate their place and give it to the public. He was exceed- ingly sorry the Government measure was not an Education Bill. It seemed tl be an ecclesiastical, Iheologicsl Bill. It was perfectly. true and a matter of
history to sty that Dissenters had not built schools. Why? Because their friends represented by the Afinister of Education would not allow the Non-
conformists to build.
To set up .now the contention
that Nonconformity bad done nothing was to forget the way in which they had put Nonconformists down, as his own church and an Nonconformist churches bore
witners. The ecclesigstics kept them out of power prPvented thee using that influence which they might have exercised' He tried to look at the education
q—u-estio-nlas it affected the national outlook and to study it not from the stindpoint of his particular theology but of his citizenship. As to the argument of gentle- _ _ _
num opposite that they had to pay for their own schools and for others in which they did not believe, it was one of the costs of progress. He had to pay

for it and not ask ror_it to come out of the rates.
rhTe
parent's right, which had been an much spoken of, was to teach religion; it was not left for the ecclesiastics. They could not. bitch men religion, hut only theology.
They could help them to cultiate. their religious life
.. but they could 'not teach it them. _ On the motion of Mr. J. N. VERNON (C., "Mlidstone) the debate was adjourned until next Thmaday evening.

"I am now eighty years old and one morning, three years ago, I was taken with a hard pain in my right side. In two days I had an attack of piles (hemorrhoids), bleeding and protruding. The doctor gave me some medicine and an ointment for them which helped me some but I had to keep using them all the time. Then I changed to the P- remedy; but if I did not use it every day, I would get worse. The doctor said the only help for me was to go to a hospital and be operated on. At this time, about a year ago, I went to using the 5-- remedies. I tried them for four or five months but did not get much help for my piles. During this time sores would come on a fleshy part of my body. They bothered me all the time; I would get one healed and another would come. These sores changed to eczema, accompanied by a terrible itching. It seemed as if I could not keep my hands from tearing ray flesh. This and the pile trouble brought on an inflamed condition. Then I got the Cuticura Remedies. I washed the affected parts with Cuticura Soap and warm water in the morning, at noon, and at night, then used Cute- cura Ointment on the irritated sur- faces and injected a quantity of Cuti- cura Ointment with a Cuticura Sup- pository Syringe. Along with the noisy opposition to the Licensing Bill with its wild statements and silly cartoons a quieter and more care- fully planned campaign intended to influence another section of the community was in pro- gress. The campaign was a literary one. Mr. E. A. Pratt produced nearly two years ago an elaborate volume under the title "The Licensed Trade," which painted the brewers as public benefactors and the public-house as the supreme necessity of a civilized society. In tens of thousands and at the cost of a moderate fortune this book was distributed among the clergy and others of their class during the discussion of the Licensing Bill.

Mr. PRATT has again placed his ingenious brain at the service of the Trade, this time to write a volume on "The policy of Licensing Justices." Its sub-title ought to be "A plea for the oppressed brewer" for it pleads with the justices to "display a more tolerant spirit" and with the police to "show a little less zeal." This volume is being sent broad- cast by post to occupants of the Licensing Bench. The justices are informed that "the tied-house has not only obviously come to stay, but no administration of the Licensing Laws can be satisfactory if based on a dis- regard of what has become a fundamental factor in present-day licensing conditions." With delightful ingenuity this slim advocate asks justices to take it for grantcd that the fullest and largest trade in intoxicants ought to be cultivated, that` brewers are the uncrowned benefactors of the race who would do far more, than they have ever done if they were encouraged instead of being thwarted by mischievous temperance reformers. Even the tied-house system "must be definitely accepted" and temperance extremists may be "judiciously overlooked when the licens- ing committees are appointed." _ _

We have read Mr. PRATT'S 150 pages with- out finding a single suggestion for the reform of the Trade,but he seems to be quite sure that the Trade if given greater privilege and liberties would gradually reform itself. It is taken for granted that humanity was made for the Trade and not the Trade for humanity, and the author indignantly accuses temperance reformers of conducting a "campaign against humanity." Is it urged that in multiplying public-houses we increase temptation? Mr. PRATT is ready with his answer. Strength of character is mainly built up by resistance to temptation, and we are left to assume that the more gin palaces there are the more morally strong the community. That people should ever blame the publican astonishes this eloquent champion of the trade ! "When the fault, defect, or shortcoming . . . is to be found in the consumer, it is to the con- sumer and not to the trader that the remedy must be applied." Temperance people are to be allowed to-pick the drunkard from the gutter, to feed his children, to pay police and support asylums, but blame the pub- lican !—the author lifts up his eyes in anguish to the skies. The public-houses are the "harbours of refuge " of the race. We feel obliged to stem this current of eloquence for a moment to interject a ques- tion. If it be, indeed, an advantage to have the public-house ever close to us how is it that the mortality of publicans is so alarming. They have abundance of opportunity to resist the temptation to drink and ought to be among the strongest of the community. What are the facts? The Registrar General shows that they die seven times as fast as workingmen engaged in trade, and the Life Insurance Companies have long since marked them off as a special risk.

But Mr. PRATT'S zeal carries him too far. With all his alertness he does not reali that his arguments, if sound, are arguments in favour of free trade in liquor. If it is desirable to give a free hand to brewers to push their trade by every device they can invent, why not leave it open to everyone else to open attractive "harbours of refuge." Possibly we should be told that the Trade is in the best hands and that free trade in liquor is undesirable. The Trade thinks so; but if Mr. PRATT'S argument be sound the licensing system ought to be abolished and free trade in liquor take its place. We do not know how many justices the trade expects to influence. We imagine that mot who read this treatise will treat it as a piece of audacious insult and effrontery and be influenced in a way that its authors did not intend. That the brewers should spend a small fortune in issuing such a volume is, as CARLYLE would .say, significant of much. Issued to Judges of Assize such literature would be treated as contempt of Court. Is it any less an offence to issue prejudiced literature to justices? There is, of course, the inevitable reminder that the State raises enormous revenue from the drink trade and that the trade should there- fore be privileged. Against this we need only place the query which JOHN WESLEY put to WILLIAM PITT, "Does it pay to raise re venue by killing taxpayers ? "
It is somewhat remark- UNRECOGNIZED able that Mr. Haldane's ACHIEVEMENTS. critics—and_ especially

Mr. Arnold-Fo-rster-L should have had nothing to say about the great reforms which the Secretary for War has introduced into our military system by the creation and development of a General Staff, and by re-organization of the working arrangements in the field, so that a com- mander-in-chief will be relieved of every detail which could preclude him from devoting his mind singly to the operations of war. In the scientific precision and exact co-ordination of parts which have always been signally lacking in our military system, Mr. Haldane's work stands out with salipnt distinction. And the creation of the Imperial General Staff, which has recently come into .existence, is a notable event to which one would have expected men who, like Mr. Arnold-Forster and Mr. Wyndham, claim to speak as military experts, would at least have made some reference.
Since writing the above, we learn with regret that Mr. H. 0. Arnold-Forster died yesterday afternoon after only two days' illness. He was Secretary for War under the last Government.
The hours of the MARRIED WOMEN m.a rried women TEACHERS. teachers in Warring-

ton schools appear be numbered. Mr. T. P. Bradshaw has put down another motion for Monday's meeting of the Education Committee which, we should think, will stand a very good chance of being confirmed. His semnd proposal is only a little less dragtic than the first, but it gives special consideration to those cases which have some claim to exemption from an arbitrary rule terminating all the engagements of married women teachers. Briefly put, Mr. Brad- shaw's suggestion is that in the case of a married woman teacher supporting an infirm husband her engagement shall be ratified. Married women teachers who cannot advance such a claim shall receive three months notice after April 30th next, and female teachers who marry while in their employ- ment shall also terminate their engage- ments at due notice. These proposals appear to us to meet the most serious difficulties • in the way of the original motion, and to give the Committee some option in each ease. In our view there is no argument worthy of considera- tion in favour of the retention of married women as teachers, apart from that admitted by Mr. Bradshaw, and the glaring cases here 1, and there of dual family appointments point plainly to the necessity for measures which will give the young entrants into the pro- fession a fair chance.

The Prime Minister's A GREAT SPEECH. speech upon Free Trade at the Queen's Hall • demonstration to a considerable extent broke new ground. The contention of Tariff Reformers that Free Trade is driving capital out of this country is comparatively recent, and the Tariff Reform programme has been modified in many direction's. It was chiefly with these aspects of the controversy that Mr. Asquith dealt. When Mr. Chamberlain started his campaign, we were told that the British investor was recalling his capital from abroad. Now we are told that Capital has fled from free imports." It is all going abroad. But, as Mr. Asquith pointed out, the total amount of British capital exported—and, of course, it can only be exported in the form of pro- duce or services—does not exceed 20 per cent. lof the whole, while another stream of foreign Icapital has been pouring into this country. It is said that we invest our capital in countries which force us to take payment in manufactured goods. But out of X 3,000,000,000 invested abroad, ,L 2,300,000,000 is invested in countries from which our only imports are imports Of food and raw material. I Nor can it be argued that this exportation of capital has, been accompanied by a denudation of the field of industry and enterprise here. Apart from the foreign capital invested in, this country, the amount of British capital invested in British indus- try last year was steadily on the increase; £56,500,000 was publicly subscribed, and a vast amount must be added for private investments that never came into the market at all. But the most striking refuta- tion of the notion that our own field of investment is shrinking while the field abroad is being extended is afforded by the figures of income-tax assessment. The gross income for 1898-9 was £762,000,000 ; for 1906-7, £943,000,000 an increase of 24 per cent, while the population had only increased 8.3 per dent. In weighty and eloquent phrase Mr. Asquith appealed to Free Traders not to underrate either the gravity of what is at stake or the ceaseless energy of the attack. Protection makes a direct appeal to instincts and inter- ests deep-seated and almost universal. The propaganda to be faced is highly organized, richly endowed, unresting in its activity, übiquitous in its range. Upon Free Traders is cast the responsibity of driving back the most formidable and most menacing attack that has been levelled, within the lifetime of this generation, against the very centre and citadel of our national prosperity.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS._
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS._
Our readers will be interested to hear that Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield enjoyed the privilege last evening of dining with the Premier at 10, Downing-street. * _

Mr. and Mrs. A. H. brosfield, on Wednes- day evening gave a musical "At Home" at their residence at 39, Hyde Park Gate. Among he guests present were :—Lord Brassey. and Mrs. Edwards, Lady Hyde- Parker, Sir John and Lady Dickson- Poynder, Lady Robson, Mrs. H. J. Tennant, Mrs. Emmott, Mrs. Birrell and Mr. Tenny- son, the Right Hon. Colonel Seeley, the Right Hon. Alfred Lyttelton, Mrs. Mond, Mrs. Spicer, Mrs. Levy Lever. the Misses Ralli, Mrs. Astbury, Mr. and Mrs. Henry, Mr. and Mrs. P. W. Wilson, Mr. and Mrs. Arcbibald Williamson, Mrs. Leech, Mr. and the Misses Maddison, Mr. and Mrs. S. Wink- worth, Miss Schilizzi, Mr. Calvocaressi, and Mr. Mitchell-Thomson. * *

The celebration of the date of Mrs. Browning's birth was a rare trap for the unwary last week. Research long since showed that Elizabeth Barrett was born in 1806, in spite of the mention of 1809 on her tombstone. The fact is that Mrs. Browning was a little older than her husband, and was extremely sensitive on the point, and her husband acted in the circumstances with delicate courtesy. * * *

• Excellent reports are to hand of the impression Mr. Joseph Howes is making in his speaking tour ' round the Attercliffe Division (Sheffield). With a racy and popular style Mr. Howes combines a wide grasp of political history, and he makes a speech any intelligent voter should delight to hear. This week he has been devoting special evenings to the House of Lords and Free Trade v. Protection. Mr. Howes is in rare form for the projected ,local debate— should it ever materialise. * * *

Evan Jones—he disdains the use of either "Rev." or "Mr."—the new President of the National Free Church Council, which met at Swansea on Monday, is in his seventy-third year. He was a printer's apprentice in Machynlleth for six yeas, and was barely "out of his time" when he became Editor of the Welsh "Punch," but left literature to return to the printing office. Printing was followed by preaching, or rather they ran together for four years, during which time Evan Jones studied at Bala and conducted his business as well. For thirty years he had a pastoral charge at Carnarvon. * * * •

In Victoria the Licences Reduction Board has recently presented a report of two years' work. Over 200 hotels, the Australian "Review of Reviews" states, have been closed at a compensation cost to the Trade itself of nearly £lOO,OOO, the average amount paid per hotel being thus about £5OO. When it is remembered that at North Melbourne some years ago some forty-eight hotels were closed under the old law with compensation averaging £l,OOO per house, it will be seen how the compensation funds were plundered under that system. The present fund is provided by a 3 per cent. levy on the amount of liquor sold. The amount of liquor sold by the houses lately closed is valued at £l,OOO per week. * _ _

A Liberal M.P. Writes to the " West- minster Gazette" of Monday "It should not be Overlooked that on Thursday night the Opposition (44 in number) divided against the Ways and Means Resolution Report to enable old-age pensions to be given during the remaining three weeks of the finAncial year. If these Tory tactics had been suc- cessful the Consolidated Fund Bill, granting £910,000 (supplementary estimate) for old- age pensions, could not have ever been introduced." The conduct of the Opposi- tion is a sufficiently pointed exposure of the claim so constantly made in the country that the credit for the pensions really belongs to the Tory Party.

* * We hope our readers will devote sympathetic attention to the needs of the Warrington Children's Summer Camp, the annual business meeting of which held last week. The year closed with an adverse bank balance of £66 12s. 9d., but this was part of an unwelcome legacy of £235 two years earlier. A year ago this figure was reduced to £139 13s. 4d., and now it has fallen to the sum stated at the retent meet- ing. This is a clear- indication of the sound business management of the Camp funds, and it should greatly encourage intending subscribers. The past season was a very successful one, no less than 399 children enjoying the benefits of the Camp, and many improvements being made. The work itself hardly needs our recom- mendation, but we would point out that its beneficial capacities are only limited by the funds, and to render the provision adequate to the needs of the town more generous help is required. * *

Beautiful unanimity prevailed at the L.G.B. inquiry held at Warrington on Thurs- day to facilitate the improvement of our four main thoroughfares. As the' deputy Town Clerk put it, this was a very unusual cir- cumstance for Warrington,—indeed the occasion deserves to be written large in the annals of the town, for even the redoubtable Mr. Gough astonished everyone by observ- ing "I have great pleasure in supporting the application." All sections of opinion are united in desiring that the great scheme of street widening to which - the Corporation set its hand as far back as 1884 should be brought within measurable distance of realization. The completion of Bridge-street has given us a fine street of which any town might- be proud, but it was stated at Thursday's inquiry that the width of Sankey-street, Buttermarket- street and Horsemarket-street is, for the most part, the same as it was at that very remote period-1465. The great obstacle is, of course, the acquiring of valuable land and property, and we re-echo the hope freely expressed on Thursday that the owners will meet the Corporation in a reasonable spirit and thus assist the town's advancement along the path of progress.

div.head: Penny Popular Concerts.
div.p: Penny Popular Concerts.

The Woodville Concert Party, of Liverpool, paid another visit to these successful concerts at told- street school on Saturday evening and a crowded audience awaited them. A bright and interesting programme was submitted, including songs (humorous and sentimental) duets and choruses, and the concert was one- of the sentimental), yet held. During an interval an address was delivered by the Rev. T. Miller. who presided.

A maiden neat and new and nice, Was skating on some rotten ice, And 'neath the surface in a trice She slid! ' They hauled her out and thought her drowned, But someone said, "Well, I'll be bound, Woods' Peppermint Cure would bring her round"— It did !—Advt.
