Price of Bread to be raised. As a glance at our advertisement columns will signify, the Warrington and District Master Bakers and Confectionery Association will advance the price of bread by one halfpenny per 41b. loaf on Monday next, March 15th.

PUBLIC BENEFIT UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Accident to Mr. H. Ambler. Mr. Harold Ambler, of Penketh, had a narrow escape from serious injury while at work at Penketh Tannery, yesterday. He fell from the roof of the lime yard and sustainW a severe shaking. Luckily no bones were broken, but the shock has necessitated his being confined to bed. Women's Circle.

Mrs. Ben Few presided at the Circle on Sunday Mrs. Broadhurst and Rose Tynan taking part. The address was given by Mrs. Lawson. Two solos by Miss Long 'were heartily received. Mrs. Farrer sang " Calvary " and Miss Alice Taylor gave a recitation "Was lost and is found." The choir gave a new setting of" The Lord's Prayer."

PUBLIC BEN, FIT.—CNDER TILE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt, Sankey Wire Mills C.C. The annual dinner and meeting of the members of the Sankey Wire Mills Cricket -Club was held on Saturday last in the Winmarlegh Café, Mr. James Evans, jun.., presi4ing.--Satisfactory reports were presented by the Secretary and Treasurer. The balance sheet showing that the club, notwithstanding considerable expense incurred in connection with the new ground at Longshaw Lane, have a slight balance in hand. Mr. E. Houghton was re-elected president. The records for 1908 were :--First Team: Played 10, won 4; lost 6. Second Team: Played 12, won 7 ; lost 5. The batting average for the senior team was won by Mr. A. B. Miles, whilst Mr. W. Woodcock captured the bowling average. The following officers were elected: Captain First Team, W. Woodcock; sub-captain, Ellis Clare; treasurer, R. Hewitt; secretary, H. Hawthorn. Captain Second Team, F. Dooley; sub-captain, P. Bladen. There are bright prospects for a successful season. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER TRE CLOCK FOR . BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. " Peter Pan " at Liverpool. At the Shakespeare Theatre, Liverpool, on Monday next, Charles Frohman presents for the fourth yearr Mr. J. M. Barrie's play "Peter Pan" or "The Boy Who Wouldn't Grow Up." Miss Pauline Chase again plays Peter. Since her last visit to this city, Mr Frolunan has presented her and the entire Duke o York Theatre Company at the Theatre du Vauceville, Pdris, for a season in June last. Mr. FrOlunan has made arrangements for "Peter Pan" and thecompauy which opens next week to have a season in Paris this summer, and under existing arrangements, June 13th is the date when the piece will be seen again at the Theatre du Vaudeville in the French • Capital. Of modern plays, there are not at present travelling which have been able to make four annual visits with the regularity and success of "Peter Pan" to the Provincial. Theatres, and there is every reason to believe that next year again will see Mr. Barrie's delightful play in this city. LAWN MOWERS nhould now be repeired for the season. Special Plant. Prompt attention.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Oddiellowshlp.--Olive Branch Lodge. .

An interesting event took place at the above lodge on Saturday evening last, the occasion being the pre- sentation of a Past Officer's Certiffeate to P.G. V(m. Winstanley. Amongst the visiting' bretlfren present were the following: Prow. G.M. Fred. Freeman, Prow. Deputy G.M.T.P. Forbes, I.P.P.G.M. Lot Brooks, Prow. C.S. Frank Webster and P.P.U-.M.T.P. Bradshaw. The N.G. of the Lodge (Bro. T. Seed) presided and was supported by V.G. Hy. G. Flood, Lodge G.M.S. Garnett, P.O. Arthur Cotterill, P.P.G.M. Alban Boyle (Secretary)' and other members of the Lodge. District G.M. Freeman in making the presentation referred in complimentary terms to the way Bro. Winstanley had discharged his duties and hoped it would be an incen- tive to the younger members to emulate his example. Bro. Winstanley had the satisfaction of knowing he had worked for a good cause, and he (the G.M.) hoped be would still continue to take a deep interest in his Lodge.—P.G. Winstanley, in 'acknowledging the presentation, said he was pleased to accept it, and he could promise them that it would be hung in a very prominent place in his house. What he had done was his duty, but hp could assure them he would still try and do his best for the advancament of the Lodge. (Applause). • LINSEED COMPOUND with warm water is an exeellent gargle for sore throat.—Advt. Warrington Workman's Death.

At the Borough Police Buildings on Ttiesday, Coroner Brighouse held an inquiry into the circum- stances attending the death of Moses Wilkes, at his residence, 22, Wellfield-street. Deceased, who was 70 years of age, died on Sunday morning last. Evidence sill:red that deceased went to his L'ork at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., Ltd., on the morning of the Ist inst. He appeared alright with the exception of a slight cold. When he arrived home his wife asked him what was the matter and he said" I'm done." On the morning of the 2nd inst. he com- plained of a pain in the right side, and Dr. Naden was called in. The next day he commenced to spit blood. On Saturday a workmate named .Sutcliffe called, and remarked that" it was that blow that did it." The old man made no reply. It transpired that deceased was handling some metal with t pair of tongs, when. they slipped and caught him in the side. The blow appeared to wind him.—Dr. Reginald Smith, who made a post-mortem examination, said that the left 'lung showed traces of pneumonia and pleurisy. There was no sign of .injury to the ribs or to any other part of the body. He could not associate the death with the accident. The cause of the death was in consequence of the pleurisy and pneumonia.—Drs. Naden and Sankey corroborated Dr. Smith's evidence.—The jury returned a verdict of "Natural causes," according to medical evidence. COAG U LIN E," EMI NX," TI4.;NASITINE.' Cements for mending all things.—Advt. Staff Dinner.

At the Patten Arms Hotel last Saturday, the staff of the Castle Rubber Co., Ltd., held their annual dinner. Advantage was taken of the, occasion for an interesting function, viz., the presentation to Mr. Thomas O'Brien, works manager, of a handsome gold hunter watch, to conimemorate the completion of 25 years' service with the firin.—Mr. Thomas A. Hampson (the chairman) in making the presentation on behalf of the directors, spoke of the recipients' attention to his duty, and expressed the desire ,that he would long be spared to serve the Tampany as well and faithfully in the future as in the p4st.-4r. Henry Greenall (director) also .made some very complimentary remarks respecting the loyalty and ability which Mr. O'Brien had so consistently displayed during his long service with the company.—The recipient, on rising to respond,, was greeted with the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow." He said he thanked them most heartily and sincerely for their kindness. That, day he had also received from the staff and work-people a splendid marble clock, and that, along with the beautiful watch then handed to him, had practically overwhelmed him. He could assure them that no effort would be wanting on his part to show the high appreciation he felt for their generous wishes and kindly feeling, and he would always do his utmost to serve the firm as well in the future as he had done in. the past. An " impromptu smoker "occupied the remainder of the evening, and was greatly enjoyed. LINSEED COMPOUND 'for Coughs and Colds.. Of proven efficacy. 9id. & is. lid. Of Chemists only.—Advt•

div.head: Wedding at Wycliffe Church.
div.p: Wedding at Wycliffe Church.

The marriage was solemnized at Wycliffe Con- gregational Church, on Thursday morning, of Mr. Bowman Hibbert, son of Mr. Charles H. Hibbert, Kendrick-street, and Miss Lucy Travis, youngest daughter of Mr. Richard Travis, 54, Winwick-road. The Rev. John Yonge officiated. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in a cream Princess costume with hat to match. She carried a book, presented by the Rev. J.Yonge,and wore a gold bangle, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaid was Miss Ethel Hibbert (sister of the bridegroom), who wore a brown costume with hat to match. Mr. J.W.Travis,brother of the bride, discharged the •duties of best man. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus.

Bac., was at the organ and played suitable selections. After the ceremony, the reception was held at the house of Mr. J. Boardman (the bride's grandfather). Folly-lane. Later the happy couple left for Black- pool, the bride's going-away dress being a pale blue cloth costume with hat to match. Numerous hand- some presents were received. div.head: ELECTION PETITION.
div.p: THE ELECTION PETITION.
COMMISSIONER'S FINDINGS.
Witnesses:, Disfranchisement.

Mr. W. J. Brooks, barrister-at-law, the Commissioner .who tried the recent election petition at Warrington, has reported his findings as follows :-1. That no corrupt practice was proved to have been committed by or with the knossledge and consent of any candidate. 2. That the following persons were proved at the ttial to have been guilty of the corrupt practice of bribery :—Alfred Wood, of 23 Longford-street ; Arthur Peacock, of Liscard, Cheshire; Abraham Smart, of 19, Longford-street ; Mary Ann Silcock, of 267, Lovely- lane (married woruan) : Albert Fisher, of 4, Philip- street; Sarah Ellen Hadcroft, of 1, Smith's Court, Winwick-road ; Richard Bailey, of 32, Oliver-street; Thomas Knight, of 2, Watkin-street. 3. That all those persons mentioned in paragraph 2 of this report have been furnished with Certificates of Indemnity in respect of the corrupt practice of bribery with the exception of the said Alfred Wood, the said Abraham Smart, and the said Mary Ann Silcock. 4. That the following persons were proved at the trial to have been guilty of the corrupt practice of -treating :—Alfred Wood,of 23 Longford-street; 'William Ryland s Alcock, of SO Vest-street; Herbert Davies, of 29 Winwick-road ; George James Cooper, of 138 Long- ford-street; Richard Bailey, of 32 Oliver-street. 5: That all those per-mns mentioned in paragraph 4 of this report have been furnished with Certificates of lademnity in respect of the corrupt practice of treating. C. That there is no reason to believe that corrupt practices extensively prevailed at the said election in the said Ward.

7. That it WM proved at the trial that the said Peter Peacock, who was a candidate at, the said election, bad been guilty by his Agents of the corrupt practices of bribery and: ^renting, hut no candidate, other than the said Peter Peicoc4, was found tp have been guilty by his Agents of any cormpt practice. 8. That no particulars were filed nor any evidence tendered upon the charge of undue influence contained in the petition.

9. That I made no order as to costs, Counsel for the Petitioner having stated at the close of the trial that the Petitioner did not ask for costs against the Respondent. Dated tho 20th day of February, 1909. W. J. BROOKS, Commissioner.

The Town Clerk has notified all persons named above as being guilty of corrupt practices that by Section 6 (3) of the Corrupt and Illegal Practices Pre- vention Act,lBB3.they will not be capable during a period of seven years from the date of the report, viz., 20th February, 1909, of (1) being registered as an elector or voting at any election in the United Kingdom whether it be a Parlia- mentary election or an election for soy Public Office within the meaning of the above Act, and (2) holding any public or judicial office within the meaning of the above Act.

div.head: MUSIC IN EARLESTOWN
div.p: MUSIC IN EARLESTOWN

Warrington Competitors to the Fore. That Welsh institution the Eisteddfod thrives in Earlestown, where it has now been successfully con- ducted for some !years by enthusiastic sons of the Principality. Last Saturday's festival was char- acterised by increased entries and fairly large audiences and Warrington competitors were, well to the fore. Mr. J. Jones, of Liverpool, was the president for the day and Mr. W.' R. Jones, of Bangor, discharged the duties of conductor. The adjudicators were Mr. H. Evans (music), Rev. Peter Williams (poetry), Mr. Edward Davies (prose), Rev. W. A. Bryan Jones (citations), and Mr Valentine, Mr. A. Dting,and Mr. B. B. Davies, of Warrington (art). RESULTS. Juvenile Choir contest. —There were two entries— Sutton United Juvenile Choir (conductor, Mr. W. Knapper) and Warrington Band of Hope Union Choir (conductor,- Mr. A. Spruce). Mr. Harry Evans awarded the first prize (23 and gold centre medal to the con- ductor) to the Sutton choir, and the second Prtze (el) to the Warrington choir. div.head: IS YOUR TROUBLE THE SAME?
div.p: IS YOUR TROUBLE THE SAME?

1 f it is your cure can be the same.", When describing, to a representative his terrible suffering and his cure by Doan's pilis,Mr.James Cawley, '2B, Lloyd-stri.et, Bank Quay, Warrington,, said: "I started to suffer with my kidneys five years ago; it came on in a most violent manner with pains in the small of my back. 1 was unable to work for seven weeks. The pains were just like a stab ft orn a kni ein my back and between my shoulders, so that. I could not turn in bed. The secretions of th.s kidneys were just like the white of an egg and very painful, especially when passing. There was a sediment of .gravel, and there was a frequent desire to pass the Secretions. "1 had rheumatism in both arms, being so helpless that I could not lift anything, and had such a great weariness in the legs that I could not walk any distance without fatigue; that was when I was up and about. I could scarcely dress myself in the mornings because of this tired feeling. I had very bad headaches at times ; I could.not hold my head up„ and even my cap was a weight on my head. Giddiness was another tiouble, and I was afraid I would fall. I was unable to sleep for more than two or three hours during the nieht and sometimes not at all. My appetite was very poor, what little I did eat seeming like lead in the stomach. Occasionally I had palpitation of the heart, and was so short of breath that the least exertion exhausted me. There were specks before my eyes and my sight was dim. "I was very susceptible to colds, which always flew to my kidneys: At the best of times I could not without a great effort get up after stooping ; but when the worst attacks of backache struck me I would have "to get to bed, and remain there a week. This occurred every few weeks.' "The doctor who treated me said it was muscular Rheumatism. I really thought I was incurable, the doctor saying the trouble would become chronic. I was always taking medicine and rubbing myself with liniments, but I cannGt say that anything gave me relief. After each attack I got to work again as soon as I could, though I was not at all fit for it. Ido not think I averaged more than seven months of work during the year. "I read about Doan's pills and started to use them; I felt the first signs of relief in seven days ; I could eat and sleep better. Then 1. noticed that the urinary secretions were as clear as crystal, and the pains gradually diminished until they disappeared altogether. A course of Doan's pills cured me absolutely. it is a pleasure to have good health. I never remember feel- ing so well as I do now; and the only thing that troubles mtS is that 1 did not use these pills earlier. I can earnestly recommend them. (Signed) JAMES CAWLEY."

Doan's Backache Kidney Pills are two shillings and nim pence per box (six boxes for thirteen shillings and ninepence.) Of all chemists and stores, or post free, direct from Fostg-McClennan Co., 8, Wells-street, Oxford-street, London, W. Mr. Cawley was cured by Doan's ;be sure that you get DOAN'S."

Warrington Borough Court. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), Dr. Markel, Mes-rs. R. T. Fairclough and A. J. Jolley. THEFT OF SWEETS.—SamueI Lomas, a youth, 66, Sharp-street, was chargeil with stealing a box of caramels, the property of the Sovereign Confectionery Company, on March 4th.—lnspector Williamson stated that a van laden with sweets, Ste. was left in Birchall- street while the driver (Mr. W. 1N hitehouse) went soliciting orders at a shop. He happened to see the defendant getting into the van and reshed out and caught him with the box of caramels in his possession. As there had been frequent thefts of this kind, the firm was unable to overlook the case.—A fine of 10s. including costs or 7 days imprisonment was imposed. CONSTABLE •ASSAULTED.—James Healey, 30, Tilley- street. was sentenced to a month's imprisonment for having been drunk and disorderly in Fennel-street the previous night and assaulting P.C. Gibson.—lt was stated tint • prisoner rushed at the officer with an axe and a severe struggle ensued before the weapon Was wrenched from him. He struck the constable several blows with his fist. On the way to the Police Station he was very violent—in fact, the constable stated that he was like a wild beast. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Wilkinson and Messrs. W. Roberts, S. Wright and G. Pilling. DRUNK IN CHARGE.—Harry Southall, Brighton-road, Stockport, was fined ss. and costs for having been , drnnk whilst in charge of a horse and lnrry at Market- gate on Saturday—P..C. Fish proved the case and the Chief Constable said it was needless to point out the danger of the offence. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Rymer Young (in the chair), C. Jackson Holmes and W. Richardson. ARREARS OF MAINTENANCE.—WiIIiam McNiullen,Fox- street, was summoned for arrears amounting to £1 6s. in respect to the maintenance of his father.— Mr. B. Shearer, who prosecuted on behalf of the Union. stated that an order of 2s. 6d. per week was made upon the defendant in November last, but he had not paid a halfpenny. During the last few weeks his wages had amounted to £1 4s. 2d. a week. He was married and had four children.—Defendant said be thought it was too much to pay 2s a week.—The Chairman : l'here is not the slightest excuse, you will have to go to prison for one month.

CHARGE AGAINST A SOLDIER.—Henry :Taylor, or Joseph Bennett., a private in the King's Liverpool stationed at Kinsdale, was charged with (1) rifling a meter at 11, Fountain-street, and stealing there- from the sum of ss. Bd., on the 3rd March, and (2) also with committing the same offence mid stealing the sum of 6s. sd. from the dwelling-house, of 53, Old-road, on the same date.— The Chief Constable stated that it would be necessary. for a remand until Monday in order to make every inquiry regarding the prisoner's character. In the meantime he would communicate with the commanding officer of prisoner's regiment, for if the man had a good character it would be ruined if the prisoner was con- victed. It appeared that the prisoner was seen by P.C. Clough spending coppers rather freely. The officer being suspicious made inquiries and subsequently arrested prisoner who admitted the thefts.—The remand was granted. FOOTBALL IN THE STREET.—For playing football in Howard-street on the 18th of February, William Wprrall (16) of 17, Howard-street, Tho nes Adams (17) 34, Howard-street, and Mark Holt (16), 12, Wakefield- street, were each fined 3s. 6d. each. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Charles White (chairman) and Alderman Smethurst* , TEMPORARY AUTHORITY.—Mr. A. Browne made an application on behalf of Mr. T. Hesketh for temporary to sell at 58. Legh-street, in lieu of Mr Jossph Warburton Robinson, who has left the town. Tne application was granted. ARREARS OF MAINTENANCE.—Joseph Rigby Vernon, Stephen-street, was charged with arrears of mainten- ance to his wife amounting to £3 18s. Defendant admitted the money was• due. He was ordered to refund it or undergo one month's imprisonment. WORLD N,vr BREAK STONES.—George Taylor, a workhouse inmate was charged with refusing to per- form his allotted task of breNking Stones at the Work- house.—Mr. Awbery (Master of the Workhouse) said that defendant had been in the House off and on since 1906. Ele bad considerable physical strength and it was the opinion of the Gtuirdians that he was able to earn his living outside the house. As be did not leave it was decided to increase his task to 12 cwt., instead of 10 cwt. This was put into operation last Monday hut the defendant absoluteld refused to perform it.—The case was adk)urned for a week in order to give defend- ant a chance.

Tit tiesDAY.—BefomMessrs. Chas. White (in the chair), J. Rymer Young and W. Roberts. SLOT METER THEFT.—John Nicholson, 15 years of age, Knutsford-rond, was charged with stealing ss. 7d. from a gee slot meter in a home .in Battersby-lane on April 30th of last year.—The Chief Constable . said the boy was sent to an industrial school in 1902. but be repeatedly absconded. He was let out on license,-and followed some enfployment for a time. The Superin- tendent of the Bolton Industrial School had intimated that he was willing to take the boy back to that institu- tion.—The case was adjourned sine die in order that the boy might he sent hack to the industrial school. BEYOND HER. MOTHER'S CONCROL.—A girl named Susannah Davison, St. Vlary-street, was committed to a reforrnatoryschool at Edinburgh for stealing some good 4, the property of William Hodgkinson,Ltd., Bridge-st, on February 22nd.—A boy in the employ of the prosecutors was directed to take a parcel of goods to a lady near St. Mary-street, and the girl represented that she was employed at the house in question. She promised to deliver the parcel and the boy gave it to her.—The mother said the girl was absolutely beyond her control. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman ~Smethurst (chairman), Messrs. James Evans, W. Furness, A. J. Jolley, H. Thornton and G. Pilling. ALLEGED ASSAULT.--Jelm Gillibrand, 15, Kerfoet- street, was summoned for wilful damage and assaulting Edith Phileurn. 13, Kerfoot-street. The evidence showed that defendant and complainant's mother had been falling out over a dog and a cockerel. It was illieged that the defendant broke the window whilst in a state of drunkenness, and also assaulted the com- plainant. Witness testified that defendant did not strike Phil burn. The magistrates disraisced the case. SEPARATION ORDER REFUSED.—John Skelton,Lower Wash-lane, Latchford, carrying on business in Sankey. street, Warrington, applied for a separation order from his wife on the ground that she was an habitual drunkard.—Ar. C. H. Unsworth appeared for the corn- plainiutt and Mr. Arthur Browne for the defendant.— Mr.Unsworth said the case was broeght before the Court on January 28. It was adjourned for four weeks, the defendant signing an agreement to be an abstainer. Since the adjournment there had been no improvement. —John Skelton said that since the adjournment he had given his wife every possible chance, but all to no pur- pose. On two or three occasions he had found her quite drunk, and in consequence he had had to do house- hold work and get the cnildren ready for school. On Wednesday last she left him for a whole day.—ln reply to Mr. Browne he said he could notgive his wife a great deal of attention on account of his business.— Vlr. Browne said it was a very sad case indeed. He contended that since the adjournment Mr. Skelton had not treked his wife properly. He would call a neigh- bour named Ars. Fogharty, who would tell them that she neglected her own home in order that she might do her best for 'Ers. Skelton. She would tell theta that she had not seen the slightest sign of anything wrong since the adjournment, and also that she catplained to 'Jr. Skelton on account of his habits.-34rs. Skelton corroborated Mr. Browne's staternent.—Mr. Browne .contended that she had faithfully carried out the agree- ment since the adjournment.—Mrs. Fogharty said that 'Jr Skelton had not the slightest ground for complaint about his wife's conduct since the adjournment.— rhe Bench dismessed the case,'aud the Chairman gave some advice to the parties concerned.

ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
"The Christian."__

• Warrington people have this week been afforded an opportunity of seeing Mr. Hall' Caine's much-talked of play "The Christian," which is presented by Mr. Wentworth Croke's company. Whatever may be . said in criticism of he work, the powerfulness of its appeal to the a-vera , playgoer is unquestionable, and each evening there as been a large and enthusiastic audience. "The C. ristian "is a play with a mission. It is a ruthless exposure of the sins of a certain section of society and seeks to awakeii the public conscience to the existence of a terrible social evil which is depicted in lurid colours. Mr. Hall Caine's inten- tions are laudable enough but his suggested remedy, if such it can be called, merely touches the surface of the question' and is in fact, almost infinitesimal. Apart from the moral purpose of "The Christian " the chequered story of Glory Quayle, the charming Manx girl, who is lured from her native isle by the attractions of a stage life, is intensely interesting and there are highly dramaticasituations, particularly in the last act when Glory narrowly escapes death at the 'hands of the over-wrought John Storm. The honours of the evening undoubtedly go to Miss Doris Gilham whose portrayal of Glory Quayle is a triumph. Glory is a creature of moods, at one time lull of child-like franlmess and impetuosity, at another plunged into despair, and Miss Gilham's acting has that freshness and natural charm which capture the sympathies of the audience from the first moment she appears on the stage. A more realistic presentment of the 'mit could not be desired and Miss Gilham thoroughly deserves the praises which have nightly been lavished upon her. Mr. Henry .Renouf; as the Hon. John Storm, throws great vigour and earnestness into his version, in fact there is 4 tendency to over-do the declamatory passages. On the' whole; however, the portrayal is satisfactory. Mr. Oswald Marshall is eminently successful as Horatio Drake and Mr. George R. Mountford does justice .to the unenviable role of Lord Robert Ure. Mr. Edwin Ling is well-placed as the fearlessly out-spoken Father Lamplugh--a great favourite with the audience—and Mr.C. T. Turpin acts the sell-complacent Ar4leacon Wealthy to perfection. Miss Margaret Broady tives R pathetic study of Polly Love and Miss Katherine Maude finds great favour as the much-wronged and tender-hearted Lady Robet Ure. Mr. E. R. Hollway is good as Lord Storm. The minor pArts are all capably sustained and the mounting of the play is in the best of ttiste. Next Week's Programme.

div.head: VISIT OF "A COUNTRY GIRL."
div.p: VISIT OF "A COUNTRY GIRL."

On Monday the Royal Court Theatre-gbers are to have a visit of that great London success" A Country Girl." This charming piece, it will be remembered, ran for nearly 1,000 nights at Daly's Theatre, London, in fact its success stood as a record for this Theatre until the appearance of that wonderful " Merry Widow." The company presenting it is that of Messrs. Dudley Bennett and T. C, Wray's. Included in the part of "A Country Girl" is Miss Anna Hickisch who played the part of Nan for a considerable time at Daly's Theatre,London. Miss Victoria Sievers as "Marjorie," Miss Lucy Lever as the Princess (late Moody Manners Opera Company) a trio of exceptional singers. Mr. Jackson Hardy, also an artist of high repute, will play Mallorden, and Barry will be in the 'hands of Mr. Coningsby Brierley, An excellent exponent of the part. Miss Elfie Vincent, a young lady who has forsaken the halls for the theatres, will appear as Sophie. A. splendid operatic chorus is with the company and this together with a new production, should prove a wonderful draw for the coming week. The company arrive by special train on Sunday from Middlesboro', where they have been breaking all previous records in. hat town. t • -

div.head: WORKMEN S COMPENSATION. A Batch of Cases at the Warrington County Court..
div.p: WORKMEN S COMPENSATION. A Batch of Cases at the Warrington County Court..

An arbitration case under the Workmen's Compensa- tion Act 1906, was heard at the Warrington County Court on Thursday beforo His Honour Judge Shires 3 Will, K.C., in which Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. B.)tiebt for the termination or diminution of the com- pensation awarded to James Fleming, 13, Booth-street, on June sth 1908. Mr. Edward Wool) (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel) represented the respondent and Mr. Adshead Elliott (instructed by Messrs. Wood and Lord Manchester) was for the applicants. Mr. Adshead Elliott said the respondent wan a bar weigher formerly in the employ of Messrs. Monks Hall and Co. In December 1907, an accident occurred tat the works by which a bar of iron dropped on the great toe of the right foot,which was burst. When the wound healed, the toe bad to be amputated. The man's weekly earnings at the time were 375. 6d. and since Decenrber 4, 1907 he had received compensation at the rate of 18s. 9d., a week up to the present time. The present application was for the terminatien or the diminution of the compensation on the ground that incapacity had ceased, and Fleming could resume his work. Mr Elliott described the process of manufacture of the iron from the puddling furnace to the time it came into the hands of the bar weigher. He said the work of the latter involved a certain am6unt of muscular strength by the arms and bands. The man had been examined by Dr. Sankey who was of opinion that he was able to resume his work, as the ball of the toe was intact and that was where the real pressure in lifting was imposed. His employers were willing to take him back at the same wages as before.

Dr. William Sankey, Manchester, police surgeon of one of the divisions, said he examined James Fleming on January sth last. Fleming complained to him of pain when walking. The great toe of the right foot had been completely amputated. The ball of the toe was intact. The Man could stand upon each the individually. There was no pain upon handling the stump. The region of the "amputation was quite healthy and completely healed, and though respondent complained of pain, witfieSs could not discover any- thing to account for that. Witness said he thought he was fit to go hack to his work. By Mr. Wool! : He considered the man fit to go to work since the wound of the operation healed. Witness did uot know that since the orieinal opera l ion the respondent had undergone two other operations. A man could balance himself with equal success if jUi had lost both phlattges of his great the if the hell of the toe CMS intact. He thought a men could lift weights just as well without the phlanges os his ereat toe. Witness did not see the respondent use a wick when walkine and he did not think a stick was necessary. By Mr. Elliott: He had no doubt that the man should go bac to his work. Campbell Rohertson, insu-ance broker, Warrington, seid he knew Fle,nine, wh visitei witness every week. He had seen the respondent walk in the street some- times with a stick.

James Fleming, 48 years of age, said that he had been employed for more than thirty years at Nlessrs. Monks Hall and Co. In December 1907, he slipped on some iron billets and the bar he was carrying fell on his toe. He was in hospital on the first occasion for 15 days, when his toe was ampotited. Tn September 1908, he again went into the hospital and was operated upon on September 26th. He remained in the hospital for four weeks and afterwards continued as an nut-patient until January Ist of this yeir. He could not walk far with- out a stick. The bars he had to handle weighed from one to two cwts. They were cool when carried. Witness could not do tbe wot k at present because he could not stand up on his foot as his knuckle bone pained him. In answer to Mr. Elliott, witness said he was not in any club, and 18s. 9d. was the only money he had been drawing- He had never asked the firm to take him back. It was impossible for him to do the work of bar weighing.

Dr. Ferguson spoke to exa-nining Fleming and found his right foot apparently in a very good condition, as it had healed uo very nicely. He required a stick when walkin7, owing to a 'feeling of uns.cority when walking. He could scarcely imagine the respondent being asked to do anything that he was less able to do than to go back to his own work. He (the doctor) was of the opinion that Fleming could not do any work which required him to stand. There was a certain amount of unomployrnent in Warringtno.nd he thought the respond nt in his present condition would have hardly any chance of obtaining work. If he obtained work he was not likely to retain it. His work in future must be something sitting or else something where the pressure was on the heel. By Mr. Elliott: The scab looked very well healed and as far as could he seen from the outside there was nothing to account for the pain. _ _

For the respondent it was contended by Mr. Wooll that there had .been nothing whatever to suggest any malingering on the p trt of the respondent. The appli- cants had not proved thtt there was any reasonable chance of the respondent obtaining work anywhere in Warrington. The only offer made by them was to resume his old work which the respondent could not perform. Mr. Elliott pointed out that the total incapacity had ceased and he Was not therefore justified in receiving the maximum compensation. His Honour said there was no evidenne that the man could go back to his old work and the applicants hd also failed to prove what work he could do. He there- fore gave judgment for the respondent and awarded costs under Schedule B.

Notice of appeal was given. • A further application was made to terminate or diminution of the amount of compensation awarded to Thomas Massey, 7, Hood-lane, Sankey. Mr. Adshetd Elliott who represented the applicants, said the man was previously employed by Messrs. Monks Hall, Co. He met with the accident on May 25th, 1907. He was carrying a railway chair weighing _ _ _ _

561hs. on his shoulder when it fell forwards and cii.ughi, the open palm of his left hand, crushing it. Compensation had been paid regularly since at the rate of Bs. 9d. weekly. Relief was now sought on the ground that the man was so far recovered as to he able practically to earn the same wagea as previously. The doctor would toll them that the little and rin,z finger was also somewhat stiff bat flexible to a certain extent. The man was only a labourer earning 17s. 6d. a week, and his employers ware willing to offer him employment of a light nature such as tidying up and give him 10s. a week. Mr. Cuthbert Smith (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel) who appeared for the respondent said he had never heard of any offer made previously. Mr. Elliott : You have it now. _.._

Mr. Cuthbert Smith: I am brought here having failed previously to get any offer. t h Lye no doubt my client will be glad to get his work back. A consultation between the parties culminated in Mr. Cuthbert Smith remarking that the offer was acc3ptel. . _

His Honour on the understanding that the employers would provide ernplornent at 10.3. per week, reduced the compensation to 3s. 9d. weekly. , A similar application was made with respect to com- pensation paid to James Thomis Wbolley. It was stated by Mr. Elliot that in view of the course taken by his Honour in the previous cases he asked for an adjournment of the case to some future date, became in this particular case owing to the present slackness of trade he was not at present able to offer the respondent his old employment. He had no evidence as to what he was able to do elsewhere."
Ntr. Cuthbert Smith said the respondent had tried to obtain work else Nhere. He asked that the case be dismissed.
His Honour said he could not take the course asked by Mr. Elliott and he should dismiss tne application.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.

The members and friends of the Bewsey-road Wesley Guild listened with unususl interest to a lantern lecture entitled " A Guild holiday in Norway," by Dr. Bennett, in the Lecture Hall on Monday evening. Mr. Frank Norman occupied the chair. The lecturer spent a holiday with the Wesley Guilds of this country at the time of the Emperor of Germany's visit to Norway. Dr. Bennett bad the happy experience of snapshotting the Emperor, and when he (Dr. Bennett) lent his camera to a friend he was afforded a double' hanpy experience of having the members of Padgate Guild taken with the Emperor himself. Tte smartness of Dr. Bennett's friend afforded pleasure and amusement to the "Guilders"

as they looke I at the scene upon the screen. The doctor described his visit in an admirable manner, the slides helping to mike his hearers fe4 as if they were spending a holiday in Norway themselves. NI r. itchell proposed a vote of thanks to the Doctor and the Rev. E. B. Keeling seconded, the resolution being heartily endorsed by those present.

div.head: St. Paul's Church House.
div.p: St. Paul's Church House.

The Hon. Secretaries (Messrs. J. W. Robinson and A. C. Binks) in their sixth annusl report sttted that the club was commenced in D.cember, 1902, and from its opening has been a splendid addition to the parish. It affords to the different organizations of the church a splendid opportunity to ,meet, together in social recreation. It affords to the young men a safe and sure place wherein to spend a pleasant evening, free from all influences detrimental to their characters. There have been two tournaments during the year, and they have been the means of greatly improving the steadiness of the members in billiards, as well its adding grist to the mill. The winners of the first tournament were: 1, Addison; 2, Bennett ; 3, Sloane; 4, H. Parkes; 5, Bailey; 6, Deakin. Winners of second tournament : 1, H. Parkes; 2, Sloane ; 3, H, Perks ; 4, E. Alarms, %V. Bobbington, T. Addison (tie 74.07). Handicap winners: A. Eland end T. Seed. Alatches had been played with the following clubs :—Parish Church (Whist and Billiards'), Widnes St. Nfary's Nos, 1 'and 2 Teams, Padgate, St. Clement's, St. George's and Whitecross S. and R.O. The year has been a succe4sful one. and it is hoped the ensuing year will be marked with the same appreciation as the one just passed. The committee thank the firm of Pearson and Knowles for so kindly decorating the billiard room, making it clean and bright.

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Church.

The Rev. Thomas Miller preached on Sunday night to a good congregation in told-street Wesleyan. Church. He took as his.subject " A great choice," his text being 'taken from Hebrews xi. 24-26. The rev, gentleman specially addressed himself to young people and instanced Moses' decision in choosing a life of hardship and of service in preference to one of else. Moses was an example of true nobility. As a young man he retained his purity, his love of freedom, and religion. Egyptian influences were weaker than his religions principles. Amongst an idolatrous people he retained his faith, and preferred an emancipator's life. His religion was patriotic. He saw his kinsmen as children of God, even whilst in slavery. His labours for their elevation were inspired by idetlism. The young people were urged to take an interest in the welfare of their country. Politics must not be fors 'ken. but purified. However, religion must not be sacrificed for politics and the politics must ever be subordinated to the faith. In conclusion he annealed to the young people not to place too high a value upon the comforts and ease of life. They should take more interest in everything that would make for the improvement of the lot of others. those who had fallen, and these who Were redeemed by, the blood of 'Christ.
--During the service thq choir rendered Gounod's "Come unto Him" very effectively.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

There was a good attendance at the 16th anniversary which was an open meeting on Sunday afternoon last. The Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Porshaw) presided and said be felt it both a pleasure and a duty to come and preside over a meeting of that kind. He-also felt. a deep interest in the work And service of their President and the Pastor of Wycliffe Church, who did not confine all his services to the church to which he belonged hut was of great service in the town generally, especially to the Infirmary and Nurses Institu- tion. The early instruction he . (the Mayor) received in the Church in his youth had never left him. That moral of spiritual teaching he had tried to carry out in a straightforward life. He wished the P.S.A. at Wycliffe a happy and prosperous tear upon which they had now just entered.—Mr. John Harrison. of Liverpool, gave a most useful and stirring address upon "True manliness." The physique, intelligence and popularity did not always make manly men. A true manly man was a virtuous man, a Christlike man, an all round man, good at hothe, good abroad, good and faithful in service. He gave some good advice to young rnenfindlwomen present, especially in shaping their lives for the future' in the craoosing of partners in life. Many lives had been blighted and many ruined, because they could ~ot say "No" at the right time. The secretary read a letter from the Rev. John Yong° who was suffering from a severe cold, saying how sorry he was not to be present to welcome the Mayor and also Mr. Harrison on that Anniversary day. The secretary moved a vote of sympathy and condolence with Mrs. Birch and family of Great Sankey, on the death of her husband and father who helped in the formation of Wycliffe P.S.A. over 16 years ago, and who had for some years taken part in its work. Mr. Farrar referred to the interesting fact. that tke first meeting ,to inaugurate this society was held on November 12th, 1890. In consequence of the epidemic of small pox, the opening was deferred wadi Marph sth, 1893. Mr. Bishop, of Whalley Range Calleee, And Mr. C. Eccles, also took part in the meeting. Mr. A. Hale sang" For all Eternity" and " Lend me your aid" which were much enjoyed. Mr. W. Rutter gave a cornet solo "Me Better Laud "in skilful style. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mt's. BAC. presided at the otaan. A most enjoyable meeting was closed by the singing of "I will guide Thee with mine eye."

div.head: Buckley-street P.S A. Mrs. Crosfield Presents the Prizes.
div.p: Buckley-street P.S A. Mrs. Crosfield Presents the Prizes.

The llth anniversary of the Buckley-street P S.A., for men and wo nen was celebrated last week-end. There was a large gati;Prina of friends on Sunday afternoon, over which Mr. W. Evans presided, and gave an interest- ing address on" Actions. Mr. Edwin Plinston gave an encouraging address on "Toe Tongue." Miss Silcock's solos. " Nearer my God to Thee" and " The-Heavenly Song" were well given and received with enthusiasm. NTiss NI. Plinston was an efficient accompanist. At the conclusion of the meeting 25 new members were enrolled.

On Monday afternoon about 180 members and friends sat down to an enjoyable tea, and afterwards the prize distribution and concert took place. Mrs. A. H. Crosfield distributed the prizes and Mrs. Charles Simpson presided. Supporting her on the platform were :—Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes, and Mrs. Letheren, Mrs. Orosaeld gave a brilliant pianoforte solo, which was applauded so much that she obliged with another. Nlr. W. Dutton was seen to advantage in " The Village Blacksmith, and M ss L Plinston delighted the audience with her song" The Gatos of the West." Miss C4rrie Hastings sang" Bid me discourse" and for an encore " Home, sweet home." Mr. G. Memben played a Bombard on solo entitled" l'he Children's Home."

Airs. SIMPSON tsaid, they ought to feel highly honoured at Mr. and Ars. Prosfield's presence. When the Society was formed they had 50 me nbers, now they were 200 strong. In connection with the Society they hsd a benevolent fond, whereby members who were ill, in trouble, or needed help, received help. The Society along with the Sunday school had bought the piano, which cost £BO, for the churvh. rhey had in the church now, workers who had been brought in by the P.S.A. movement, and they were a great benefit. (Applause). Mrs. CROSFIELD, who was enthusiastically received, said it was a pleasure for her to go there and hear about the admirable work they were doing for progress. She had lived in the East for a good time, and she knew something of the religious beliefs of the Dancing Dervishes and the Mohammedans. The Mohammedans were very devout people ; but they did some of the most curious things. In their worship they made some of the most gruesome sounds—they literaly howled.

Their howling in many cases OOntinued for hours and without them feeling it. Some of them on a certain day in the year formed a procession and cut each other with knives in a most horrible manner. The Moham- medans were very pious and prayed three or four times a day, leaving their business or anything else—however important—to go and pray. It would be very much better if instead of that grusome worship they stretched forth a helping hand to their brothers. (Loud applause). Mrs CIIoSFIELD then distributed some of the prizes. Mr. Straw (President of the P.S.k.) said that on Sunday they first gave the pure Gospel, second they gave all members a hearty welcome, third, they gave the best speakers, fourth, the best solos, and fifth the best books. They had got very big for 18 years old. They had certainly cut their wisdom teeth—(laughter) and they were on the right road to progress, and God helping them they would prosper. (Applause.) Mrs. Crosfleld had been speaking to them about the religion of foreign countries. It was very strange that their Committee decided to present her with' two books called "The living races of mankind." (Applause.) It was the first time they had seen Mr. and Airs. Crosfield in Buckley-street, and they hoped shortly to have them again. (Loud applause.) Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD said his wife had asked him just to say a word or two on her behalf, as she had already made a very much better speech than he could attempt to do. (Laughter.) It was only fair that there should be a little division of labour—or division of pleasure— and that he should on her behalf say just a word of thanks for the extremely interesting and comprehensive books that had just been presented to her. She would value them even more because of the kindnesses and the real hearty welcome they had given to her that evening. It really was quite a little coincidence that her speech should touch upon those diversities of race and religion which were comprised in the books presented to her. He did not mind telling theia. that he was with her a spectator of both the dancing Dervishes and the howl- ing Mohammedans. Those poor people were sincere enough, and certainly amongst the Mohammedans they found a wonderful amount of religious sincerity, but it was very different from what religion was in this country. Still, there were many ways of making their way to heaven. In conclusion, he said it had been such a pleasure for them to go into such a splendid gather- ing and for his part, and his wife's part, he thought our friends in the East would be wiser if they thought perhaps a little less about the working out of their own salvation, and took a leaf out of our books, and helped each other. (Applause). Mrs. CROSFIELD then distributed the rest of the prizes, and the Doxology concluded the meeting.

div.head: Baptist Church, Golborne-street. Minister's Anniversary.
div.p: Baptist Church, Golborne-street. Minister's Anniversary.

Special services in celebration of the first anniver- sary of Rev. R. E. Letheren's settlement as minister were held on Sunday. Brightness was evidently the order of the day; the flowers that set off the pulpit being but a symbol of the feeling in the hearts of the people. The sermon in the morning seemed at first to strike another note. The subject was "A minister's milestone" and the text ii. Cor. iv. 16, "We faint not." But after an apt introduction Mr. Letheren showed that tbough it seemed a little thing to say it was in reality a great deal. • In the Christian life continuance is triumph. The words,quiet as they are,speak of a con- quest of circumstances little short of sublime. They revell a courage that the most malignant foes were not able to master. They are instinct with a stroag conviction that steadfastly resists all temptations to compromise. They breathe a serene confidence that spite of waning enthusiasms around "bates not a jot of heart or hope but still bears up and steers right onward." These thoughts amplified with appropriate illustrations, of which one was Matthews Arnold's Sonnet of the Spitalfields preacher, served to make the somewhat sombre text yield a messagp heartening and u'plifting, and more than one bore witness to its helpfulness. In the evening the subject was " The Snow of Lebanon," Jeremiah 18-14, and a special feature of the service was the delightful rendering by the Orpheus Quartette of "Perfect in Christ" and "The long day closes." Mr. Letheren made a brief reference to his first year's ministry in Warrington. Thanking those who had helped to make the day's ser- vices so cheerful, he added, "I shoeld like also to record my sincere appreciation of the very kind words of confidence and approval to which the members of the Church gave expression through all the deacons at, the Church meeting last Thursday evening ; a meeting at which it was a pure and unalloyed pleasure to be present.; a meeting fragrant with the atmosphere of friendliness and good fellowship lam very thankful for that meeting ; quite as thankful for the proof it I afforded of the appreciation the Church manifestly has of Mrs. Letheren's work as of my own. I ant the more thankful because the expressions of opinion were unexpected and informal, and therefore the more likely to be genuine. I am most thankful because although the opinions confirmed my own observation yet I mtvt confess I have been more than a little anxious. 'The story of the past Came up before my view. Should it be said to suit us still? • Old and yet ever new.' So far at any rate last Thursday night's meeting confirmed me in the belief that the Church means to go forward and looks upon the work done this year as moving upon lines that seem likely to lead to success. Thirty new members have been added during the 12 months and others are moving forward. That is in itself some- thing to he very thankful for. At the close of the firsi, year of this minktry both church and minister may 'Thank God and take courage.' Services in continuation of the Minister's Anniversary were held on Thursday evening when Rev. J. E. Roberts MA., 8.D., of Manchester, preached a much appreciated sermon. The attendance was good. The text was Mark ix. 28-29, "Why could not we cast him oilit ?" The preacher referred to the general discussion of the "Arrested Progress of the Churches" and said that it did not mean that churches had ceased to give or to work. They had never been busier. And vet the work was not done which most wanted doing. The forces of liquor, gambling and greed flaunted themselves before us. The Church was in the world to accomplish a Divine mission. The world would believe in it when they saw it was doing what nothing else could do. The t lta rch was on trial and if it is to con- tinu it must prove its worth. What w.is the Maser doing during his absence on the Mount? He AS praying. The disciples were not. Prayer is the divi ing force in spiritual work. It is not a luxury. It

is a necessity. It puts men into contact with the springs of power. It needs the powet of God to drive out devils. It is for the church to transform and transmit the love of God into healing energies for men, to bring it to where it is needed and in what form it is noeded. The prayer life of the individual and of the church is the measure of their public service. The choir rendered the anthem " Lift up your heads." Mr. S. Rickets presiding at the organ.

div.head: Spiritualist Society. .
div.p: Spiritualist Society. .

Mr. J. Henley, ol Manchester, delivered addresses at the meeting of the Warrington Spiritualist Society on Sunday, this being the first visit. In the afternoon he gave a brief adclress on "Prayer," followed by clairvoyance. In the evening there was 'a good con- gregation, and after giving a recital of" A Legend of Chertsey," with considerable elocutionary ability, Mr, Henley spoke forcibly on "Spiritual progress." Omi Monday evening, Mrs. Griffiths gave a large number of clairvoyant descriptions and psychometric readings.

div.head: ALLAN LINE ENTERPRISE.
div.p: ALLAN LINE ENTERPRISE.

IMPROVEMENTS TO A POPULAR STEAMER. The famous Royal Mail tyrbine steamer, Virginian which sailed from Liverpool for Halifax and St. John, N. 8., last Friday, has on board about a thousand passengers. This is her first voyage since lying up for the winter, during which opportunity was taken to re-decorate her throughout, and to alter and improve two of her apartments. What was pr6viously the saloon music from has been transformed into a most seductive lounge and cafe. It is an extremely comfortable room, luxuriously furnished with easy chairs, settees, and handy tables, a notable feature being the profusion of plants, charmingly arranged, which considerably enhance the appearance of the room. The library has been arranged as a retiring-room or boudoir for ladies. It will prove especially attractive to passengers who appreciate a quiet hour in a comfortable armchair with a favourite book.

div.head: DOWAGER EMPRESS OF RUSSIA.
div.p: THE DOWAGER EMPRESS OF RUSSIA.

Our photograph was taken last autumn when Queen Alexandra was in Denmark. Beside her is the Dowager Empress of Russia, who has just arrived on her annual visit. Her Imperial Majesty crossed from Calais to Dover in the Royal yacht Alexandra and was received with an imposing naval welcome. At Victoria the Prince and Princess of Wales met the illustrious visitor. She is now in deep mourning for the Grand Duke Vladimir, her brother-in-law, and on that account she will not be seen at theatres and picture galleries as in previous years. Her stay will be spent chiefly at Sandringham and in the Isle +DI Wight.

While attempting to enter Portsmouth Harbour, after carrying out exercises in the Solent, the submarine known officially as Al 2 went on the Haslar Wall and, as the tide was falling, was forced to remain in that undignified position for some hoars. The spot is a soft mud bank close to the creek where boats of the class are ordinarily stationed. The Photograph shows the members of the-crew making the vessel secure with hawsers so as to prevent any possibility of her heeling over and so doing heavy damage. Fortunately nobody was hurt as a result of the accident, and, as was expected, the midnight tide lifted the submarine so that she could be got off. So far as has been reported, no injury was done to the vessel,

A most regrettable accident, of which there seems to have been no other cause than con- tinuous bad weather, brought about the death of fourteen labourers at Birkenhead. They were Working on a night shift in an excavation immediately behind an immense dam protecting the new dock, which would now be practically finished but for the addition of the Great 9ates. With no more than a moment's warning the wall of timber, soil, and clay cracked in the centre. Voluni"s of water rushed through, swirling and filling the-pit where the men were imprisoned. One only of these and the crane man and boy escaped in marvel- lous fashion. The rest still lie buried under the debris, but attempts are being Made by divers to recover their bodies.

Mr. E. Plinston %as re-elected a member of the Education Committee for the next three years. Mr. Plinston has been a member of the committee for six years and he was h,mrtily thanked for his services. MR. HAMPSON'S CANDIDATURE.

Mr. PLUMB proposed the endors.t.ment of the candida- ture of Mr. James Hampson in respect to Orford Ward election. Last November he fought fairly, and it had been proved without question that the others did not fight fairly. Mr. HALEY in seconding, said that Mr. Hampson was the one man in the contest who fought with clean hands. He was in the hope that both political parties in the town would have held their hands and allowed Mr. Hqmpson a clean walk-over. Many people had said that what they considered a fair and reasonable issue would have been that Mr. Harnpson should have taken the place of those two candidates.
