div.head: TALES OF A COUNTYWOMAN.
div.p: TALES OF A COUNTYWOMAN.

"One day last Summer," writes my friend the naturalist," "I was far out on the Moors, away from the furthest fringe of civilisation—and I was woefully hungry. Coming upon a one-storeyed cottage, packed away in the shelter of a small coppice, I knocked at the door, and, after a minute, was admitted by an apple- faced old dame, who bad an unmistakable odour of baked cakes about her cotton-gown. I may live to be ninety, but fashall never forget the taste of the currents in that good woman's girdle-cakes Ever since that day I have made a practice of eating currant girdle-cakes whenever and wherever possible, and hive found them the most satisfying and delicious of all cakes."

div.head: FWARRINGTON CHAPTERS.
div.p: FWARRINGTON CHAPTERS.
WARRINGTON AND THE CIVIL WAR.

Speculation concerning what might have been is always alluring and to no one more than the student of history. In the life of nations as of individuals great events have turned upon small, and great currents have been deflected in their courses by small impediments. There is a great " might have been " in the story of the Civil War, and as it touches Warrington in a peculiar way the facts can hardly fail to interest our readers.

The early months of 1642 found King Charles I. in a desperate position. He had demanded the arrest of five members of the House of Commons and the Commons had refused to give them up. London seethed with discontent and its streets were filled by day and night with armed men. Upbraided as a coward by his Queen, Charles fled to York, and those who sympathised with him began to flock to his side.
These things are matters of familiar history and need not be mentioned except in reminder. It is with the inner and hitherto untold history that we are here concerned.

Among those who joined the King was Lord Strange of Knowsley, heir to the earldom of Derby. The York Conference was momentous, for the subject of discussion was the setting up of the Royal Standard and the organization of the Civil War. With London under the power of Parlia- ment Charles had to choose a centre of operations to which he could best gather his army and which for the time would be his capital. Many places were mentioned as having great advantages. The claims were urged of York, Chester, Shrewsbury, Oxford and Nottingham, but from the multitude of counsellors one voice spoke with clearness and conviction. WARRINGTON CHOSEN AS HEADQUARTERS.

"With • humble submission" said Lord Strange" I conceive Lancashire to be the better place as a centre to which the loyal parties can gather from Yorkshire, Cumber- land, Westmoreland, Cheshire, Shropshire, North Wales and Notts." He urged the loyal disposition of the people and promised that he himself, though the unworthiest of His Majesty's lieutenants,would contribute 3,000 foot and 500 horse at his own expense, and made no doubt that he could in a few days enlist 7,000 more. The burden of the speech was that by rallying at the quickest speed they could reach London before Parliament could furnish its•army and by their presence make good the King's claim to rule his people. The speech and argument prevailed. When it came to the choice of a centre, the Council accepted the opinion of Lord Strange that Warrington should be the Kings head- quarters, and that his standard should be raised there without delay. Charles issued his famous order to "array, train and muster the people" and the Civil War had begun. Lord Strange was even better than his word. He raised in central Lancashire no less than 20,000 pike men, and before long could show a total of 60,000 men gathered in Lancashire alone by his influence. He was proceeding to call out-the forces of Cheshire and North Wales with the same energy when a most unhappy experience befell him. His absence from the King's presence gave opportunity to envious tongues, and Charles was induced to believe that ,Lord Strange had other than loyal intentions in raishig these huge forces of battle. It was s}lggested that he had designs upon the crown and hoped to snatch it in the day of turmoil. The close connection of the Derby family with Royalty lent colour to the report, and it was argued that too much power ought not to fall into such hands. CHARLES' FOLLY.

The conduct of the King at this most critical period forces to mind the Rornan proverb that "whom the gods would destroy they first make mad." Charles was always pliable and easy going and quite unequal to the desperate campaign he had entered upon; but upon this occasion it would seem that his last gleam of judgment left him. At the request of the envious helpers at his feet he renounced the absent lord' who was doing more for his cause than all the rest combined. There is nothing in the corres- pondence to show that Lord - Strange had opportunity to make a defence. Upon the advice of jealous gossips Charles drove from his side the most powerful and loyal helper his cause possessed. , Warrington had already become abnor- mally busy by reason 'of the men and horses gathered and in training, when by order of the King the arrangement was cancelled.

The same order fixed Nottingham as the centre of operations, appointed Lord Rivers to act with Lord Strange in the lordship of Lancashire, and placed Lord Strange as lieutenant of Cheshire and North Wales. Deep disappointment fell upon the men of Lancashire. Disgusted at the insult heaped upon 'their leader they returned to their homes and decided to remain neutral. ' Others in the warmth of their indignation joined the Parliamentary forces. Lord Strange would have been more than human if he had not felt the slight. By the folly of the King his work was undone, his troops melted rapidly and he was left a disappointed man. It says much for his sincerity that his loyalty rose above the slight. He him- self was reduced to impotence and almost to despair, but his belief in the cause was not affected by personal suffering. In striking contrast from' the pitiable folly of the King is the devotion of hi follower. "Let my master be happy though I am miserable" he wrote, "and if they consult well for him I shall not be much concerned what becomes of me. If my prince and my religion be safe, I shall bless even mine enemies who do well for them, though in my ruin." That Charles should have had such devotion and failed to recognize it is a sufficient explanation of what befel him.

div.head: FATAL LOSS OF TIME.
div.p: A FATAL LOSS OF TIME.

J. a. • - _ Five months later, on August 25th, the Royal Standard was raised at Nottingham. The King was present, and everything was done to make the occasion impressive. But the troops did not arrive as was expected, and Charles quickly realized his danger: His unwisdom towards Lord Strange seems to have early come home to him, for there is preserved a long letter written in his own hand, by which he urges him to bring the men of Lancashire to his help. Lord Strange responded nobly, but five months of delay and diappointment had made great changes. Manchester had been seized by the Parlia- mentarians and Lancashire, bitterly resent- ing the King's treatment, was neutral. From his own tenants he raised three regiments and led them to the King at Shrewsbury. The long march was no sooner accomplished than the King sent him to capture Man- chester. The men were led back and the siege organized, but before the attack could be made a letter came from Charles demand- ing that he should instantly return to help the King at Shrewsbury against Lord Essex.

He arrived to receive a crowning indignity. By Royal order he was removed from the command of his Lancashire regiment. Smarting and indignant Earl Stanley (he had now succeeded to the title) said, "Sire if I have deserved this indignity, • I have also deserved to be hanged, and if it had come from any man living except the King I would have pitched the calumny from his lips with the point of my sword." Charles' hour of opportunity was past. Delay and folly had given time and strength to the Parliament and Cromwell arose to weld troops of Iron- sides which Charles could never break. Of the situatiOn that arose through Lord Derby's desposition and how Parliament approached him when at Warrington, we may tell in some future chapter. For the present it is enough to reflect upon the might have been." • As far as the facts and forces can be measured it seems probable almost to the point of certaintST that Charles' cause would have triumphed and the course of English ' history been strikingly changed if the Standard had been reared at Warrington instead of Nottingham. [I have to acknowledge indebtedness to the late Earl Derby and his librarian for access to the information upon which the foregoing narrative is based.] A.M.

div.head: OUR MISCELLANY.
div.p: OUR MISCELLANY.

It has come as a pleasant surprise to our readers to learn that Hill Cliffe is Lewis Carroll's Wonderland and many expressions of interest have reached us. The story told by Mr. John Naylor of the dedication of the "conic sections book is'explained in the fact that Lewis Carroll was a tutor in mathematics. A similar story is told of a gentleman who was so delighted with " Alice " that he ordered the publisher to send anything else he might write. He was amazed to receive in due course a volume full of abstruse discussion upon conic sections and the differential calculua. ** * *

An article • in " Harper's Magazine" renews the reminder that there is an interesting side to our vulgar dialect. It is written by Professor Lounsbury under the title "Archaic Speech of the Uneducated." As the Professor dwells on the other side of the Atlantic he is remote from English dialects, and those of us who live in daily contact with one of the most interesting of them could give him points innumerable to illustrate his theme. The examples given are mostly from South country dialects. We imagine that he could have built up a much more interesting article had he studied our Northein speech. ** * *

To take an example which comes first, I have just heard an errand boy assuring a friend that they "never gave me nothing to bring back." His schoolmaster had doubtless told him many a time that a double negative becomes a positive and that such expressions are an abuse of English. But tradition is stronger than the schoolmaster.

In the days of Chaucer the errand boy's sentence would not only be counted good but commendable. Take Chaucer's own method of giving the emphatic negative. He never vet no villainy ne said In all his life unto no rnaimer wight.
In modern English we should say that "he never used any abusive language to any kind of person." Chaucer however uses four negatives never no ne and no and the effect is cumulative and crushing.

The custom of multiplying the negatives to give emphasis is one of the commonest things in vulgar speech. When we hear a mother—as I have done—warning her girl to " never do no such thing never again while she lives," we may solace ourselves 'with the reflection that five centuries ago it was good grammar and would have been yet if somebody hadn't brought in new rules. * *

To mention only one other survival, Lancashire people often make their plural by adding en. In our accepted Eng Hash this lingers in oxen and children, but in the older language both nouns and verbs formed their plural in this way. Thus Chaucer When they from riehesse aren throwe Fully to knowen, withouten were. They maken foolis glorifye. One has but to linger among the colliers of Wigan or ,Westhoughton to hear these forms of speech in common use. The verbs take a distinct plural form as in Chaucer, and we have they know-en," "they went-en" or "sent-en." This is why the eyes are always the " een." ** * *

These bits of fossil speech are not so plentiful as they were, and with Education Acts at work may pass more rapidly than ever. My schoolmaster friends must forgive me if I say that I am half sorry at the prospect, for they are antiquities ancient as our oldest castles and not a whit less interesting. ** * *

A new fragment of Ruskin's prose is always welcome. I am able to give a characteristic passage by the courtesy of Messrs. Sotheby who • sold some autograph letters of his last week. This is how Ruskin spoke his mind to the vicar of Coniston on the subject of the Church of England clergy. " I must really put this matter of the church at rest between you and me, by speaking clearly out for good and all. There are not above half-a-dozen clergymen in the Whole number I know—whom I would not pay—if I had it—their annual stipends to if they would only hold their tongues—in the pulpit and out of it."

div.head: COMING SPRING
div.p: THE COMING SPRING

Ah ! never ending dome Of blue, With all the stars of night, Amid the short and stormy days, How blessed is your light. The sun is warm, the wind is cold When Spring and Winter meet; • The lofty mountains capped with snow, Warm sunshine at their feet. The heaven-descending spreading beams Grow warmer day by •day. Until the frosty morning winds With us no longer stay. Arising as from sleep of death Where all was bleak and bare When nature wakens into life What can with her compare. How welcome is returning Spring So sweet the sunny air And cheering are the longer days, When all is bright and fair. The brook goes rippling through the wood And warbling in the deli! The nesting birds in joyful notes Their songs of gladness tell. Ah yes, the earth in sprines gay With all her budding flowers, And passes with unfading charms To summer's happy hours. • S. KENYON
Ribbleton, March, 1909,
MY LIFE STORY.
ci)i-NCITA_,OR T. 13IRTLES

div.head: Early Warrington Recollections.
div.p: Early Warrington Recollections.

My life up to a short time ago has been one of attention to a profession demanding my personal application. I have lived devoting my time to this ! and to the claims of a numerous family. It is only in the evening of my life, when the shadows are lengthen- ing, that I realise how little 1 have done for my 'native town. This has made me resolve if I have an opportunity, to further any work taken in hand for the public good. . My ancestors belonged to a Cheshire family, settling in Warrington about '2OO years ago, and are buried in the graveyard of the old 'Parish Church, on the north side. The last one, my father, Edward Birtles, died in 1-848, aged 32. years. My grandfather Edward Birtles, was in the Battle of Trafalgar with Nelson and was slightly wounded by a cannon ball. (He carried the marks of this to the end). He afterwards returned with a pension and medal. Two of his brothers were in the American Wtir of Independence, one being shot from a ship's- rigging, dead. The others was killed in action. Another brother, Thomas, served in the Peninsular War, but he returned home without a scratch. He also received a medal with -pension. These four brothers were taken by the press gang from Liverpool while on business, and at once sent-to sea.-

I was born in Mersey-street and early went to a ' Dames' School, afterwards to the National SchooLand • the Blue Coat School as a day scholar,but my education really commenced after leaving school. My mother was left with four children on the early death of my father,and I being the eldest had to turn out. and com- mence work at about 12 years of age with Mr. Robert 'Garnett the founder of the firm of Garnett and Son, cabinet manufacturers, and grandfather of the present Mr. R. Garnett. The house I lived in has recently been pulled down, to make the new street through to Rylands-street. I lived here and in Sankey-steet for 'a period Of 50 years. On the advice of Mr. Owen . (father of Mr. W. Owen, architect) I joined the Mechanics Institute, Mr. Owen selecting for me my . books to read, from the. catalogue. I got in harness thoroughly and liking my work made rapid strides, Mr. Garnett giving me every encouragement and con- sideration. was at the first ~ meeting called, to consider the formation of a• school of design and listened to an address given by Mr. Hammersley, of Manchester, in the Old Academy, ori Art. Shortly , after the lecture, the school was formed and Mr. R. Collinson .from the Manchester School appointed first master. I became one of the early studtnts, Mr. Garnett paying my fee. My mind was made up to become a designer, and to this end I worked at the school all the time I could get in. Getting my drawings through (1 had a medal for freehand dra*ing) I was not long in learning the good news that I had got the Scholarship. and became pupil teacher under Mr. Collinson. Mr. Collinson soon afterwards got the appointment of Painting Master at South Kensington and removed to London, Mr. J. C. Thompson being appointed at Warrington. I thus became the Joint Assistant to Mr. Thompson, and it is with great pleasure I say that an unbroken friendship remained to the end. Mr. Garnett was very good in encouraging me, and I have in my house a writing desk he gave me, as the result of one of the prizes he offered for competition. The transfer of the school to the new building in Bold Street was made. and I attended the day classes as assistant two hours for three days in the week. I got settled in the new quarters at the Museum, working late with students like Warrington Wood and ' others, and being pressed for time to get works sent • for National Competition, I frequently kept the school • going after midnight. On one of these occasions more noise than usual being made, the Curator, Mr. Cooper (sleeping under our room) was roused to indignation and demanded to know what 1 was dis- turbing them for. He appeared in a long nightshirt, with a candle in his hand. The young men began to . laugh and make game of him. He left and brought a magistrate (Benjamin Pierpoint) from St,. Austin's to turn me out. After an eAplanation about the drawings. all was peace and he retired. Now came the turning point in my career. The , works I had sent:up were accepted for entrance as a Master in training at South Kensington with an allowance of salary. Ir went to London ' in .1856-7 tnal entered South Kensington. I had - three National schools , to visit each week .and give a blackboard lesson in freehand and model drawing. The first school I visited, singular to say, was St. George's in the East. Our late Rector the Rev. William Queckett had just been appointed from there to Warrington •Rectory. I did not remain long at South Kensington, returning to Warrington in a had state of health, and entering again the service of Mr. Robert Garnett. I was not . long settled before I got married to the eldest daughter of Mr. John Lon...shaw, photographer of Sankey- street. At this early history of photography, I could see a future for it. Looking out for an opening I settled upon Northwich and it was here I started to erect my first temporary studio. Wet plate photo- graphy meant work, and I had to make my own baths collodion and chemicals and prepare my own plates. Fiat a change to-day! I soon got a good connection, and in a short time I built a good and permanent studio and shop with work room—the first premises built in Cheshire of a permanent nnure for photo- graphy. About this time I had the satisfaction of being elected a member of the Northwich Local Board. I photographed the first salt mine lit up by electricity in the country, 28 years ago, in the Thompson Rock Mine, Witton, for The Hammond Electric Light Com- pany. In my profession I was receiving support from the leading county femilies of Cheshire for miles around. I kept in touch with Warrington and opened a studio at Market Gate over Mr. Eaude's music shop in" 4-878, keeping Warrington as a branch. On the death of Mr. Thomas Davies at 'Legh House, 'Mr. Robert Garnett purchased the whole of the premises. I again became a tenant of the family and built my . fourth studio in 1880. Whilst in Northwich I became acquainted with Mr. Edward Leader Williams, engineer to the river Weaver. He carried out the construction of the first hydraulic lift in the country, taking a boat from the upper canal and lower- ing it to the River Weaver. He was also an expert amateur photographer. Sir Edward Leader now of Ship Canal fame, on his appointment by the Canal Company commissioned me to take all process 'liews on the Canal. I had a free hand from Eastham to Irlam, where all the heavy • work was done. My work was the only series of views- accepted by the contractors. Under his orders 1 macje the set of views and prepared the folio that was presented to our Queen Victoria when she 'opened the canal I opened a branch studio in Knutsford, in conse- quence of my having the engagement with the Kimtsford County Prison to photograph prisoners. I had this contract with the Government of the day for some years. In the early stages I had many lively scenes with prisoners who evidently knew the law as well or better than the Governor. • To go into a few of these would take up too mach of your valuable space and therefore I must content myself with giving you just one. I was summoned very early to photograph some prisoners whose time was up. Being a wet morning I stood in the corridor watching them leave the chapel and I suppose I was looking dejected, for one of the prisoners serving 14 days for poaching met me a few weeks after this in Northwich crossing the street, and holding out his big hand exclaimed. : "My heart bled for thee lad, whatever

had ta been doing to get time at Old Gallop's Farm" (prison), it was Rodney Weedle, a notorious poacher. I walked in the procession of trades at the peace rejoicings in May 1856, this being a great day for Warrington—tournaments on the river, sculling matches and boat races, greasy pole climbing for legs of mutton, rough and tumble tilting„men falling over- board,. and struggling in the river: The boats started from Mondock Bay racing to Wilderspool Brewery and round by Walton Arches. Easter Day at that time was a great day for the factory girls, who use to rope the men at the bottom of Orford-street. When they saw a likely man coming along the road, the rope would enfold the victim, a dozen smart girls surrounding him with willing hands and , throwing him up by legs and arms crying out " All lift, all lift." They -generally managed to turn the victim over until his money came out of his pockets. Carol singing at Christmas was very much , favour, mixed choirs going to the various members of the congregation. " Hark the Herald • Angels sing" and " While Shepherds watch their flocks, by night" sung. by a good choir in the stillness of the night was a treat in those (lays, and a great loss to the present generation. Another musical treat was the celebrated Hunt's Band Billy "Hunt's Baud), with (accompaniments; the members forming a circle in the street and carrying a lamp on the top of a long pole played "Christians Awake" and" Hail smiling morn." The "Love feasts" at Friars Green Chapel, with the varied experiences of its members, were n delight to listen to. I Was at the laying of the foundation stone by Mr.Beamont of our Museum and Library and in my time all the buildings from St. Austin's to Bank Quay station have been built Standing ,on the Town Hall steps and looking South- West not a house save one in Slutchers' Lane, Arpley- street, existed, all being green fields with Cheshire in the distance. The Ship Building Yard at Bank Quay was in full swing at that time, building ships of the ocean. 1 saw the " Tayleur " launched with all the red, white and blue streamers floating in the breeze, :Cannot this last industry again flourish in our midst for we have the facilities and a good river? I was at the opening of Bold-street Chapel, and was working in the Chapel with workmen to the last moment of people coming in. The opening ceremony was a great day-for Wesleyans in Warrington. I heard the famous orator, J. B. Gough, deliver one of his great lectures on "Temperance " in this Chapel, and after the close of a famous peroration he was so exhausted they had to carry him to Mr. William Nield's house - wrapt in a blanket (Mr. Nield lived next to the shop now occupied by Mr. Gerrard) We had a few characters in the town, giving the lads fine sport. You might find some morning a barber's pole 4ken down .and fixed over some other premises, or a brass plate removed from one door and fixed upon another. The police had not come on the scene then. One morning at about 5.45 a coffin plate was kicking abont Sankey.street, having been -taken from a coffin used as a cupboard; this was broken up and thrown into the road.

We had only three policemen, Dan Dagnall being the Chief. One of these, ;lick Hayes. would clear Bridge Street on a Sunday afternoon and I have seen Irish labourers dart up passages and make for Friars Gate out of his way. He used a truncheon right and left, which to-day, would be brutal of course. I have fished- in our river and caught eels and dace, and drunk its waters when going to school. The packet stage was a busy scene with the " Jack Sharp con- veying to Manchester the fustian pieces from shops in town. This was one of the great industries of our town we had six cotton mills then. Boats at the the packet stage could be hired, 4and many a six- pennyworth have I had and a sail as far down as Walton Arches and back. Saturday afternoon was the time for the fishermen to go down the river to Hale Bank finking, and returning on Sunday afternoon with their catch of fluke. I have seen plenty of fish landed.

I remember the L. & N.-W. Railway low level being opened and the first station a Bank Quay called White Cross, and I had a treat to Sankey Bridges. I think the fare was 1 ld. There was a fair held at Bank Quay called Korgin Fair, toffee stalls, swing boats and nuts and gingerbreads, with an halfpenny staked on the red or white for nuts. There was only one cab on hire then, Allison's ('ab. Eagle and Child Yard, kept in use mostly by Mr. Beamont. The tradesmen wore tall bats, workmen all caps (no bowlers) the women poke bonnets and long cloaks. I was present at a Council meeting in 1848 when the Council Room was in Market Street over the Fire Engine Shed. I remember the Election of 1847 between Creenall and Allcard and the factory girls parading the town singing '` Greenall for ever, Alleard is a beggar." The post office wasa small place in Mill Street and a very primitive affair. I listened to the great debate between Mr. A. Mackie and Mr.Bradlaugh in the Old Music Hall. To conclude with a few brief biographical details I was elected a membei of the Council of the Sehool,of Art in 1889. This was an honour from the committee

I much appreciated after being a pupil. I am a member of the National Society of Professional Photographers of England and have been on the Council since.the formation some years ago. I was elected a member of the Royal Photographic Society of Great Britain and made a Fellow of the Society in 1895, a great honour then: I was elected to the Warrington Town Council in November last, and hope to be vouchsafed the opportunity of rendering some service there.
I cannot close these disjointed notes without tribute o the memory of a good woman—my late wife—a levoted mother to her childt,n. Hers was a sacrificing mture to all. Through her I am what I am.

div.head: ANOTHER CARROLL STORY Told by Mr. John Naylor.
div.p: ANOTHER CARROLL STORY Told by Mr. John Naylor.

Sir,---Your article in Saturday's impression re Lewis Carroll. ' A friend of mine once told me that one of the greatest pleasures of his life was to have known Lewis Carroll when at Oxford and that when be wrote "Alice ,Wonderland " the Queen (Victoria) was so delighted with it that she commanded him if .ever be wrote another book to dedicate it to her.

Lewis Carroll was at that time engaged on an abstruse work on conic sections and when it was _ published in book form it came out as "dedicated by express command to her most gracious Majesty, &c." The Queen expected another" Alice in Wonderland " and it is very doubt, 1111 whether she yank nay interest in " conic sections " but my friend cited this as characteristic of the man. Lewis Carroll he said did not like the Sea and when at Oxford wrote a sea dirge which was published at the time but he said was now out of print. I enclose you a copy of it.

div.head: Yours truly,
div.p: Yours truly,
JOHN NAYLOR

Beeston Towers, Tarporley, March Bth, 1909. , A SEA DIRGE. There are some thing like a spider, a Ghost, The Income Tax, Gout, an umbrella for three, That I hate, but the thing I hate the most, Is a thing they call the sea. Pour some salt water over the floor, Ugly I'm sure you'll allow that to be, Suppose it extended a mile or more, That would be like the sea. Beat a dog till he howls outright, -- Cruel, but all very well for a spree, Suppose that he did so day and night, That would be like the sea. . I had a vision of nursery maids, Tens of thousands paAlrl by me, Each carrying children with wooden spades, And that was by the sea. Who eould havVinvented those spades of wood? Who was it cut them out of the tree? None, I think, hut an idiot could— Or one who loved the sea. , It is pleasant and dreamy, no doubt, to float, With thoughts as boundless, and souls as free, But suppose you are very unwell in. the boat— Then how do you like the sea? Would you like coffee with sand for dregs? A decided hint of salt in your tea? And a fishy taste in the very eggs? Then by all meal; choose the sea. And if, with such nties to drink and eat, You prefer not a vestige of grass or a tree, And a chronic condition of wet in your feet, Then-1 recommend the sea. There is an animal people avoid, Whence is derived the verb to flee; - Where have you been by it most annoyed? In lodgings by the sea. Once I met a friend in the street, With wife•and nurse and childreifthree ; Never again such a sight may I meet, As that party from the sea ! Their looks were sullen, their steps were slow, Convicted felons they seemed to be,— • " Are you going to prison, dear friend ?"—" Oh no, We're returning from the sea."

div.head: SYNOPSIS.
div.p: SYNOPSIS.

HraRY GISTONARD, a student of sculpture in Paris, nas been left a fortune of seven thousand pounds a year on condition tnat he is earning five hundred pounds a year by his own labour and talent by the time he is twenty-five. If that condition is unfulfilled the money is to go to a cousin. Gastonard is now twenty-four, and there seems to be no prospect of his ever receiving the fortune. lie wr,tes to his friend Paddy O'Connell telling of his acquaintance with Mimi—" The Show Girl "—and an ad- venture with a gang of Apaches, who attack him in Paris, having designs upon a gold and diamond cigarette-case which they think be carries, but which is actually in Mimi's possession.

div.head: CHAPTER I. (Continued).
div.p: CHAPTER I. (Continued).
[Being a letter from Henry Gastonard of the Maiklon du bon Talmo at Paris to his friend Paddy O'Connell of Glendalough, County Wicklow.]

Had there been but two or three there gathered together, I don't doubt they would hdve dealt with us as men deal with chickens at Easter; but their very numbers, defeated a set purpose, and the lights of the cabaret forbade a murder.. For • a little while we swayed about as a ship caught in a vortex; the lamps, shone down upon faces besotten with drink or fired by greed; I could see the room behind us. the figure of the patron who still gesticulated, the gaunt form of Jean-le- Mont now risen to his feet; and it seemed to me to take the place of a pleasant harbour one had quitted in despair. Then I think a ruffian tried to pull me down from behind; but the press was too close, and I caught nis hand in mine and went near to breaking nis wrist. This was a mistake, for he also pos- sessed a knife, and drew it, and it needed an iron hand upon his throat to silence him. I am going deeper than I meant intcf these police-court news, Paddy, chiefly that you may understand my present difficulty with Mimi La Godiche. Let me tell you that when the fun really, began, when fists were busy and hats were flying down the Butte, when the women shrieked and fled and the men called upon their fellows to make an end pf us, I discovered that she had .friends, even among such as these, that she could call them by their gutter-names and that they would answer her. It may be that many of them hung back just because it was Mimi of the booths and the files foraines, and by no chance could she be credited with the posses sion of sixpence; but, the reflection apart, my spirits sank when I heard them recognise her, anti a sense of degradation, impossible to define, afflicted me anew. _ _

What a position for Henry Gastonard.to be in—self-sought, inevitable, the price of this gipsy's game upon the Butte; , the conse- quence of a chosen masquerade and a self- imposed war upon civilisation Were there not a thousand devils of my Saxon self-respect crying at my elbow to have done with it—to pitch them a handful of money—to say to them, "There is your sister in the arts; take her by the hand and lead her to her home?" A flash of thought it may have been, while I dealt with the gentlemen of the pavement and calculated the chances with a greater precision; but there it was, and while it ran stre;ng in my head, the g.r4 herself lay almost in Inv very arms, smiling still, a very gamin enjoying a brawls asom mon incident in her daily life. Doyou .won- der, Paddy, that I clung to my wreckage and refused to part with it to any other robber upon the shore? By heaven and earth, swear she is the best plucked 'un that eve, wore a red silk stocking or showed it on a booth to a gaping nitOtitude. And that you shall come to believe for yourself presently— when I take you fifty paces further from the cabaret and show you in a line just why we were not I murdered. Do you remember the Rue St. Vincent, that narrow lane by the Assassins, with the great black buttresses and the dingy oil-lamp we used to deride together? Well, it was just by there thau we seemed in for the worst just by the very corner that you would not have paid the half of a brass farthing for out chances.

I had as good as given it up, and fallen to wondering what it feels like to have six inches of steel in your vitals while twenty hands are picking your pockets and twenty more are rifling your shoes. That this was premature, the unexpected but quite gentle- manly appearance of some fifteen agile sr- gents de ville immediately assured me. They had been fetched, it seemed, by the "cipi, or municipal guard, at the cabaret, who, while he would not have lifted a finger to gave Mimi La Godiche, was by no means willing that an Englishman should be papered to- morrow, or., found drowned um' the follow- in 'g morning. Thus the company, armed to its very teeth, and thus the rate scuttling ta their holes, the women left to slither down the steep, the men crying that Mimi La Godiche was une • guepe, and that they would settle with her upon another occasion. I thanked the guard, Paddy; thanked Des- mond Barrymore for his kindness to the girl; and bidding him "good night" (it should have been good morning), I climbed the mountain to that verdant alley wherein my home lies, and took Mimi to the parlour with me. Her first act was to return me my dia- monds. I need not particularise as to where she had hidden thejn, or what was her inspi- ration. She is here as I write this, like d dog upon my carpet. She has been for twenty hours almost in the same position—but what am I going to do with her, what provision make for her, or how am I going to smuggle her in safety from this mount of thieves, I know, my dear Paddy, no more than your estimable self.
So let me have your consolations. All places ,are filled with fools, says Cicero—but there are but two at the Maison du bon Tabac, and one is Mimi La Goclich'e and the other—
Yours eternally, HENRY GASTONARD.

div.head: CHAPTER 11.
div.p: CHAPTER 11.
[The response of Paddy O'Connell of Glerida- lough, County Wicklow, to his friend, Henry Gastonard of the Maison du bon Tabac at Paris.]
Glendalough, County Wicklow, May 18th, 1905.

Dear Henry,—Your letter is. received; I gather therefrom two facts:-1. That you are making a fool of yourself in Paris. 2. That this occupation is congenial to you and the lady of the circus upon whom you ap- pear to have bestowed your patronage.—Be- lieve me to be, My dear Henry, Yours sincerely,
PADDY O'CONNELL.
CHAPTER 111.
[I letter from the fame brief author ad- dressed to the Rifterend Arthur Warring- ton of Beldon, Suffolk.]
Glendalough, County Wicklow, May 18th, 1905.

Reverend Sir,—Your. reques. t that 1 would favour you with such news as I may from time to time receive from my friend, Henry Gastonard, permits me to assure you that he is now established in Paris and appears, by his diligent habit and assured gifts, to be do- ing all that will presently entitle him to .the permanent possession of the fortune, condi- tionally bequeathed to him by his late father, Henry Gastonard of London and Bor- deaux.—My dear Sir, Yours very faithfully, THE O'CONNELL of Glendalough.

div.head: CHAPTER IV.
div.p: CHAPTER IV.
[Henry Gaetonard continues itte story in a letter to his friend Paddy O'Connell.] The Hotel St. Paul, Paris. May 24th, 1905.

Dear Paddy,—Permit me to ignore the Battering document I had the honour to re- ceive from you three days ago. Friendship, my dear Paddy,- culls for something more than a pious expression of opinion upon the reason or conduct of a friend. It demands a sympathetic endea- vour to understand, and an unshaken deter- mination to accept such facts as are con- fided to us and call for our judgment. To tell a man he is • a fool is often to tell him the truth. But I am not aware of many who have become lees foolish for the knowledge, or have derived any consolation whatever from so bald an utterance.

Now, Paddy, you know as well as I do that you are all agog for further news -)f Mimi La Godiche ; and were you in Paris this little chit of the booths would have your warm friendship, and you would lay scalps upon the green should • any defame her. Can- not I see you with your feet upon an his- toric mantel-shelf, and your eyes (so far as tobacco smoke will permit) upon a regal ceiling, reading that same letter for a, second time, and willing to barter all Ire- land and the people thereof for one week of the Butte, one month of this rolling world of gilt and tinsel and all its. spangled joys. Admit the truth of it, and write me some- thing sensible. For, Paddy. I have need of you—there is the devil to play, and the game grows interesting. You will remember that I left Mimi La Godiche upon my hearthrug. Barrymore aad left us: the time was the ear)y morning of the day; the canaille of the Assassins had pine God knows where. Save for the old soldier, who is at once my valet-de-chambre, butler, I cook, housemaid, and scullery wench, there was no one with me in the Matson du bon Tabac.

Depict the scene, Paddy, and -bear with a recital of my virtues. A room as large as an opera box; about its walls the drawings of Caran d'Ache, Henri Riviere, and Willette a couple of armchairs, as ragged as the beggars at the door of St. Eustache ; yacht's piano bang against the wall; a buffet with all the drinks that are not good for us; the very worst novels littering all the tables: cigarettes and cigars everywhere; uipes in. all the nichegf—such is the, mountain home of Henry Gastonard, gentleman., And upon the hearthrug of this charming apartment, style Louis de Montmartre, the tousled-haired Mimi squatting like any lady of-the harem, her legs crossed, her feathered. hat in her hand, her cheeks as rosy as a picture from a Christmas-book. Now, Paddy, I have told you something of Mimi, the Simpleton • but, to be as frank as the priest of thanconnell. 'tis precious little that I myself know of her, anyway. I can no more tell you whether she be vir- tuous or otherwise than recite ten chapters of the Koran. This is a difficulty, to be sure, which my friends of the Hill will never un- neTstand. I can hear the roar of laughter uhich Nionla attend its expression either in the neighbourhood of Neuilly or in that of in Galette. Mimi La Godiche virtuous! Then was Catherine of Russia a latter-day saint, and Lucretia herself as misunder stood as all the historians woiskl now have us to believe: This would be the opinion of the Butte and of Neuilly. It ,is not my opinion—l cannot tell you why; nor do 1 trouble myself for reasons.

She sat upon my hearthrug, I say, her legs 'crossed and her great feathered bat in her hand. When I questioned her, her answers were often monosyllables; sometimes node and smiles; long sentences but rarely. Of her past she appeared to know nothing at all. Her birthplace she named as Vendome, but was not sure of it. She could tell me nothing of her childhood; the Fair she spoke of with dread; the lion-tamer Cassadore stood to her for all terrors, past, present, and to come. She would have burned her band in the fire rather than return to him.
"Have you no remembrance of your father?" I asked her.
She shook her head many times, aa one who wished to think but could not.
"And your mother?" "There was someone at 'Orleans, Monsieur Henry, and after that Cassadorel Oh, Cas- sadore always,, I assure you."

",`You must be able th tell me more than that, Mimi. Somewhere, somewhere in your life, there was a woman who was kind to you. Now, don't you remember when?" "I remember a very old lady, Monsieur Henry—that would have been at Orleans. And then the road—the great, white, open road—so many days, so many nights . . . and after that Cas'sadore always until you came. Monsieur Henry."

div.head: "Why did you not run away, Mimi?" __ _ ,
div.p: "Why did you not run away, Mimi?" __ _ ,
"To Whom shoti:d I run?" "Anywhere away from Cassadore. You are young . . . you can work; why did you not leave him?"
"It was im'possible, monsieur—as well ask the Abbe to run : away from his church."

"You mean that the life had become neces• sary to you?" ' "Yes, yes, I mean that—would you put me in the 'kitchen, Monsieur Henry?" "Certainly not, Mimi—but, you ,see, you can't stop any longer in Montmtertre, and what then?" •
Her face clouded, but only for an instant. "I, shall gb away with you, Monsieur Henry." "Why should you go with me?" "Because I do not wish to go with Cass dors."
"There are plenty of others who would take you away, Mimi. Why do you think of me?"
"I cannot tell you, Monsieur Henry--you must know yourself why, it is."

"And .if I do, what then? Suppose I can- not take you away?" "I shall ask Mr. Barrymore." "Oh, Barrymore would not be of any use to you." "Then I shall go back to Cass.adore." "It wouldn't be safe for you to stop in Montmartre now—l suppose you understand that much, Mimi?"
She laughed a little at the suggftstion. "Jean-le-Mont is very angry," she said, "I am afraid of Jean-le-Mont.
"When did you steal my cigarette case, Mimi; how did you know that Jean-le-Mont had it?"

"He came to Mr. Barryrsore's atelier three days ago—the Italian who makes the models told me that Jean had the box. At the Lapin Ag,il I gave him a rose, Monsieur Henry, and then put my arms about his neck. Ah,.the droll—he discovered it at once, but he did not wish to tell because the others would know and rob him afterwards. Then Mr. Barrymore came in because he saw me there, and I told him, and we sent for you—" "And this was the first time you have stolen anything, Mimi?" "Monsieur-henry, you know that it is."

Observe, Paddy; the reiteration of this. I know that she is virtuous; I know that she is honest. No reasons 'given or asked, as they say in the thieves' advertisements. Upon my, word of honour, the good faith of it is aston- ishing! For Ido know, Paddy . . . and I would stake my fortune (or what is left of it) upon the truth of my astonishing creed.

"1 have a story for you. When will a good comrade hear I shall net fatigue you with further particu- lars of this amazing morning. For a eonple of hours, perhaps, I slept upon my bed, and Mimi upon the hearthrug; but at viz o'clock I waked her, and stopping only for coffee and a roll, I was out of the house by seven and upon my way to the Paris of law and of civili- zation. All my instinct told nte that the thieves of the Butte would make short work of Mimi La Godiche if she remained in their neighbourhood. • Let her go to the old haunt this night, and a knife in the back or a ool- larette of rope would certainly be her reward. You know Montmartre; you know the parti- cular kind of blackguard and of black- guardess it can vomit from its cavernous and detestable mouth. From these I fled with Mimi at my side—whither, the great Saint Christopher, patron of travellers, alone might tell me.

You are aware that. I have an apartment at the Hotel St. Paul, and thither first took the child in the hope that inspiration would come and a swift solution of a pretty problem be found. Be sure the excellent patron stared not a little and that Madame, his wife, sniffed more Of the morning air than had filled her ancient lungs for many a day. But a better entertainment was that provided by Narisse of the Faubourg St. Honore, who came round with his hand- maidens to dress her, and must take my directions three times before assuring him- self finally of the madness of this English traveller. •

Oh. Paddy, cannot you hear this man as he exclaims to heaven upon the feathers oi Montmartre, and sees a national infamy in the fine, if tattered stuffs of Belleville? iNc doubt I Bhould have gone not Che; Narisse but to the Magazin du Louvre; there bought not silk and chiffon but good honest seizes, a hat to fit a governess am lace suitable to the deaconess of a Sunda: school. But, Paddy, lam a man, and know the name but of One costumier in al Paris, and he is Narisse, and he made o Mimi La Godiche a veritaule beauty in les, time than you or I could finish a rubber o bridge at the club. Ah, these mad English men--they still exist it appears, and • blessec is Paris because of them! And what shah be said for the girl herself, and what must she do upon the instant but sing the man a song after the fashion of Jehan Rictus, just because of the clothes he had put upon hei back. Believe we, when I tell you that the models themselves came near to joining in the chorus, and that Narisse was speechless before the end of the second verse.

Mimi, then, is dressed and in her right mind. Will you follow me as I lead her forth about the hour of twelve !o'clock, and ask Myself, what next? There are many in Paris who know me, and not a few whc stared with some astonishment. Whatevei the costumier's art, my dear Paddy, it can not disguise the walk, the airs, the mannei of the Butte. I am a person of some sen sibility out of doors, and I object to tha• freedom which grips ,you hysterically by to, arm, at odd intervals, to drag you to a . sho, window and exclaim upon a rope of/ pearl which would ruin a Maharajah, or al emerald bracelet none but a Rothschild caul. buy. It is not a .joy to me when my corn panion has the wit and the language whicl silences enterprising cabmen or calls for Ln4 retort discourteous of the foot-passenger vim has been obstructed. Publicity has no charms for Me; I prefer to give the wall to the humorists and to go in obscurity. We lunched at the Café of the Cascade in the Bois. There was a goodly company pre- sent, and "her ladyship" fell in love with the Baroness &chard, who was with Pechala, of the Spanish Embassy. I think the grand manners of many of these far from grand dames somewhat astonished her; but the size of the asparagus tickled her sense of humour. and the bill was ever in her mind.

"What will happen to us if you cannot, pay the bill, Monsieur Henry? " "We shall go to prison, Mimi." "Cassadore went to prison once—at Cha- lons-sur-Marne—l do not wish to go to prison, Monsieur Henry." "Then we must try to find some money, Mimi. How much have you now?"
The question should not have been Put, for Mimi carries her money where she carried my cigarette case, and made no secret of the matter."

I was but just in time to prevent a dis- play which might have brought us the bill on the spot, and, as it was, Etienne, the waiter, grinned from ear to ear as he floated to. us with a sole it la Victorine.
"Did they not tell you in the Rue Pigalle that I am rich, Mimi?" "You could never be rich, Monsieur Henry.; you are not clever enough.". _ .
"El-Ili:Mimi. am I not a sculpror?" This appeared to .her a droll saying. ShA. laughed quite honestly and again appealed tc my candour.

"You know that you will never be a sculp tor; you have no talent, Monsieur Henry. even I have more. talent than you. esides, if you were "—she added wisely—"how poor we should be." "It is not good to be poor in Paris, Mimi." "It is not good to be poor anywhere, Mon- sieur Henry."

"But if one has no way to get a I have not, what then, Mimi?" "Oh, then one sleeps at the Hotel of the Belle Etoile. I have stayed there often wher I used to go to the Fetes. It is a very larg, hotel, and • you can see the stars while yoi. lie in bed."

"Would you go back there, Mimi?" "Jesu—no; why do you speak of it whet- one is no longer hungry, Monsieur Henry?" I did not pursue the subject further, but paid the bill and went out with her to the Bois. A shabby cab made the usual granc tour with us and helped us to pass a pleasant hour. Perhaps it astonished me to discove, that the Bois impressed her but little—bu. then she had been accustomed to the spangle. all her life and could make little of a pas:- able equipage with a fat Baroness in it, or costly motor driven by a man who looke4 like an Oneida Indian. Her exclamation were few but her observation unfailing. Sh detected me at once when I nodded to Lei d'Alencon, who drove a pair of cream- coloured ponies near the Cascade. " Whv did that lady look so angry, Mon sieur Henry? Are you in love with her?" ' "Why should I be, Mimi? She is the wife of Captain d'Alencon of the Engineers." "But she is in love with you—l am sure of it. And she is very angry with you." "Then I cannct help it. Let us get out and walk, Mimi, and ask ourselves where wt are going to stay to-night. That will be more interesting than Madame d'Alencon." "You wish to see her pass again—is no that the reason, Monsieur Henry?" Well, of course it was, and she had guessed wisely eaough ; but what was I to say to her: Lea is one. of my virtues, as I have told yot, before, Paddy. When I wish to balance tilt. 32.tge maralitiGua pb.. day ncl
it?"

!eager, Lea crAiencon 6tftii•eim zzr. valuable 'of my assets. She is to clever to be anything else, and yet you might call her the, most amorous woman; and one of the most dangerous in Paris. Just a, hundred times, perhaps, has she advised me to get out of this delectable country and go back to Eng land. I might have done so but for her pro- mise to visit me there upon an early occa- sion. Be sure, Paddy, that I have no desire whatever to cut the Captain's throat merel3 to prove myself a good Parisian. Lea is charming as a friend. She would be all the malignities impersonified otherwise. I should tell you that I had recognised her when she passed me, and that this astonished her considerably. It is considered less than nothing at all in Paris to drive in the Bole with a cocotte—but to recognise your lady friends when thus employed must be named little less than an infamy. So here was a pretty problem for this majestic Astarte with the raven locks and the liquid black eyes and all the langour of the trained voluptuary. Either I wished to insult her or it were pos- sible that my companion might be introduced. This she must have told herself, for the chariot reappeared presently and was drawn up at the pavement not fifty yards from the place where we stood. "Bonjour, Madame d'Alencon." "Bonjour, Monsieur Gastonard." "I have a story for you; when will a good asasaada hear it?"

••^Ally not at rive Veloca ; my nuramma 13 at Valerien. Is it a story of the theatre, Mon vieur Gastonard?" "It is a story of virtue, madame." We laughed together This poor old Pal taloon Virtue still provokes a smile—if his name be ever mentioned—in such saloons as Lea d'Alencon and her kind have made famous. Some spirit of sheer devilry must have prompted me to this confidence, Paddy; but behind it lay a firm belief in the sagacity of this shrewd woman of the world and in her honesty. She would place Mimi the Simple- ton in some possible situation—l had not a moment's doubt of it. How we laughed together over the whole story when I went to her rooms an hour later. Mimi, meanwhile, hod been dispatched to the Hotel St. Paul, and there entrusted to the safe custody of la patronne. I myself sat in a wonderful cradle chair and wretched Lea pour out really excellent tea from a Chinese pot that should have been behind glass. She had changed her gown for a delicate robe of lace and chiffon, and thrust the prettiest pair of feet in all Paris from a petticoat over which a costumier must have shed tears of joy:
l'Who is this girl?" he asked me. I told her that I did not know. "Why has she become virtuous?" . ."A natural condition, Lea; why is not marble chalk?"

Observe, Paddy, that Lea and I have been soine months at the point when "Monsieur" or "Madame" provokes ridicule, and no for- mality clouds our brutal frankness. Had it been otherwise I could not have spoken to her of Mimi La Godiche at all.

"Let me tell you the girl's story," I said, "or what I know of it. Six months ago she was performing outside the Walls of Paris with a monster of a man named Cassadore, whose riches are three lions and whose ward- robe a pair of spangled tights. I was in the tent when this child vgas taken into the cages with this man, and I did not fail to remark two facts: one, .that she was absolutely lack- ing in a sense of fear, and, secondly, that she might become eventually one of the most beautiful women in Paris. Five francs judi- ciously expended obtained an introduction to her—a hundred francs- bought her of the lion- tamer. Rejoice, my dear Lea that in our society women are not sold for a hundred nor for ten hundred francs. or who can tell what I might not bid for you, at an auction.. In Mimi's case the bargain was soon made. After all, the tamer had a dozen girls of her station ready to be driven into the cages at his -nod—what was this girl to him? I bought her and took her to the Butte. Febry, of La Galette, gave her a chance to get hissed upon his stage, and she did not disappoint him. I tried her again, paying a thelisand francs for the privilege at the Quat-Z-Arts and the Coq d'Or. Again, my dear lady, she was a hop- less failure. No femme de chambre acting iii the, kitchen could have failed so dismally. And yet I continue to believe in her; my faith is unshaken. I am ready to declare that she will become a great actress, astonish Paris, and end in an apartment not a third of a mile removed from the Arc de Triomphe or the Avenue Marigny. It is this faith which brings me now-to the house of the charming Lea d'Alencon. I come, foi d'honneur, simply to seek a salve to my vanity. How shall I get this child taught? Where shall I place her while she is being taught? You, of ail may friends, can best advise me upon that point. Do so, and you shall not find a more grate- ful man in Paris to-day." _ _ _ •
Well, I could see tiial I had impressed her, but I had not continced her, as the next ques- tion proved. a, "Why do you say that the phi] (1 is irt lI- OUS ? " she asked me.

"Because I know her to be so," was my re- tort. "Put your hand upon the marbles at the Madeleine and wiil they burn you? It is true that a fire might be conceived of such a nature as to melt your marble and cause it to run as liquid steel—but, my dear Lea, we are not talking of the forges, but of the facts. This child is virtnoirs because she is utterly devoid of any desire to be anything else. The wisest up on the Butte recognise the truth and are proud of it." "And now these very people drive her out. Did you not tell me tria't she cannot return to Montmartre, Henry?"
"Certainly not--at least, to the only quar- ter of Montmartre where it would be pos- sible for her to live. The thieves have marked her down—she would not be alive a week if she remained up there."

"And you propose----?" "My dear Lea, nothing of the kind. I have no matrimonial intentions, believe me. It is you who will propose." She laughed a little wickedly. The talk had drifted apart from my idea, and I could not but be amused by her sudden vorite face. "Louis does not 'return from Valerien until to-morrow," she said quickly. "I am sup- Posed to dine with my sister Lucille. Where are you going to take me, Henry?" "Alone, Lea?" She looked me straight in ths face. "Let us ask the Cure of the Madeleine." "By all means. And while we dine we will make plans for Mimi." "Let us dine on the island," she crivl. ignoring it; "there is the safest place Paris.'
- "I will be at the Cascade at a quarter to seven. Of course, it may be a tragedy." "The tragedies, my dear Henry, are alwa.vs for to-morrow."

Atid so, Paddy, arnittoie root min iT, 113, consented. It will be no surprise to you to hear that the Cure of the Madeleine had another appointment, and could not turn up. But of this dinner and of all the ab- surdities which followed upon it, I will write to-morrow. your

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
By Veronica.
POWIMAIT U R E.

It is astonishing that many amateurs for their early photography in photoraphy generally select portrait work. I suppose it is because they wish to show their friends what they can do, and so create a personal interest. There is no doubt; however, that portrait work is much more difficult for a beginner than ordinary landscape work.; In many cases the early attempts in portrait work are most appalling. It generally happens that the friend who is the victim of the occasion is seated in a chair looking straight at the camera. Undoubtedly it is purely 'want of thought that no trouble is taken in posing. The best pictures, how- ever, are those that have the head turned a little away from the camera, aml where the body and the head are not quite in the same_ direction.

Portrarits that are taken in doors are frequently spoilt by the background. Pictures on the wall, etc., very often mar what might otherwise be a pleasing result. A simple way out of this trouble is the utilising of a background, and for this purpose nothing is more, effective than cedar felt which is used for laying underneath carpets. This is obtainable in a size of about 6x4 feet. To make the background nail a couple of wooden uprights on two of the sides then curve the felt in a semicircular form, nailing another piece of wood across the top to join the two sides together. It can then be keptin this semi- circular position. Then using the background near a window it can be so arranged that you got a grada- tion of light and shade owing to its circular form, and when taking photographs looking towards the light you will get the shadowed side of the background behind the strongest lighted side of the face, and the lightor portion of the background against the shadowed side. This, if the light is not too strong; gives a very pleasing effect. Should the gradation on the background be too severe it can be reduced by putting a piece of tissue paper over the top. So much for portraits taken indoors.

Ifor out-door portraits select a position so that the main source of light comes a little from one side. This is managed by seating your subject near to a wall or the side of a house. A little time spent in the watching of different effects of lighting by moving the model a little more one way or the other will Convince any one of the gain in modelling effect by having the light cut off on one side. Engineers often make the mistake of taking a portrait out in the open light. In the majority of cases this gives so great a flatness that the result proves anything but satisfactory

div.head: COPYING ENGRAVINGS,
div.p: COPYING ENGRAVINGS,

In one of the American publications there appears a very novel method of copying engravings and half- tone reproductions to obviate the screen effect which is otherwise very accentuated when these are copied for use as lantern slides, It is this :—obtain a piece of rough glass and place it in contact with the engraving to be copied, having the ground side outside. In this way),ou copy from the glass, and if it is desired to accentuate any particular part this can • be done by oiling the ground glass in the spot to be accentuated. It is claimed that by these means negatives can be made and lantern slides from them so as to almost resemble the originals. a

div.head: NEW DEVELOPER,
div.p: A NEW DEVELOPER,

" Certenial "is the name of a new sinkle solution, concentrated developer that has been introduced by Ilford Limited. For developing negatives it is diluted from one to thirty times with water_ One in twenty is the advised strength for correct exposure weaker. It is a very clean developer and quite free from fog, and suitable for developing either negatives, bromide or gaslight papers. The name of Ilford has so long been associated with the manufacture of reliable plates that that in itself should be sufficient recom- mendation for this new developer. ,

div.head: USE OF STOPS,
div.p: THE USE OF STOPS,

There is considerable ignorance as to what is accomplished by using different stops.- This is .more so where the worker has n camera without ,any focussing Screen. For those who wish to have the action of ,stops proved to them a simple way is as follows :—Put a chair out in the garden, say six feet in front of the camera, and then four or five other chairs at intervals of about three feet between-each. If you have a focussing camera focnss on to the nearest .chair with tour lens at full aperture. Then rack your camera in Until you have the chair that is farthest away. Now rack it out until you get the middle distance sharp. Both ends of the rows of chairs can now be brought sharply into focus bv using a stop which yon can easily find out: Of course if the camera does not possess a rocn:4;ing 'screen the only way out of the difficulty. is by taking a succession of negatives following the same directions as above.

div.head: ENSYNA PAPER.
div.p: ENSYNA PAPER.
In one of the photographic weeklies there appears the7following interesting note from a correspondent : _ _

—" Ilaving—overlooked The point in the directions for Ensyna which states that Wesh developer should be used for each print, I. got some prints which, NI dry- ing, were badly stained. As they were spoilt, and so could come tr no,further,harm, I mixed a,. solution of potassium bromide and 'potassium fern-cyanide and bleached them. I then re-developed them with metal- hydroquipone, and was agreeably surprised to see the prints restored to their original chocolate colour, but minus the old purple stains. They had lost slightly in depth, 'so that. the method would seem to be a safe one to reduce an ever-developed print,as well as to get rid of stains: This method may be very useful to those who are unfortunate enough to get stains through in- correct working, the most common error being in using a developing dish, that to t‘ll appearance is clean. yet
unless the dish is made of very hard enamel, such as graniteen, solutions permeate into the ware, and so afterwards contaminate new solutions that are put into it.

div.head: SPORTING ATTIRE.
div.p: SPORTING ATTIRE.

-- With, the mention of sport one's mind turns almost automaticallv to Burberry's for this famous firm have earned the thanks of every sportsman or sportswoman by the intelligence brought to bear on the all-important question of sporting garments. Comfort and freedom of movement are absolutely essential qualities which must characterise any article ,of clothing intended for sporting use. Looseness was formerly thought to secure freedom, and one saw appalling examples of the Norfolk jacket, all pleats and bulges, in which the wearer has as much difficulty in raising his gun to his sboulder as if he were trying to shoot in a frock coat. Time after time inventions have appeared that were to abolish all restriction of arm and shoulder; but though in theory excellent, they were found wanting and soon abandoned. Burberrys, however, came to the rescue of the distressed sports- man with the now famous patent pivot sleeve, which is constructed on sound anatomical principles and made to follow the lines of the muscles that are responsible for good or bad shooting. The ordinary tailor binds these important muscles by placing an inflexible band in the form of a seam com- pletely round the' arm-pit, the very point where the greatest liberty is essential. Even when the arms are at rest these seams are often most uncomfortable. On arising the arms, the muscles expand and take double the space they did before, the seams now cut into them and it becomes impossible to move without a pain- ful sense of restriction and a great drag on the body of the coat. Pivoted sleeves do away with all transverse seams and allow perfect freedom for easy movement, an advantage that the sportsman readily appreciates. A speciality of Burberrys, without which no male or female sporting kit can claim to be complete is the Burberry Slip-on, that ideal form of coat made in "Gabardine "—a very light thin cloth that offers the same sturdy resistance to rain as oilskin without any of the attendant drawbacks of that unpleasant material, for it combines its waterproof qualities with natural self-ventilation, which is a sine qua non if the wearer intends indulging in pursuits necessitating rapid move- ment and consequent perspiration, The Slip-on is cut on liberal one might say voluminous lines, with very loose sleeves that allow the arms to move in any direc- tion withont a constant tug to remind you that you are wearing an overcoat. It is made in various thicknesses euitable for the different seasons of the year, and is useful for motoring and travelling as it is for shooting, golfing and every other out-o'door pursuit. ' On the point of going to press, we bear from Messrs. J. and W. Dutton, that Burberrys have arranged to hold a special exhibition of the lattst Burberry productions at their premises in Sankey-street, on March 15th and 16th. The display will include all the 1909 novelties in Sporting, Motoring, Travelling, Town and Country Kit for ladies and gentlemen. A representative from Burberrys Loudon house will be in attendance, who will give our readers any information they require oon- cerning the various devices utilised to secure the utmost comfort and protection for wears of Burberry- Proof garments.

Grappenhall. LIVELY PARISH MEETING.

14:rh, e.re were lively scenes at the annual parish meeting .; Ad In the Grappenhall schoolroom on Tuesday even- Lister Kaye was voted to the chair and there w-es Et large attendance. The cause of the discussion ft the much-vexed question of the Johnson charity. i-ee Chairman explained what had passed between the r ish C)uncil and the Charity Commissioners' the °.e.heil having agreed in committee to ttike no furbber Zielgeh in the matter. The charity is administered by t e Rector and churchwardens, linen beinu distributed eh the poor of the parishes of Grappenhall, Christ whereh and St. James', Latchford. Mr. S. H. Jeakins, th'e as previously raised the question, contended that. s: Parish Council were not justified in forcing them- pz.iee into committee and discussing the question in vete- He bas strongly maintained that the charity Zl3ht to be administered by the Parish Council but, on 8 .tiler hand, it is stated that the will provides that 40143' be administered by the Rector and wardens.— p-Lre, ef Mr. Jenkins' remarks in which be took the ant'se Council strongly to task for having debated the chat in private were strongly resented, and the trrnan said that if Mr. Jenkins would not withdraw Yi'euld have to leave the chair. Mr. Jenkins was rapattrate and Hr.
