div.head: Penketh and Sankey.
div.p: Penketh and Sankey.

WESLEYAN CHEL.—The Wesleyan Men's Bible Class held their open service on Sunday.. The members of the class had given the Sunday open service over to the Salvation Army to hold a meeting. Mr. C. E. Parker, who presided, in speaking on behalf of himself and class said how pleased they were to welcome Major Bas. and the two sisters who had come to sing. He also said he was sure that all present would agree that the Salvation Army was doing a great and grand work. Major Bax, who has been abroad as a missionary and is now stationed at Liverpool, gave a very interesting address and spoke of the work they did in Liverpool in the way of free meals andsoupat midnight to the poor. He also instanced several cases where men and women had bcen lifted from sin and were now followers of Christ. The two sisters, Captain Moorey and Sister Platt of Warrington, sang a duet in a most charming way. The Bible Class choir led the singing, and Mrs. Parker officiated at the organ. A collection was taken and divided between the Salvation Army and the Trust Funds of the Chapel. DEATH OF AN OLD INHABITANT.—It is with regret we report the death (done of the oldest paristkione-s in the person of Mr. John Johnson who passed away at his reswence on AI onday. The deceased, who was 85 years of age,had been ailing for some time. A bad attack of bronchitis was the caure of death. Mr. Johnson died at his birthplace, Ye Olde Ferry Inn, on the river side. As landlord be managed the business up to the time of his illness. The deceased was highly iespected by all who knew him. He served nis time as a cabinet-make- with the late Mr. Robert Garnett's father at the Penketh works. On the death of his father he took over the management of the Ferry Inn. Deceased took a great liking to making bowls and a great many of his bowls are still in use. He also took great interest in painting and when a young man won a prize at the Warrington School of Art. Many of his pictures can be seen at the Ferry Inn. The funeral took place at Great Sankey on Thursday at 3.30. The deceased leaves four daughters.

THE LATE MR. A. Bincx.—Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, enquired on Saturday into the circumatances attending the death of the late Mr. Arthur Birch. who died at his residence, 217, Liverpool-read, Great Sankey, on the 3rd inst. Mr. H. Roberts appeared on behalf of the Associated Iron and Steel Workers of Great Britain, and also for the relatives of the deceased. Mr. Eilis, of Wigan, repre- sented the Wigan Roll Mills, where the deceased met with ancident on February 16th.—The evidence showed/that decealed fell and caught his foot upon something on the floor and fell heavily on an"i ron horse,"the foot of which caught him on the right side of tbe chest. He went home and had not been able to follow his employment since.—Dr. Smith, who made a post-mortem examination, said the sixth rib on the right side was fractured; the heart was in a state of fatty degeneration and weighed over 16 ounces. He we of opinion that the came of death was failure of the hclrt's action.—ln answer to the Coroner, witness said the fracture of the rib would accelerate death. Deceased was in such a condition that the shock and the injury would have more effect than it would have had upon a perfectly healthy man.—lt was stated that the deceased was a very active man and a life-bag teetoteler. The jury returned a verdict of" Death from heart failure, ac c elerated by the injuries, the death being accidental."—On Saturday the funeral took place at the Sankey Cemetery, the Rev. John Gunnell officiated. The chief mourners were :—Messrs. Frank (Wigan), James (Belfast), and Fred Birch (Warrington), sons'; Thomas Birch • (Warrington), brother; and Messrs. Allen and Simpson. There were also present : —the Rev. J. R. Jones (vicar of Sankey), representa- tives from the Great Sankey Parish Council, and the National Amalgamated Asaociation of Iron and Steel- workers.

div.head: Lymm
div.p: Lymm

THE CHORAL SOCIETY.—The fourth session of this society will 'come to an end next Tuesday, the 16th inst., when the' annual business meeting of members and subscribers will be held in the Council Offices at eight &dock. Offioers and Committee for the ensuing year will be elected at this meeting and the work of the next session will be discussed. LIBERAL WOMEN PLEASE NOTE.—A Women's Liberal Association for Lynnu is being started on Thursday next the 18th and Mrs. W. .1. Crossley is inviting any ladies interested to meet her at Hirst's Pavilion at 3.30 o'clock on that afternoon. 'rickets or invitations are not necessary and Mrs. Crossley will welcome all women interested in the Liberal cause.

RETIREMENT OF MR. JOHN WINSTANLEY, FARMER.— Mr. Winstanley who has for over 30 years been one of the most successful farmers iu the district this month vacates his holding in order to take a well-canted rest. Mr. Winstanley has kept pace with the times both in methods and in the WM of up-to-date machinery and consequently leaves his farm in a remarkable state of efficiency which is extremely creditable to him. He carries with him into his retirement the best wishes of a large circle of friends and acquaintances. His work will be carried on by his son.

LyMM MAY QUEEN.-A public meeting was held in Hirst's Pavilion on Friday last, the sth inst., when it was decided that the Tradesmen's Association be approached with a view to ascertaining whether the May Queen Compittee could look to the tradespeople of Lytum for a fair amount of financial support, if the festival was carried on and 11lossrs. F. P. Cooke, A. H. Fray and .lames D. B. Smith were deputed to wait upon tho Association. The meeting was adjourned until Tuesday next, when the report of the deputation would be given.

OUGHTRINGTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— On Monday, the Ist inst., a Parliamentary debate was held in connection with this society, when Mr.O. G. Smith introduced a "budget." Mr. J. ThompsoA moved a "Tariff Reform" amendment. The debate which followed proved so very interesting, and as at the time of closing several members had not had an opportunity of taking part in the discussion, it was decided to adjourn the debate to the following Monday. The adjourned meeting was duly held and proved equally interesting. The next meeting of the Society will be held ori Monday, the 15th inst., when Mr. Cecil H. S. Wilson, M.A., will give a paper on "Cambridge and its Colleges," illustrated by limelight views.

THE! LATE MR. S. STARKEY.—The funeral took place at Bowdon Parish Church on Monday of Mr. Samuel Starkey, Brook Farm, Agd3n, who died suddenly the previous Thursday. The service was conducted by the Rev. R. E. Roberts. Mr. Starkey, who was 52 years of age, was born at Brook Farm, where he Si, as preceded by several generations of his family, who had held the farm for nearly 403 years. He also represented the township for some years on the Bucklow Board of Guardians and the Rural-District Council. He was also a member of the Committee of the Altrincham Agricultural Society It is only six weeks since the death occurred of the deceased's wife, and the double bereave- ment of the family in so short a time has csused the deepest sorrow throughout the district.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL BAZAAR.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL BAZAAR.

The Lymm Congregation!il school was bright with streamers and other decorations on Thursday afternoon when a three days' bazaar in connection with the Congregational Church was opened. On tastefully- arranged stalls a great variety of useful and fancy wares were temptingly displayed, and members of the con- gregation and elder scholars gave willing help as stall- holders. There were the usual attractions of a bazaar, including an " art " and curios exhibition, and a miniaturiz rifle range at which mould-be marksmen could test their skill. A novel feature which constituted a pleasing souvenir as well as a source of revenue, was a book of quotations and proverbs collected by Mrs..). D. B. Smith I rom a large circle of friends of the church. The object of the bazasr was to raise £2OO towards tho deficit on the church accounts, to meet the expenses of repairs in the Sunday school and to augnlpt the chief rent fund. The officials, who worked most energetically to promote the success of the enterprise, were :—President, Rev. A. Barnett; chairman, Mr. J. Hardy Holt ; treasurer, Mr.J. E. Bell; hon. secretaries, Messrs. F. P. Cooke and

J.D. B. Smith. Mr. A. A. Haworth, M.P. had promised to open the bazaar on Wednesday, but unfortunately was unable to be present. Mrs. Haworth performed the ceremony in the presence of a large gathering. Mr. L. L. Noar, of St. Annes-on-Sea, a former deacon of the church, presided. After devotional exercises, led by the Rev. A. Barrett, The Chairman, in a brief address, said the work of that church bad their deep interest and he hoped they would have the satisfaction of seeing their labours in connection with that bazaar bear good fruit. He was very glad indeed to be there amongst so many old friends. They bad been in different paths, some of them in different towns and countries and had seen many faces, but be could tell them that hardly a day passed without his thinking of Lymm and of Lymm friends. If good wishes could have made them happy they would have been happy indeed. The old times could never come again and there were no friends like the old ones. When he was in office at that church he knew the consolation they felt in remembering the kindly feelings of the Bowdon friends. One of those friends—Mrs.Haworth—was with them that day, and he bad pleasure in asking her to declare" the bazaar open. (Applause). Mrs. Haworth expressed on behalf of Mr. Haworth his great regret that owing to his belt% so busily engaged in London, he could not be with them. He sent his good wishes for the succds of the bazaar. She was sure they bad a very up-hill fight in that part of the world, as in all the countiy districts, and they were making a very brave fight with a very good leader at their head, for she knew Mr. Barrett well of old. (Applause.) She bad much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause). Mr. J. Hardy Holt, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Haworth and the Chairman, said it was pleasing to see some engaged at the stalls that afternoon who some few Tears ago were scholars in Mr. Noai's class at the Sunciay school. The name of Haworth belonged not only to Lancashire, or to England, but was world-wide. It stood for all that was free, in more things than in Free Churches (Applause). Mr. J. B. D. Smith seconded, and said be did so in the absence of Mr. Bell, the treasurer, upon whore Ooulders a large share of the work entailed by the bazaar bad fallen.

The vote was enthusiastically passed. The amount realized on Thursday was :—donations, .£5B 6s. ; stalls, entertainments, Ix., 163 175. 9d. ; total £122 3s. 9d. Yesterday the bazaar was re-opened by Mrs. H. P. Bedell, Mr. Bedell presiding.

div.head: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAVING.
div.p: COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAVING.
MR TOVVIIROE'S SUMMING UP.

The high level of idealistic thought reached, and so ably maintained by Mr. Harold Gray in his criticisms of the series of articles on Compulsory Military Trainitia 'makes it difficult for the victim to answer, if he 1 c no, supplied with 'philosophic wings or an aeroplane worked by gas. For Mr. Gray has not even troubled to study with care the arguments for National Service, and dismisses the whole of the last article with the remark, the question of physical development is merely subsidiary to the military issue." THE PHYSICAL QUESTION.

Now the passionate enthusiasm shown by many members of the National Service League is created largely by our knowledge that in States where national service exists,the character and health of every citizen is of parathount value. Every mother is honoured. Every child is a national asset. England spends nearly sixty million pounds 'a year—(see Poor Law Commission p.* 52) upon poor relief, education and public health, and yet to secure 5,000 men for our Navy, we have to reject 35,000 as physically unfit. We of the N.S.L. feel most strongly that the appalling physical degeneration, representing the invasion of disease and decay due to the hosts of microbes which have effected a landing in feeble systems, is far more dangerous than military invasions by any army in the world. Many of our strongest supporters, like Mr. T. C. Horsfall and the Rev. J. A. Campbell are engrossed in social reform rather than in soldiers' reforms. And yet Mr. Gray says " the physical development is merely subsidiary !' I challenge him to produce any practical scheme for improving our national physique more strongly supported by actual figures and experience than regular physical drill in schools .followed by a period of 'open air life and strenuous work Such as is only possible under national service. Surgeon-General Sir Alfred Keogh puts admirably our convictions in ,these words : " Military training, of course, assists first, of building up, in feeding, housing, and clothing the recruit and then gradually setting him to his military exercises. If we never required an army to fight for us, we should still, spealAng from the medical point of view, regard medical training as physical training, and as the finest thing for the race, and for future generations." I have at hand quotations from Sir Lauder Brunton, Sir James Chrichton-Browne, Sir John Tweedy, Dr. Hanson, Dr. Dabbs, Dr. Caton of Liverpool, and other famous medical men. They all say the same: " Our youth can be best saved from degeneration by a course of military training." Will Mr. Gray confess that he has misrepresented our airfis in calling physical development a subsidiary issue? Compulsorymilitary training will enable us to fight both consumption and conscripts. The former foe is more terrible than the latter.

div.head: INVASION PROBLEM.
div.p: THE INVASION PROBLEM.

Mr. Gray in the same summary fashion dismissesthe whole of the second article with the modest remark that "I do not posse-Ss the requisite knowledge to discuss the technicalities involved in this question." The problem of invasion, in so far as it has to bo considered by the man in the street, is not a technical one. Seventy-three Admirals tell us" that our Navy is not

sufficient both for the defenc-e—ofm-r- Empire and our shores. The'Y warn us that it is not wise to put all our savings in one stocking. Mr. Haldane acknow- ledges that the Regular Army cannot always be kept at home to act like a nursemaid guarding a baby. We English must he able to defend ourselves,and not hire patriotism by proxy to -protect us. Hence the Territorials. But can 300,000 young men—cajoled out of a population of 44.000,000—wh0 nobly consent to put on putties and undergo in the first year 40 drills, in their second year merely 10 drills of one hour each, plus a short annual stay in camp of eight to fifteen days, minus Sundays, days of arrival, inspec- tion and departure, can such men hope to •face regu- lars? The idea is worthy of" Alice in Wonder- land." Can an amateur boxer hope to face a pro- fessional? Common sense, not technical knowledge, is required. Therefore we are in full agreement 'with Mr. Haldane's dictum that ' a nation in arms is the only safeguard for the public interests." Close friend- ships with officers and students in both France Belgium and Germany restrained me from making the personal references to international politics indulged in for half a column by Mr. Gray. The League is most 'anxious to avoid adding fuel to the fire of rivalry. It simply says that the majority of experts are agreed that invasion is within the verge of possibilities, and that we are not ready to oppose troops once landed. Are we going to make more adequate preparations?

div.head: "THE HAPPIEST TIME IN MY LIFE."
div.p: "THE HAPPIEST TIME IN MY LIFE."

But Mr. Gray refers indirectly to the trained men of certain continental armies as ".dumb-driven cattle." What a parody of the truth! Let me quote from a speech made on March Bth, 1909, by Mr. Hilaire Belloc, Liberal member for South Salford, formerly an artillery man in the French army.—" I believe I am the only man in the house who has been under a Compulsory system and I would never argue against it on the score of hardship—the time so spent was the happiest time in my life." Can our opponents dis- regard such evidence ?

div.head: EQUAL OPPORTUNITIES TO ALL.
div.p: EQUAL OPPORTUNITIES TO ALL.

Mr. Gray, however, professing to criticise, leaves aside altogether the military necessity, the .physical and moral advantages, the actual facts , of universal training, and is content to dub it anl" autocratic military regime." In truth he is so carried away in a 'whirlwind of words and quotations from Quaker poets that he forgets this work-a-day world. For the obligation to b trained trained for four months could exist only by the will of the majority of the people. The law by which the British would compel themselves to be trained would be in fact the expression in a business-like form of , the will of the majority. In such * a force all would have exactly the same obligations, cobbler's son and Lord Mayor's son alike. No man could become en officer without first doing his duty as a private and proving, further, his qualifications for promotion. Such Is the Swiss system. Such a system we propose. Where is the autocratic military regime? Lord Rosebery said in his speech at Edinburgh on December 4th, " I myself am a believer in the Swiss system, by whiqh every able-bodied man is compelled to train for a short time so that, at any rate, he may be capable, at a pinch, - of being produced as an efficient soldier. I believe that is the most democratic system of defence. Switzerland is the purest democracy

existent in Europe, and would not endure any but a democratic system of defence." Ur. W. If. Hughes, a minister in the Watson (Labour) Admistration, writes : "I do not hesitate to assert that this universal training is not only democratic, but that, wanting it, democracy must perish." Mr. Gray writes that our proposals are "unfriendly to democratic aspirations. Another perversion of truth and fact! -

div.head: PEACE AND GOODWILL,
div.p: PEACE AND GOODWILL,

" War is wholesale murder," writes M. Gray. So in place of artillery he would institute arbitration. Rules would oust rifles. All who appreciate the waste and misery of war must be in the deepest sympathy with this movement. But we are dealing with a tough old world, not with an imaginary society. Even the most peaceful envoys at the Hague Conference could not persuade the rulers of Germany to give up the use of those devilish devices—floating mines. Suppose we adopt the needs of the Peace advocates and rely- ing on arbitration, relax still more our home defences. We shall soon be in the position of the conductor on the tramcar held up by a Tottenham murderer. The tramcar will be the "British Empire " ; the conductor, the Prime Minister of a defenceless country; the armed desperado, who has slipped past the policeman of the Navy, will be any power you like. For all the powers are Nations in Arms except U.S.A. and self-confident little Britain. The world is not ripe for the amiable rule of the Peace Party. The Berlin Treaty, the most binding inter- national law existent, was entirely disregarded last Autumn by the Emperor of Austria, Law by itself is not enough. Behind the magistrates' verdict is the policeman's truncheon. Behind an organised Trade Union is a War Chest. Behind a Foreign Minister is an Army. All organized force is in degree war, and upon organised force the world has progressed and still progresses. The ultimate act of an individual, trying to prevent someone hindering him at work, must be a blow. As Captain- A. T. Mahan writes "The dykes of Holland withstand bydirect opposition the natural mission of the North Sea ‘o swallow up the land they protect." Our Army and Navy are the dykes of England. "These are the dykes our fathers made, but we would not look to the same. Time and again we were warned of the dykes, time and again we delayed, Now it may tall we have slain our sons as our father: we have betrayed." INTERNATIONAL NONSENSE.

The truth is that Mr. Gray is obsessed by a windy idea to which he gives the name " Internationalism " or "Inter-Dependableness." If on a side issue he proposes to give the public political philosophy, let it be good not bad philosophy. To try to build a philosophy on Internationalism is like a blind man looking in a dark room for a blacliohat which is not there. It has been a sign of national decadence when such washy doctrines, called in Greece "Epicureanism," in Warrington " Inter-Depeadableness " receive public confidence. Both the Greek philosophers, Plato and Aristotle, revolted against this idea of a man disdaining to identify himself with the citizenship of a single state but claiming to be a citizen of the world. Who is there in Warrington who can feel the same regard for the Grand Lama of Tibet or the Emperor of Japan as he does for his Majesty the King? This talk of Inter- nationalism is philosophically wrong and inhuman. For every nation has a unique faith, or purpose. The national or imperial state is the widest organization which has the common experience necessary to found a common life. Each State like each individual has to work out its own salvation and destiny. Mr. Gray, diregarding this national purpose, vocation, destiny, proposes a federation of Europe. Even then he would not have solved the problem of doing away with war and armies. For the 400,000,000 inhabi- tants of China might apply for land in disarmed Eurqpe. Arbitration would say "Keep off the grass," Chi& might easily reply "Our views are not your views. Might is right. We are coming." Talk of " Inter-dependableness " would have little effect against the yellow peril. Most of us in such a case would lament our weapons laid aside and prepare to fight for our homes and our religion. .

A TRIBUTE. Hitting out from the shoulder is perfectly con- sistent with a strong respect for one's opponent. I cannot close this counterstroke without paying a sincere tribute to the wealth of literature, the evident earnestness, the welcome seriousness with which Mr. Gray has championed his ideals. But have his negative criticisms touched the main issues? "\(a). Compulsory military training is necessary; for oui voluntary soldiers can never afford to spare the. time necessary to be trained sufficiently to fulfil the purpose for which they are created. (b). It is just, for then everyone would perform a . common privilege and duty. ' (c). It offers the certain advantages of national safety, increased self respect, improved physique. Let Mr. Gray in his reply, honestly tackle " these main issues "and not cleverly "dribble the off the main ground. Let him justify .his opposition to national service by facts and not by fancies. B. S. TOWNROE.

div.head: FISHGUARD AS A PORT OF CALL.
div.p: FISHGUARD AS A PORT OF CALL.

The advantages of Fishguard•as a port of call for ocean liners was very clearly demonstrated on the 4th inst., when the S.S. " Hilary," one of the largest vessels of the Booth Line, disernliarked a number of passengers from South American and Spanish ports. The liner archored inside the Breakwater at 5.30 p.m., the neces- sary Customs formalities were gone thrvugh, and the "special train started from the Harbour Station at 6.5 p.m. arriving at Paddington at .10.46 p.m., after a stop at Cardiff for South Wales passengers. The throughout run of 260 miles therefore occupied less than 4i hours. Tbe passengers expressed tben3selves highly pleased with the arrangements of the Great Western Company, and were in town within 51 hours after the liner had anchored.

div.head: QUESTIONS • FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
div.p: QUESTIONS • FOR TARIFF REFORMERS.
XXI.—If Import duties do not raise prices, why did the German Govern- ment raise tht3 Corn duties with the express purpose of raising price?

When the last German Tariff was introduced into the Reichstag, in 1902, the German Government pub- lished with it a printed explanation of why they pro- posed to raise the corn duties. They said: , "A means whereby the agricultural interests are enabled to cover their coat oi production is to be found, under the given circumstances, by creating a factor which will determine the inland selling price through relative Protective duties. . . . INLAND PRICES ARE RAISED, SO FAR AS A CONSIDERATION OF THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE LAST TEN YEARS WILL ALLOW US TO JUDGE, in proportion to the duties. This is seen from the following tables. . . ." The tables (which are too long to print here) showed that the Berlin price of wheat in the years 1889-1900 was higher than the London price of wheat by about the amount of the German wheat duty. The German Government memorandum then said: "These tables show that the difference between the inland price and the price of foreign wheat (exclusive of duty) varies according to the amount of duty. It is therefore to he expected that a rais- ing of duties will favourably affect our internal agricultntal interests." L. G. C. M.

[COPY]
We are obliged by your letter, but if you will refer to our _previous communications yen will see

that we distinctly stipulate that you sho-uld nominate a local member of your league to debate .this question with us. As we said at the - outset, we are great believers in home industries, and do not. think it at all necessary to import an outsider, however able, to discuss this matter. We are of opinion that Warrington is quite capable of conducting this controversy and coming to a sensible decision thereon and if you will nominate a local member of your League we shall be happy to nominate one of our local members to meet him.—Your faithfullys
J: E. MACKEY, G. H. WARBURTON STEEL, Hon. Sees. Warrington Tariff Reform League. To Messrs. J. Howes. jr. and J. Morton, Bewsey-street, Warrington.

Compulsory Military Training. Sir,—Your correspondent H. Gray made rather a -weak show in his last article by quoting Napoleon as a Peace advocate. There wasn't a more bloodthirsty commander during the last century than Napoleon, nor one more reckless with regard to human lives, ,as every student of history knows. The peace Napoleon desired was one on his own terms and only that was to count. Europe was to be his Empire and Paris the capital. That was a favourite desire of his. With regard to the general trend of El. Gray's argument he could havp sammarised his position in a dozen sentences. I would respectfully suggest he clip those wings of his, so he can't rise too high. He seems to have his head in the clouds: Mother Earth is the scene of our operations at present,and we are living in the ever present.—Yours, E•Wilderspool-road.
AMOS WILLIAMS.

Sir,—lf in my previous letter I had set out in any way to ridicule, except to show the methods of "the N.S.L. and conscriptionists in " persuading " the people of England to adopt their ideas, I should most certainly have held up the discreditable document of the "Daily Telegraph." Surely never has a cause had to stoop so low for support of its proposals as when we have one of its chief exponents in the North of England appealing to the organ of the Confederates on the strength of an inter- view for which the author had not the courage 4' to sign his nlme. Captain Crosfield makes me smile indeed when he quotes Lord Derby as saying"the men who want to be compelled more than anyone else are those who have money and leisure." I do not think it squares with his action on the Licensing Bill, by which he refused to compel these men of money and leisure to give up extracting some of their money out of a monopoly that is in my opinion a greater danger than any foreign foe and ought to be fought by all true patriots. Mr. Crosfield says if we had National Military Training every one would have to go before a . doctor and that our political leaders on thus becoming aware of the bad physique of the country, would make a great effort to ameliorate the conditions of the people. Comical,. Mr. Editor, indeed. I have stowed .away in one of my drawers the report of a Departmental Committee of the House of Com- mons on Physical Degeneracy, which reveals a state .of affairs that I hope the. N.S.L. will never eclipse. Yet nothing seeins. to be done to remedy matters.

Perhaps our political leaders have never heard of that report, one never knows. Mr. Crosfield says he believes in compulsion for everyone on the ground of safety and because it is far juster than trading on the patriotism of the few. Now let us see how it works out in practice. Suppose the miner says his trade is dangerous, because every time the clock measures 20 niinutes of every " working day there is a Man or a boy injured and every two hours there is a man or a boy killed. Therefore on the score of danger every man ought to be compelled to serve part of his ,life in the mine and so share the danger and responsibility. Or take another case, neither • Mr. Crosfield nor myself are producers of food stuffs, we neither of us make two blades of grass , grow where one grew before. Has the farmer any right to say that we shall not consume any of the produce that he rears*? No. The farmer knows that both Mr. Crosfield and myself are accessories, therefore for the exchange value that we can give him he will give us of his products. Exactly so in military matters. Let the man who wants to fight his brother whom he has never seen nor who has never done him any harm go and volunteer for the job. As for compelling every man to be a soldier against his wish, well I hope and believe it is a long way off yet.—Yours etc., _
HARRY WARDMAN. 10, Wilkinson-street. March 10th.
A Joke for a Joke. Sir,—Ha, ha, ha, ho, ho, ho, he, he, he ! " Whatever's. _th' matter wi'th mon ; tha're gooin'

choke thyself' if tha're not careful. At ever g—ooin' stop laughin' ? was the demanding enquiry of the better half. " Whatever's making thee carry on such capers" she added. I handed her the" Examiner." "Just, ha, ha, just read Mr. Parker's reply to my letter on th' drink question"? I asked her. "Read from the'er," I said, pointing to the middle of Mr. Parker's letter. She found the place and began to read aloud. "Thus the value of the discovery increases because we have several alternate methods. Surely it makes the year, and the "good old town" of Warrington famous. Is not the discovery worthy of some per- manent recognition in the Borough? Why not com- memorate it by the erection of a monument in the centre of Market Gate. Four representative figures could be placed on a handsome base. The chief figure will of course be your correspondent—she stopped reading the paper, glared at me, and wsped. a Does th' mon mean to have thi statue at Market Gate? Seems to me he's an out-of-work architect after a job. But I'll give him insulting my mon like that, I tould thee summat 'ud come through thee sitting up these cold nights writing letters." She went to the door, where her hat and jacket hung, and placed them on. • " Wheer does 'th mon live ?" she asked. I want an explanation. I tried to pacify her. "Oh, tak no notice; it's only his fun," I said. She slowly divested herself of her clothes, sat herself down andthen looked at me. " What does th' mon waant do that for? she asked, Does t' remember Ramsay Macdonald being at'h Parr Hall speaking for th' 1.L.P.? "Aye, I do," she said. "Well Mr. Parker didn't agree with something he

said on th' temperance question and said so in th' " Examiner " a week or two ago. This is what he said." I took down a previous issue of the " Examiner " from the paper rack and read: "I contend that efficiency, and the elimination of waste due to intemperance, other things being equal, would increase the call for employment, and tend to make unnecessary the dismissal,which Mr. Macdonald considers inevitable of efficient and temperate men."

Dost' see what he means?" I said: He means if there is less drinking there will be more employment. I proved by facts and figures that temperance would make matters worse. Mind you. I did not say that more drinking would make matters better, but I went oft to say that I thought a more equitable distri- bution would. Mr. Parker seems to lose his head, completely forgets his own contention, ignores my reply, thereto, and accuses me of advocating more drinking as a remedy for unemployment, then straighways proceeds to wriggle out of the situation by indulging in satire at my expense. "Just fancy him saying that tha wants everybody to get drunk," interjected the better half. "Thee, whose been a lifelong teetotoller, a non-smoker, and has so tender a conscience and so fastidious a palate as tha weint touch flesh of slaughtered animals. The idea of him."

" Aye," I continued, " It's a good way to avoid 6ickling cold facts. And the knows it would give me great .joy to see such vicious habits as drunkenness and flesh-eating done away with. But I'm not going to say it would benefit the people financially. The benefits are physical, and more physical efficiency in the workers means efficiency in production and there- fore must create more unemployed. And besides economy in wages expenditure re-acts upon wages paid. Economic circumstance compels the worker to accept the lowest possible wage of subsistence. The teetotal, non-smoking vegetarian worker can live cheaper than the alcohol drinking, smoking, flesheatmg worker, and when unemployed has to compete with more unemployed for work. This competition lowers the price of labour and the worker accepting the lowest wage gets the job. Production to-day is carried on for profit and any method which will reduce the cost of production is adopted, whether it be by the means of improved machinery, reorganisa- tion or taking advantage of the temperance of the worker. Temperance is good in all thihgs. But if the workers want a solution to poverty and unemploy- ment, abstinence from drinking alcoholic liquors will not solve it. Only the reorganisation of society upon a co-operative basis, with the land and capital co-operatively owned and controlled, can provide the community with a free, full and happy life.—l am yours,
LABOR 01(NU VINCIT.

div.head: WARRINGTON GYULISTS.
div.p: WARRINGTON GYULISTS.
A Successful Season Reviewed

The members of the Warrington Cycling Club are a jovial company, and sociability and good fellowship are the keynotes of all their gatherings -not excluding the, annual business meeting, which they contrive to invest with a great deal of interest and pleasure. Whilst puffing the fragrant weed on Thursday evening, these ardent wheelers recalled the many delightful outings of last summer, perpetrated jokes about appointing honorary officers " at the usual salary," thanked all and sundry who had had a share in the season's success, and made handsome presenta- tions to two esteemed officials. The meeting was held at the club's headquarters, the Patten Arms Hotel, Sergeant Major Delmage, the popular captain, pre siding over a large asgerubly. In an ably-compiled report, the Hon. Secre- tary (Mr. J. T. SAMPSON) dwelt with satisfac. tion upon the continued progress of the club. "I do indeed look upon it as a privilege to be associated in the capacity of hon. secretary with a club, whose formation reaching back as it does to the infancy of cycling, can justifiably claim to have been one of the pioneers of the sport, and although on the threshold of its twenty-fourth year has lost none of its vigour, the membership during the past season having been the highest attained within its annals." Applause greeted this encourag- ing statement. In picturesque language the secretary then reviewed the outstanding events of the year. There were humorous allusions to the " Irish walking match ' mode of arrival at Warburton, the mirth-provoking fishing contest where the catch was "more conspicu- ous by its quality than quantity "and to the cricket match with Warrington Thursday when "our boys, probably through want of practice, had to submit to defeat on the stroke of time." The attendances at the club runs had been about up to the average, the prize winners being: A Spinks, W. Delmage, and G. H. Anderton. Special reference was made to the visit to the President's (Mr. John Naylor's) lovely home at Beeston- the 13th annual outing to that charmiiag retreat—the Secretary observ- ing that another link had been added to a chain of delightful memories. The members of the Warrington C.C. pride them- selves on their prowess as bowlers and a portion of the report was devoted to chronicling their achieve- ments on the Sankey Chapel House green, placed at their disposal by Mr. W. Unsworth. Turning from the more strenuous side of the club's doings and taking a survey of the winter programme, there were references to successful smokers, whist drives, and the annual dance—" the great event of the social Reason."

Feeling allusion was made to the losses sustained by the club in the death of Mr. Edgar H. Clare and Mr. Alfred Scattergood. The season as a whole was voted "highly satisfactory" and the Secretary concluded by expressing regret— which was shared by all the members—that be was obliged to relinquish his office. He bespoke the same kindly: assistance for his successor, as hs personally had received and said that whilst such loyalty continued to be shown, there could be no doubt of a continuance of that success which had marked the progress of the Warrington Cycling Club. Mr. E. PICKAVANCE, who moved the acceptance of the report, naively remarked that it was not quite as poetical as some previous effusions—a personal touch which was greatly relished—but ass a good, sound practical report. Mr. A. BOOTH, another ex-secretary, seconded and the report was heartily approved. Mr. F. GARNETT, the hon. treasurer, had a bright picture to present, the club now having a balance to its credit of £37 10s. as against £29 9s. last year. "What we are going to do with so large a balance, I don't know" remarked Mr. J. CRITCPILEY, who pro. posed that ale balance sheet be passed. Mr. W. LITTON, an auditor, who seconded, was equally complimentraj., and the accounts were unani- mously accepted. Then came the pleasing duty of thanking all the officers for their past services, and we learned that the Captain had delighted everyone by his genial presence and kindly manner, that the sub-captain (Mr. T. P Throssell) had contributed to the social element by hiss musical accomplishments, being ever ready to "finger the dominoes' as as one member termed piano playing, that the hon. treasurer was " a past master in the art of working things on an economical basis," that the lion. secretary had worked with whole-heartectenergy, and that the committee could not be improved upon., Electing the officers was the next item, and the follow- ing were chosen :—President, Mr. John Naylor; vice- presidents, the Mayor of Warrington, Messrs. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., Robert Pierpoint, W. Pierpoint, J. C. Parr, Roger C. Parr, W. Peter Rylands, and T. Mather; captain, Mr. T. P. Throssell ; sub-captain, Mr. Arthur Spiroks ; hon. secretary, Mr. Carey Berry; hon. treasurer, Mr. F. Garnett; committee, Messrs. G. H. Smith, F. Fieldhouse, J. T. Sampson, j. B. Poole. A. G. Robertson, C. Houghton, G. A. Anderton and ,W. H. Bellian • auditors, Messrs., W. Litton and B. Podmore ; delegates, Messrs. A. Booth, E. Pickavance and C. Berry. Mr. Burleigh, of the Patten Arms Hotel, was heartily thanked for his many courtesies to the club, which a highly appreciated. The formal business over, there was a mysterious pause; no one seemed inclined to lEave. In a moment or two, however, the hon. treasurer was seen to dis- appear behind a screen and to return carrying a hand- some clock,which he deposited on the table before the chairman. The worthy sergeant-major then disclosed the pleasing intelligence that be had been asked to band the time-piece to the retiring hon. secretary (Mr. Sampson) as a token of goodwill on the occasion of his approaching marriage. He spoke warmly of Mr. Sampson as the worthy son of a worthy father and wished him every happiness. Mr. SAMPSON, who was heartily applauded, said the gift would always remind him of the pleasant times he had spent with the club both awheel and at the various s•icial functions in,Warrington, and last, but not least, of the many friends he had amongst the members of the Warricgton C.C.

The titne.piece having been removed its place was taken by another which it transpired had been sub- scribed for by the committee and some friends as a present to Sergeant-Major Delmage who is removing to Chester. Clock number 2 was handed to its recipient by Mr. W. 11. Bellian who appropriately voiced the rosard generally entertained for the sergeant-major. Sergeant-Major Delmage returned thanks and said that the pleasure he had derived from the performance of any little duty to the club had been more than ample payment to him. He was looking forward to being able to join tbe members occasionally when they had a spin in the direction of Chester.
Take Woods' Great Peppermint Cure, for Coughs and Colds; it never fails. is. lid., 2s. 9d.—Adv.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOSEPH PODMORE.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOSEPH PODMORE.
An Old Warringtonlan.

A familiar and respected figure has been removed from our midst by the death of Mr. Joseph Podmore, who passed away at his home, 37, Allen-street, at nine o'clock on Monday evening, at the ripe old .age of seventy-three. So recently as Friday last Mr. Podmore was apparently in his usual health, and was out of doors looking as bright and cheerful as was his wont. During the night he was seized with illness. Dr. Martin attended him, and he took a decided turn for

the better on Monday morning, but at five o'clock in the evening he had a relapse, and the end came at the time stated. In 18734 Mr. Podmore had a serious attack of rheumatic fever, which resulted in heart affection, and this was the cause of his death. He leaves a widow, five sons and threle daughters, with whom the deepest sympathy is felt in their unexpected bereavement.

div.head: LATE MR. J. PODMORE
div.p: THE LATE MR. J. PODMORE

Mr. Podmore was a native of Warrington and had a great affection for the old town. He was born in Mersey Street on April 27th, 1835, and was the sou of Mr. George Frederick Podmore, who carried on businesa as a shoemaker and was a very noted man in his day. The late Mr. G. F. Podmore was a Chartist, a strong Radical and temperance reformer. He took a great interest in Parliamentary elections and *as prominent at meetings held in support of the late Mr. Peter Rylands' candidature- The subject of this memoir received the rudiments of his education at a dame school. Afterwards he attended the National School, Church Street, and finally he was under the tuition of Mr. Jackson—generally known as" Quaker Jackson "—at the Academy which stood in Academy Street. As a youth Mr. Podmore entered the trade of a hairdresser, at the shop of hia luncle Mr. Randall, in Bridge-street. When he reached the age of twenty he took a shop at the corner of Bridge-street and what is now Rylands-street, and carried on business there for forty-three years. When the Corporation required his premises for street improvements he removed to temporary premises at Friars Gate and latterly he had assisted in the busi- ness in Ryland§-street along with his son Mr. Joseph Podmore, jun. He had many interesting recollections of the Warrington of bye-gone days and had witnessed remarkable changes and developments in local affairs. For thirty-seven years Mr. Podmore had resided at 37, Allen-street. .

Mr. Podmore was enrolled into the membership of Wycliffe Congregational Church in 1816, and 10 years later (in 1886) was elected a Deacon. With marked ability and earnestness, and to the great satisfaction of his fellow members, he continued in office for 20 years, and though re-elected in the hope that he would retain his position, he firmly declined, as he felt that his health was failing. The members then elected Mr. Podmore as an Hon. Deacon for the rest of his life, and at their request he consented to still administer the Poor Fund of which he had been Treasurer for many years. His wise distribution to the poor and needy was greatly appreciated, for it was always deme in that quiet and unobtrusix,e manner so peduliarly his own. -

As a manager of the day schools Mr. Podmore rendered -valuable assistance for many Years and by kindly words of encouragement, together with a firm adhesion to strict economy, he helped both teachers and officials in this difficult work. _ _

Mr-.Podmore's connection with the Sunday school was probably as long as his membership with the Church. Nothing pleased him more than to be amongst the infants, where by his genial manner, interesting addresses, and love of music he delighted the children and his regularity of attendance was a splendid example to all. Only so recently as January 11th last (to quote the "Wycliffe Record"), "the infant scholars had their animal party in the Memorial Hall, and the room was thronged by parents and friends, who came to see and hear the little pebple; and not least to cheer and encourage the venerable, but ever youthful leader of the Infant Scholars,our honoured and beloved friend Mr. Podmore. His endeavours were ably supported by Messrs. Colley, James Brown,. and Miss L. Wallington. The first part of the evening was given to a beautiful Service of Song" The Childrens' Jesus," compiled and prepared by Mr. Podmore himself. The connective readings which were exceed- 'ingly good, were well read by Mr. Joseph Owen. It is impossible to particularize the details in our narrow limits, but this we gladly put on record, that the children did their parts exceedingly well, and the whole thing was most enjoyable to every one present. Mr. Podmore is much, to be congratulated on his devoted labours in this branch of the Master' S Service. He talks of laying down the work he so deeply loves, but both scholars and teachers are intensely anxious that he should continue in his work so long as ever his strength will allow, and hope that he will try how becoming. a 'Half Tinier' will enable him to still brighten his owli life and give joy to the children by his fre4uent presence." Mr. Podmore was one of the best known members of the Order of Druids. His father was the founder of the Druids' Hope Lodge and one of the points which he insisted upon in drawing up the rules for its conduct was that no meetings should be held on licensed premises. That principle has been faithfully adhered to up to the present. The Lodge was founded in 1844 and the late Mr. George Frederick Podmoro was appointed the first \ treasurer. Mr. Joseph Podmore joined the Lodge at the age of eighteen and on his father's death in 1868 he succeeded him in the treasurership. He took a very active interest in the Widows' and Orphans' Fund and in the Royal Arch Chapter and he was also most regular in his attend- ance at the Lodge meetings His genial and good- hearted nature made him a great favourite with the members and two months ago they decided to recognize his services by presenting him with an illuminated address and purse of gold. It is a pathetic circumstance that the presentation had been arranged for next Thursday evening. Mr. Podmore had filled all the offices of his lodge but owing to the demands of business he was unable to undertake district offices.

Mr. Podmore's chief hobby was music and he took a great delight in composing or transcribing instru- mental pieces. As a boy he was a member of a drum and fife band in connection witb the National Schools and later he formed a Good Templars' Brass Band at the old Dallam Lane Chafiel. He had played in the Wycliffe Band under the conductorship of the late Mr. Ellwood and considering that he was 'entirely self-taught, he possessed wonderful musical abilities. In politics Mr. Podmore was a Liberal and in his earlier days he took part in several municipal con- tests. Latterly, he had not figured prominently in political affairs. He was a cheerful, kindly old gentleman, particularly devoted to the children with whom he was a great favourite, and .hi si ever-wel- come presence will be greatly misssd by a wide circle.

div.head: FIJNERAL.
div.p: THE FIJNERAL.

In the presence of a large gathering of relatives and friends the funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday afternoon. Before the inter- ment a service was held at Wycliffe Church, and was conducted by the Revs. John Yonge and Harry Wall. The hymn " Brief life is here our portion," was sung by the congregation. The Rev. JohnYonge in a brief address said they could not help feeling as they looked upon that coffin bow it hid from them a face they all loved to see. He did not know that anyone who knew him had an evil thought of Joseph Podmore. Many lived who loved him, as his minister loved him, and

who had reason to love him. No one knew except himself of the • unspeakable help he often rendered him ( \lr. Yonge.) When he used to go into that Church on the Sunday morning in the middle of the service after having been teaching the infants and the younger scholars, he used to look up to him (Mr. Yonge) in the pulpit and smile. He (Mr. Yonge) used to love to look for that smile, and it was like a ray of sunshine on the darkest morning. He knew it was not a formal greeting. They all sympathised with the family in whom that death had come, and they bore them on their hearts. They trusted that when they passed away they might leave behind them memories as sweet, as beautiful, as bright and as helpful as he left to them.

The chief mourners were: Mrs. Podmore (widow), Mr. and Mrs. G. F. Podmore, Mr. and Mrs. William Podmore, Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Podmore, jun., Mr. and Mrs. Frank Podrnore, Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Podmore (sons and daughters-in-law), Mrs. Ford, Mrs. Batty (daughters), M r. and Mrs. S. W. Jeffery (son-in-law and daughter), Messrs. Richard Cooke, J. H. Knowles (brothers-in-law), T. E. Knowles; and J. Young (nephews). Amongst others present were :—Messrs. J. div.head: ORFORD WARD ELECTION.
div.p: ORFORD WARD ELECTION.
Polling Next Tuesday.

On Tuesday evening the electors of Orford Ward will be called upon to elect a representative on the Town Council to fill the vacancy caused by the unseating of Mr. Peter Peacock. Polling will take place at the Silver-street schools from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. The Liberal candidate is Mr. James Halliwell, boot and shoe dealer, Market-street,and he is receiving most enthusiastic support. , Although Mr. W. Mc Niel Sloane's nathe appears on the list of candidates it is not his intention to continue his candidature and the election will therefore, to all intents and purposes, be fought between Mr. Halliwell and Mr. James Hamp- son, general labourer, ?A Garibaldi-street who is the Socialist nominee.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

•Of music hall novelties there is no end. Nothing more odd has been seen at Warrington for some time than the performance this week by Master George Wood," the world's greatest juvenile artikte." What age Master George is we do not pretend to know, but he looks about five and makes his first stage appear- ance in the nttrsery in short frocks and white socks and bare knees. He even has his nurse with him and cheeks the lady in the most precocious manner while he is undressed and put to bed. Once the inurse has gone, George rises and takes the boards. Though not much more than knee high he has all the self-confidence of a matured comedian and gives imitations of George Lashwood, Harry Lauder, Vesta Tilley and Camille Clifford with remarkable skill. Altogether, George is a remarkable youngster. Developing at the same rate it is impossible to imagine what he will grow up into. The bouncing Dillons, Willie and Hilda, con- tribute a novel bouncing and gymnastic turn. The bouncing " bed " is an attractive idea and the manage- ment has catered for popular fancy by instituting a " bouncing " competition, open to all comers, Uproarious mirth is provoked by the efforts of the novices to bounce, and the performance of the ladies last night was a screaming farce in more senses than one.. J. •W. Rowley was a favourite comedian 30 years ago and he is a favourite yet. His songs and patter are of a superior kind and there is no questioning the warmth of his reception. Rowley could entertain for an hour, but he packs a lot into 15 minutes. The Seven Wulfrunas present a comedy acrobatic act entitled "Fun in a CaftS." The mounting of the show and the acrobatics rank Al, but the fun is somewhat trans- parent. Nevertheless the act is well-received. Jack Hayworth essays rather a big task when he appears as a Scotch comedian of a distinctly Lauder type, but he has originality and humour of his own which go down well. Sybil Montague sings such favourite ballads as "Alice where art thou" and "Queen of the earth," in a sweet and flexible soprano and earns her share of the applause. Mr. Widdop's orchestra excels in some of German's dances, and the biograph pictures are, as usual, novel and attractive, , FLYING MATINEE, "DOLLY REFORMING HERSELF."

For Monday afternoon, Mr. 3/facnaghten has arranged a flying matinee, from the Haymarket Theatre, London, of the brilliantly • successful. comedy "Dolly Reforming Herself." This engagement is one of the forty flying motor matinees which this company will play in the provinces prior to their return to London. Miss Aimee ,be Burgh will appear as" Dolly" and will be supported by an excellent all-round company. This splendid attraction should be witnessed by a crowded house. We understand that Mr. MacNaghten has already secured several first-class companies for future flying matinees.

div.head: EASTERN AGRICULTURE.
div.p: EASTERN AGRICULTURE.
Lecture at Stockton Heath.

Under the title "Eastern Agriculture as illustrating the Bible "Mr. A. Mounfield gave an interesting Bible class lecture in the Independent Methodist school room last Wednesday evening. It was pointed out that in the East a system of communal land obtains. Villagers who desire to till the soil assemble each year and cast lots for the available land. A number of stones bear- ing signs are put in a jar and a-child is brought forward to draw them and hand to the would-be farmers. Each recipient holds up the stone and says "This is my lot, may God maintain my lot." The mystic signs are then interpreted and each man learns which piece of land he is to have. Under this system the farmers rarely have the same plot two years together. The plots are defined by imaginary lines drawn from one landmark to another. The lecturer pointed out that the custom explains many passages in the Bible such as "The lines have fallen unto me in pleasant places," " Thon maintainest my lot," and also the solemn laws relating to landmarks. Many other Bible references were explained and illustrated in a very interesting way. Several similar addresses are promised for succeeding Wednesday evenings.
For Children's tacking Cough at night, Wood's Great Peppermint Cure. is. li. 2s. 9cl.—Advt.

div.head: WARRINGTON OF THE FUTURE.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON OF THE FUTURE.
An Inquiry into Street Improvements.

Alluring visions of the Warrington of the future were oonjured up at a Local Government Board inquiry held at the Town Hall on Thursday with reference to the widening of the main thoroughfares of the town. The Town Council had petitioned the Board to issue a Pro- visional Order to empower them to put in force, with reference to certain lands required by them for the widening and improvement of Bridge-street, Butter- market-street, Sankey-street, and Upper Bank-street, and for the construction of a new street at the rear of Buttermarket-street, the powers of the Lands Clauses Acts with respect to the purchase and taking of lands otherwise than by agreement. The inquiry was con- &toted by Mr. F. H. Tulloch, M. Inst., C.E., and there was a large attendance, including the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw,) the Deputy Mayor (Aldermen Smethurst), Aldermen Bennett and Evans; Cduncillors Evans, Craik, Skelland, Birtles and Pemberton; Messrs. A. T. Hallway (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), W. H. Woodcock (borough collector), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), A. M. Ker (assistant surveyor) and other Corporation officials ; Messrs H. Roberts, W. Hickman, F. Pendlebury, W. R Throssell, S. Gough, W. Isaac, Herbert Hatton (Messrs, Robert Davies and Co., solicitors, representing several large owners of property) and R. Dobson. Mr. HALLAWAY explained that this proposed street widening was not an isolated case. The Corporation had a definite scheme in view,which was started so long ago as 1884. The Bridge-street improvement was com- pleted last year and the line of widening which had yet to be undertaken proceeded on the right hand side of Horsemarket-street as far as the Central Station, on the right hand side of Sankey-street from Market Gate to the municipal buildings, and on the right of Butter- market-street down to the King's Arms Hotel— generally a convenient stopping place in Warrington. (Laughter.) The Corporation had carried out the widening of Bridge-street and had re-instated all the businesses there, with the exception of two, with the result that they had preserved to the town the valuable assets which old-establised businesses undoubtedly were and had saved the town the expense of buying. them out—in all probably some £150,000. If one went down Bridge-street to-day one saw the same ns.mes that were there fifty years ago. That was the policy the Corporation hoped to pursue in completing the scheme. Buttermarket-street was particularly affected by the present application. It would no doubt be interesting to the Inspector to know that the four main streets in Warrington had been in existence for a great number of years, in fact a local guide stated that " from a detailed survey of Warrington prepared in 1455 we find it had even then its present contour and was penetrated by the four main streets which met at Market Gate." With the excep- tion of Bridge-street and a slight alteration to the eastern end of Buttermarket-street, the four main streets remained at exactly the same width as in 1485, and in Buttermarket-street one of the old properties was still remaining. Buttermarket-street was a portion of the main road from Liverpool to Manchester and, with the improved methods of traction, tlaffic was increasing every day. The gradient of the street Was very steep and this, combined with its narrowness, made it highly dangerous to traffic. With regard to the proposed new street, th 6. Corporation considered it absolutely necessary that there should be at the back . of an important highway like Buttermarket-street a secondary means of access to the various premises and, in accordance with their byelaws, the street must be open from end to end. The INspEaroa : Then the necessity for the new street is commercial convenience.

Mr. HALLAWA Y said it was not intended to proceed with the formation of the new street right through to Bridge-street at present, but negotiations were in progress which might probably result in that being carried out.

The INSPECTOR: It seems desirable, if you can do so, to get it right through; or Ido not think it will comply with your bye-laws. Mr. HALLAITAT explained that it was the Corpora- tion's present intention to carry the passage through from Buttermarket-street to Upper Bank-street. The present entrance was by means of an archway which was undesirable and would be taken down. The present width of the street was 15ft. 91n. and they proposed to make it 40ft. Alluding to the proposed circus at Market Gate, Mr. Hallaway said it was one of the first circuses to be commenced in this country in the present century. The Corporation originally proposed to run their electric tram cars right through the four main streets but the Board of Trade refused to grant them powers on account of the inconvenience at Market Gate. Aperson wishing to go by car from thenorth of the town to the south had therefore to break his journey and walk 400 or 500 yards. The proposal was that when the circus was completed there should be a circle of tram lines so that they could be switched off in any direction. The accepted design for the cireis was in the old Georgian style and was in keeping with the characteristics of the town. It was proposed that Temple Court should be closed. Mr. Hallaway concluded by remarking that the application met with the unanimous approval of the town—a most unusual thing in Warrington. There were eleven objections, mostly formal, eleven people assented and seventy-five were indifferent. I Mr. William Iss.Ac said he believed the assessments of businessmen who had been re-instated had been nearly doubled, and they were thus placed on a much heavier expense. Mr. HICKMAN (president), said the Property Owners' Asitociation were in favour of the scheme, as they con- sidered it absolutely necessary. In reply to Mr. Isaac, Mr. HALLA.WAY said that if the Corporation and the owners could not agree on prices they would go to arbitration. It had, however, been the policy of the Corporation to agree upon the, price in almost every instance. It possibly might have been better if they had gone to arbitration in some of them. Alderman Beerairr, as Chairman of the Street Improvement Committee, said it was a source of great satisfaction to him and to his committee to find that for once the town was really unanimous in favour of this improvement which was undoubtedly urgently neces- sary. Perhaps he was somewhat of a faddest but he thought even the width they had decided upon for the four main streets-60 feet—was scarcely adequate. The general opinion was that the circus would be an artistic feature and that it would have many practical recommendations, particularly in allowing of a through tram service. He hoped the property owners would meet the Corporation in a reasonable spirit, as the Cor- poration did not want to go to the expense of arbitration. It would greatly facilitate municipal improvemedts if the Corporation themselves had power to rebuild and he also considered it a misfortune that when they had carried out improvements they were obliged to sell all surplus land. Alderman SMETHURST, as chairman of the Tramways Committee, supported the application, and stated that had they been able to carry the tram service through the centre of the town eight years ago it would have meant a saving of something like £20,000. Councillor PEMBERTON said 'he hoped the property owners would try to meet the Corporation and get the scheme through as quickly as possible. If they would only be reasonable the Corporation would meet them, In the past the street widening' had taken too long, and there had consequently been great displacement of trade. Mr. HICKMAN : The safety of the public demands this alteration. Mr. GouGH : I have great pleasure in supporting the application. The inquiry then concluded.

div.head: NIGHT ATTACK.
div.p: A NIGHT ATTACK.
Warrington Territorials' Interesting
Manoeuvres.

There was warfare by night on the Cheshire side of Warrington on Thursday, a contingent of 100 of our local Territorials engaging in some highly interesting manceuvres. It was supposed that troops of a Con- tinental power had effected a landing at Weston, while our Atlantic and Channel fleets were engaged on the East Coast, and their Com- manding Officer had determined to make a reconnaissance in the direction of Warrington, with a view to discovering the strength of its garrison. Two companies—represented by D and F Companies of the Territorials—were detached from Moore as a right flank guard with orders to advance along the following line—Walton Hall, Appleton Hall, and Grappenhall. To repel the invaders the officer commanding the Warrington Territorials had decided to estab- lish the follewing outpost line for the protection of Warrington :—Winwick Quay, Bewsey Old Hall, Sankey Bridges, Walton Bridge,Appleton Hall,Stretton. A and B Companies were ordered to hold from the cross roads north., of Appleton rifle range to the third mile-stone on the Warrington Tarporley-road, rstiblishing communication with companies on their ight and left. The defenders, under the command of Captain Crosfield, left the Drill Hall at 7.30, and the attacking companies, under Captain Roberts, followed half an hour later. The other officers on parade were :—A Company, 2nd. Lieut. Harvey Adams; B Company, Lieutenant Egerton Fairclough ; D Com- pany, Captain Williamson and 2nd Lieutenant McClure. The umpires were Major Brereton Fairclongh, Captain and Adjutant Mott, and Major F. M. Appleton. The evening proved a highly instructive one. The attackers rushed the left of the defenders' position, but whether they would have been able to get through in actual warfare, with bullets whistling around, it is impossible to say. They entered Appleton Hall Park and worked round to attack the picket in the rear, but the commander of A company on learning that the left position bad been driven in, took out a strong reconnoitering patrol to find out where the enemy was. The two forces came into collision in the park and commenced fire, which continued until the umpires called " cease fire." It was a novel and some- what picturesque spectacle to see the repeated flashes of fire in the darkness amongst the trees and bushes. Refreshments were jerved at the cross roads and the Territoriala returned to the Drill Hall at 11.40.
